messages.body_plain:
You need to define assign_to_var() for fwd-mode
auto-dif vars.  It basically just does an assignment.
You should only need to define the case where both
the left-hand side type is a fwd-mode auto-dif var
and the right side type is double or int.

We can talk more about this tomorrow.

- Bob

messages.subject: new commit/push policy?
messages.body_plain:
We've been getting lots of broken pushes
lately (missing tests, missing doc, code in
the wrong namespace, etc.)  I'm as guilty as
anyone here, if not more so, so I hope nobody
takes this as an implied criticism.

The problem will probably only get worse as we have more
developers as we haven't made our coding standards
particularly clear.

What I'm wondering is whether we should go
to a system where we pull request rather than
push ourselves and where there's a forced code
review by someone other than the person issuing
the pull request.

Thoughts?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new commit/push policy?
messages.body_plain:
I'm torn.  More formal code review would probably be good for us and
getting into the habit would make it easier for other people to join
the process (as we would be more used to the "pull request" workflow).
 That said, for some cases it seems excessive.  E.G., I pushed some
commits which made changes to the printed output of BFGS...hardly in
need of code review.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: separating dependencies
messages.body_plain:
The recently pushed

   src/stan/agrad/rev/matrix/assign_to_var.hpp

lives in agrad/rev, but has this include:

   #include <stan/agrad/fwd/fvar.hpp>

There shouldn't be includes of fwd from rev.  In this case,
this include's not doing anything, so I just removed it.

As an illustration of my previous point (that I'm as
much to blame for bad commits as anyone, if not more so),
this whole file's in the wrong place, which was my doing.

We'll move it so the assign is at the top level and just
deals with scalars and std::vector.  Then we'll have one
that does promotion for reverse-model LHS in agrad/rev
and another one for fwd-mode in agrad/fwd.

- Bob

My vote is for pull requests. I'm against process as much as everyone else, but I think it makes sense to go that route. Especially with the potential of others helping out. If someone is waiting for a decision, I am willing to make the decision for the group.

My suggestion:
- start the new process on Tuesday, May 7, at the Stan meeting.
- pull request does not guarantee a full code review
- I'll try to get the Jenkins github pull request plugin working. That will allow one of us to kick off the unit tests for the pull request and we can view the results of the tests before the merge.

I've got more below.

>
> Part of the problem is that too many commits are going to the master branch too soon. Like "I'll push the code now and the tests / doc / etc. later". Part of the problem is that we don't enforce a push hook that runs test-unit. I think Bob sent an email a couple of weeks ago about the 5 steps needed to add something to Stan, but we don't really have any formal guidelines.

Unfortunately, I don't think we can run a reasonable post-commit hook through github. The issue is that our unit tests now take 20+ minutes, distribution tests run close to 2 hours, and then another 2 hours for model tests. As of right now, we've got our Jenkins box testing on commits. I wish we could use a post-commit hook, but I don't think we can work that out.

Regarding only one person knowing the code: that shouldn't hold us back from using pull requests.

Should we start managing our TO-DO list as issues? Then individual pull requests would could be tied to things that we want to accomplish.

On a bit of a tangent, I'd like to add that the slowness of the tests
is an issue for me running them more often right now.  I haven't timed
things but it's slow on my laptop (~3yrs old dual core MacBook Pro,
using clang), definitely more than 20 minutes, probably closer to an
hour.    If I've nothing else to do (going to make dinner, whatever)
that's fine, but as a rule it's a burden.  A way to have a decent
machine (Jenkins or otherwise) available where I can say "run the for
me" and have it return in a decent amount of time with informative
output would be a big win.

Also, I don't think we need to do formal code review on everything.
Most things probably just need a quick look to catch anything obvious.
 It also helps to ensure that more people know what's going on with
different parts of the code.

Finally, we should consider the workflow where not everything gets
done together.  E.G., one person writes code, someone else writes the
tests/docs.  This has happened a few times for me (thanks Bob!).  Does
it all get staged in a different fork before it's finally pulled?  I
don't know how hard it is for me to give someone else push access to a
fork on github.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
I included the following pair of signatures in the generated
model code, but would be happy to reconfigure if others
have suggestions.  If these are OK, I can do the same thing
with names.

    void write_array_params(std::vector<double>& params_r__,
                            std::vector<int>& params_i__,
                            std::vector<double>& vars__,
                            std::ostream* pstream__ = 0);

The above would call the following with a dummy RNG
and the include_tparams__ and include_gqs__ set to false.

     template <typename RNG>
     void write_array(RNG& base_rng__,
                      std::vector<double>& params_r__,
                      std::vector<int>& params_i__,
                      std::vector<double>& vars__,
                      bool include_tparams__ = false,
                      bool include_gqs__ = false,
                      std::ostream* pstream__ = 0);

This second one's a bit tricky because including the
generated quantities (gqs) requires including the
transformed parameters (tparams). I could make this an
enum or something, with values PARAMS_ONLY, PARAMS_TPARAMS_ONLY,
PARAMS_TPARAMS_GQS.

Also, the int parameters are currently ignored --- we don't even allow
them yet.  I have a feeling a lot of the code involving int
params, which is just stubbed for now, will have to change.

- Bob

[re-posted on stan-dev]

sort() is definitely useful.

If we have sort(), is there a reason to also have rank()?
(That wasn't meant to be a rhetorical question.)

I'd like to see at least one realistic example where something
like Kahan summation makes a difference before including it.
Did you work on it because of an applied problem you were
having?

Does anyone else on the list have experience with this?

Did you test gradients for summation?  Writing custom
gradients is critical for speed, but the gradients need to be
tested even if they're not custom.  You should just be able
to use the gradient already there for sum.

Also, which signatures did you go with for sum()?  It
should probably work over the same types as sort: real[],
int[], vector and row_vector.

Could you perhaps break these into two separate pull requests
(sort/rank vs. summation).

Thanks!

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] primitive types in auto-dif: three options
messages.body_plain:
The one advantage that option 2 has over option 3 is that option 2
could significantly reduce the amount of duplicated code we have
hanging around for mixed type operations.  In other words, instead of
having three versions of a function, e.g.,

var dot_product(var, var)
var dot_product(var, double)
var dot_product(double, var)

we could have one

enable_if< is_same<var,T1>::value || is_same<var,T2>::value, var>
dot_product(T1,T2)

Cheers,
Marcus

On Mon, Apr 29, 2013 at 4:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I want to outline three options for dealing with primitive
> arithmetic types (only double and int in Stan) in our functions.
> This is related to the bug I just closed that was preventing
> int arguments to matrix ops (they were getting cast to stan::agrad::var
> instead of double due to argument-dependent lookup of the other
> arg, which was a stan::agrad::var).
>
> Proposal 1:  Brute force expansion, no templates
>
>     template <int R, int C>
>     inline Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>
>     multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>& m,
>              double c) {
>       return c * m;
>     }
>     template <int R, int C>
>     inline Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>
>     multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>& m,
>              int c) {
>       return c * m;
>     }
>
> Proposal 2:  Explicit use of boost::enable_if
>
>     template <int R, int C, typename T>
>     inline Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>
>     multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<typename
> boost::enable_if_c<boost::is_arithmetic<T>::value,
>                                                              double>::type,
>                                  R, C>& m,
>              T c) {
>       return c * m;
>     }
>
>
> Proposal 3:  no-op encapsulation of enable_if
>
>     template <typename T>
>     inline void
>     validate_is_arithmetic(const typename
> boost::enable_if_c<boost::is_arithmetic<T>::value,
>                                                              T>::type&
> /*v*/) {
>       /* no op helper function */
>     }
>
>     template <int R, int C, typename T>
>     inline
>     Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>
>     multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<double,R,C>& m,
>              T c) {
>       validate_is_arithmetic<T>(0);
>       return c * m;
>     }
>
>
> The problem with (1) is the additional code and that it's not
> general for types other than int and double (and see below about
> return).
>
> The problem with (2) is that it's hard to type and to read.
>
> The problem with (3) is that we need to lean on the compiler to
> compile away the no-op function.  (The argument 0 could also be c here.
>
> To truly generalize our types to allow float returns, what we'd need is
>
>     template <int R, int C, typename T1, typename T2>
>     inline
>     Eigen::Matrix<typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1,T2>::type, R,
> C>
>     multiply(const Eigen::Matrix<T1, R, C>& m,
>              T2 c) {
>       validate_is_arithmetic<T1>(0);
>       validate_is_arithmetic<T2>(0);
>       return c * m;
>     }
>
> Now there's not a good value to pass in for T1 (the matrix could be 0 x 0),
> so it really has to be 0.
>
> Given that reverse mode auto-diff is double only and we don't foresee
> ever using float scalars or int matrices, I think we can get away with the
> simpler version in proposal 3.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] a (fairly) painless way to implement discrete sampling?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] a (fairly) painless way to implement discrete sampling?
messages.body_plain:
I think this is valid from a language perspective, but it probably
won't ever be fast from an algorithmic perspective. The problem is
that the posterior will become discontinuous unless a is completely
isolated from the rest of the model. (In which case there's not much
point.) Each time you cross a cutpoint you get an abrupt change in
energy, which basically hoses your chance of maintaining a high
acceptance probability.

That said, I seem to remember Mike talking about an integration scheme
that might be able to handle that sort of problem.

Matt

On Thu, May 2, 2013 at 3:56 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> Hi all (especially Bob).  During the times we've discussed discrete sampling, one possibility we've talked about is to work with latent continuous variables.  We've talked about this as a possibility but I always had the sense that it might be tricky to get the distributions right.
>
> But, thinking about it, I think it's close to trivial.  For simplicity, suppose our model has only two parameters:  a N-dimensional discrete parameter a (which can take on the values 1,2,…,K) and an M-dimensional continuous parameter b.  We can define a new continuous parameter z defined on [0,1], along with K probabilities p (i.e., simplex[K] p).
>
> Thus, we expand our model from:
>
> parameters {
>   integer<lower=1,upper=K> a[N];
>   real b[M];
> }
>
> to
>
> parameters {
>   real z[N];
>   simplex[K] p;
>   real b[M];
> }
>
> Now, z relates to a in a very simple way.  In the model, define
>
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> cutpoints[K]
>   cutpoints <- cumulative_sum (p)
>
> Then, y=1 if z<cutpoints[1],
>   y=2 if z is between cutpoints[1] and cutpoints[2]
>   . . .
>   y=K if z>cutpoints[K-1]
>
> This can all be implemented in Stan.
>
> That means, I think, that we could implement discrete variables internally:  if we have an integer-valued parameter "a", we just define the corresponding "z" and "p" parameters and set up the model as above.
>
> All this so far only works with finitely-valued discrete parameters, but I think we could do countably-infinite sets too, by just defining a preset Zeno-like sequence of cutpoints.
>
> What do you think?
>
> A
>
> P.S.  I tried this out by implementing the standard mixture model using the latent-data formulation and then testing it out on fake data.  It seemed to work, but it was very very slow to converge.  So that's another concern.  But if we can get the model set up, improving convergence might be possible using various Matt and Mike tricks...
>

messages.body_plain:
One question is:  How slow would it be on problems of interest?  If it is implementable and slow but not prohibitively slow, it could be a useful step along the way, so that users who really want to implement discrete variables will be able to do so.  But of course if Mike could whip up a better algorithm, that would be great.
For some models (for example, or multinomial logit), I could actually imagine the continuous parameterization being not too bad, in that the underlying continuous parameter has a statistical interpretation.
A

messages.body_plain:
If you wanted to bound the discrete variables, that could be done directly in the model.

In any case, I'm sure there are examples where this would be slow.  What I like about my proposal is that it could all be done internally in Stan, I think.  That is, instead of us having to recommend that users apply "the continuous variable trick," we could just let them specify discrete parameters and Stan would do the sampling under the hood.

Of course, we'd want to make it clear in the manual that, as much as possible, users should integrate out latent parameters so the program will run faster.

You are answering your own question rather than the one I was raising. Ideally, you would want to map

binary ~ bernoulli(1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-mu));

to the same thing that you map

binary ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));

to, but that would entail a massive amount of pattern recognition in the Stan parser. So, it wouldn't be feasible to support and internalize all the Stan syntax that would be legal if binary were fixed, which is why I think we would first need to make it possible for the users to do latent variable constructions in their .stan files and that would entail being able to pass vectors of lower and upper bounds. With that infrastructure, it would be possible to internalize a finite number of common constructions like

binary ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));

or

binary ~ bernoulli(Phi(mu));

Ben

messages.body_plain:
How would Stan know to use a truncated logistic distribution for the latent variable whose observation mechanism determines binary if the user writes

binary ~ bernoulli(1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-mu));

unless Stan pattern recognizes that as the standard logistic CDF? Or it could be some other CDF or a CDF parameterized a different way, or a quasilikelihood thing where the variance depends on the location instead of being fixed to 1.

I'm just saying it would be really hard to be able to internalize syntax that is arbitrary but legal if binary were fixed, so you would want to make that possible by allowing users to do the latent variable constructions themselves, even if most of the time they were using common constructions that could be internalized.

Ben

On Thu, May 2, 2013 at 10:56 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> I would augment
>
> binary ~ bernoulli(1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-mu));
>
> with the same thing:
>
> real<lower=0,upper=1> z;
> real<lower=0,upper=1> p;
> binary <- int_step (z-p)
>
> This would still work, no?  I'm not expecting Stan to parse "1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-mu))" to "invlogit" (also, I think/hope it would be ok to use "1" rather than "1.0" in this expression!).  But that's the least of our worries.  We make it clear in the manual that it's best to use canned forms where they exist.
>
> On May 2, 2013, at 10:47 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> > You are answering your own question rather than the one I was raising. Ideally, you would want to map
> >
> >
> > binary ~ bernoulli(1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-mu));
> >
> > to the same thing that you map
> >
> > binary ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));
> >
> > to, but that would entail a massive amount of pattern recognition in the Stan parser. So, it wouldn't be feasible to support and internalize all the Stan syntax that would be legal if binary were fixed, which is why I think we would first need to make it possible for the users to do latent variable constructions in their .stan files and that would entail being able to pass vectors of lower and upper bounds. With that infrastructure, it would be possible to internalize a finite number of common constructions like
> >
> > binary ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(mu));
> >
> > or
> >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: new functions: sort, rank, Kahan summation, ???
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: new functions: sort, rank, Kahan summation, ???
messages.body_plain:
On 5/2/13 4:00 PM, Marco wrote:
>
>> sort() is definitely useful.
>>
>> If we have sort(), is there a reason to also have rank()?
>> (That wasn't meant to be a rhetorical question.)
> I thought about efficiency, as using sorting could be slower for big data, but I don't know how often the need of these
> functions show up in the models, probably not often as JAGS hasn't defined them (in fact JAGS has rank(v) similar to R's
> one which serves a related, but different propose).
>
>
>>
>> I'd like to see at least one realistic example where something
>> like Kahan summation makes a difference before including it.
> I think you are right and the said truth is that I couldn't come up with a definitive case where any of them are  better
> than sum(), so there's no reason to include them, at least not yet. It seems that these algorithms only help with very
> big data, but very big data (as my model) takes too long to converge.
>
>
>> Did you work on it because of an applied problem you were
>> having?
> The motivation is that model I described a few weeks ago in stan-users. I'm still having a lot a trouble to deal with it.

Are you sure it's a problem with summation precision per se?

I want to understand where you need to add numbers of
vastly different scales AND the lower-order numbers
matter.  That is, when do you do (1e-30 + 1e10) and
the 1e-30 term matters in the sum?  We try to handle
the gradients separately, and in the usual ways to do
sums (+ and sum()), the gradients are handled independently,
so you get the right answer there even if the 1e-30 term
drops out of the sum due to underflow.

So what I'm wondering is where higher-precision summation
will make a difference.

The integrator we use to simulate the Hamiltonian dynamics
has a higher error than floating point precision.

>>
>> Does anyone else on the list have experience with this?
>>
>> Did you test gradients for summation?  Writing custom
>> gradients is critical for speed, but the gradients need to be
>> tested even if they're not custom.  You should just be able
>> to use the gradient already there for sum.
> I've done, but I sadly lack knowledge to extract useful information from them.

You basically want to implement a complex summation
so that the gradients are done in the same way as for
sum(), but the value is calculated to higher precision.
In a sum(), the partial is just 1 for all of the components,
so there's really no more precision to be gained there.

>> Also, which signatures did you go with for sum()?  It
>> should probably work over the same types as sort: real[],
>> int[], vector and row_vector.
> I tried a lot of different ways, but I decided to use just a single eigen vector to sum.
>
>      vector [nZeros] summads;
>      for (i in 1:nZeros)
>          summands[i] <- log1p_exp(-zeta0[i]-exp(eta0[i]));
>      1 ~ bernoulli_logit(zeta0);
>
>      yy1 ~ poisson_log(eta1);
>      0 ~ bernoulli_logit(zeta1);

What I meant is that if you implement kahan_sum(), you probably
want to implement it for real[], vector, and row-vector.  Forget
what I said about int[], because you won't get any extra precision.

>> Could you perhaps break these into two separate pull requests
>> (sort/rank vs. summation).
> I started them in two different branches and it looks like it was a wise decision after all.

Great.  Send us the pull request for sort() and rank() when
you have them.  Just please make sure to run fairly extensive
tests.  Testing these functions is usually harder than writing
them, so it's not doing us much of a favor to write the function without
extensive testing.  For sort, you'd want to test zero size arrays/vectors
as input, and cases where all the numbers are the same, and some random
ones.  There's no issue with gradients here because neither rank() nor
sort() have gradients to calculate.

- Bob

vectors of lower and upper bounds.  They're not too hard
to do by hand if they're in vectors, but not something we
probably want users messing with on a regular basis.

- Bob

Ben
I'll have to take a look, but my first thought is that you may be making it more difficult than you need to be.  You're expressing the model using these truncated distributions (the way that Bugs does latent variables).  I think it will be ok to express the model using untruncated distributions.  As I see it, the full joint distribution is untruncated; the truncation comes conditional on the discrete variable, but that will come out naturally in the model.  I could be missing something, though (of course).
A

>   int<lower=1> K;
>   int<lower=K> N;
>   matrix[N,K]  X;
>   int y[n];
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> R[N];

>   vector[N] lower;
>   vector[N] upper;
>   int n_miss;
>   n_miss <- N - sum(R);

>     else {

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] a (fairly) painless way to implement discrete sampling?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] a (fairly) painless way to implement discrete sampling?
messages.body_plain:
My guess is it'll be significantly worse than JAGS, for a few reasons:
it's throwing away the advantages of HMC, it's not exploiting the
conditional independence structure of the model, and it's imposing an
order on variables that may not have an intrinsic order (e.g., to get
to a=5 from a=1 you have to go through a=2–4, any or all of which may
be arbitrarily unlikely in, say, a mixture model).

But it's worth testing! It may be that there are some scenarios that
it works ok for. (In particular, it's worth testing before we get too
deep into the language issues involved in doing it automatically.)

Matt

On Thu, May 2, 2013 at 6:14 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

>>> One question is:  How slow would it be on problems of interest?  If it is implementable and slow but not prohibitively slow, it could be a useful step along the way, so that users who really want to implement discrete variables will be able to do so.  But of course if Mike could whip up a better algorithm, that would be great.
>>> For some models (for example, or multinomial logit), I could actually imagine the continuous parameterization being not too bad, in that the underlying continuous parameter has a statistical interpretation.
>>> A
>>>
>>> On May 2, 2013, at 7:27 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>>
>>>> I think this is valid from a language perspective, but it probably
>>>> won't ever be fast from an algorithmic perspective. The problem is
>>>> that the posterior will become discontinuous unless a is completely
>>>> isolated from the rest of the model. (In which case there's not much
>>>> point.) Each time you cross a cutpoint you get an abrupt change in
>>>> energy, which basically hoses your chance of maintaining a high
>>>> acceptance probability.
>>>>
>>>> That said, I seem to remember Mike talking about an integration scheme
>>>> that might be able to handle that sort of problem.
>>>>
>>>> Matt
>>>>

>>>>> Hi all (especially Bob).  During the times we've discussed discrete sampling, one possibility we've talked about is to work with latent continuous variables.  We've talked about this as a possibility but I always had the sense that it might be tricky to get the distributions right.

For simplicity, suppose our model has only two parameters:  a N-dimensional discrete parameter a (which can take on the values 1,2,…,K) and an M-dimensional continuous parameter b.  We can define a new continuous parameter z defined on [0,1], along with K probabilities p (i.e., simplex[K] p).
>>>>>
>>>>> Thus, we expand our model from:

>>>>> }

On 5/2/13 6:56 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi all (especially Bob).  During the times we've discussed discrete sampling, one possibility we've talked about is to work with latent continuous variables.  We've talked about this as a possibility but I always had the sense that it might be tricky to get the distributions right.
>

> But, thinking about it, I think it's close to trivial.  For simplicity, suppose our model has only two parameters:  a N-dimensional discrete parameter a (which can take on the values 1,2,ï¿½,K) and an M-dimensional continuous parameter b.  We can define a new continuous parameter z defined on [0,1], along with K probabilities p (i.e., simplex[K] p).

>
> Thus, we expand our model from:
>
> parameters {
>    integer<lower=1,upper=K> a[N];
>    real b[M];
> }
>
> to
>
> parameters {
>    real z[N];
>    simplex[K] p;
>    real b[M];
> }
>
> Now, z relates to a in a very simple way.  In the model, define
>
>    real<lower=0,upper=1> cutpoints[K]
>    cutpoints <- cumulative_sum (p)
>
> Then, y=1 if z<cutpoints[1],
>    y=2 if z is between cutpoints[1] and cutpoints[2]
>    . . .
>    y=K if z>cutpoints[K-1]
>
> This can all be implemented in Stan.
>
> That means, I think, that we could implement discrete variables internally:  if we have an integer-valued parameter "a", we just define the corresponding "z" and "p" parameters and set up the model as above.
>
> All this so far only works with finitely-valued discrete parameters, but I think we could do countably-infinite sets too, by just defining a preset Zeno-like sequence of cutpoints.
>
> What do you think?
>
> A
>
> P.S.  I tried this out by implementing the standard mixture model using the latent-data formulation and then testing it out on fake data.  It seemed to work, but it was very very slow to converge.  So that's another concern.  But if we can get the model set up, improving convergence might be possible using various Matt and Mike tricks...
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] a (fairly) painless way to implement discrete sampling?
messages.body_plain:
Because of the loss of gradient information in the continuous
representation of the discrete parameters, this is effectively doing
something like Gauss-Metropolis in those variables while doing
HMC/NUTS in the regular continuous variables (although the Hamiltonian
in that case would be very badly behaved).  The performance of the
sampler would likely be limited by the performance of the Metropolis
portion though, so this will be a huge drag on the sampling.  (Plus,
if you're going to loose gradient info anyway, you might as well do
real x; int y; y<- round(x); I have a hard time seeing a huge
advantage in other parameterizations.)

I suspect that the few direct discrete samplers that would be
relatively easy to implement in Stan (Slice, Gibbs, etc) would be more
efficient than this.

Cheers,
Marcus

>>>>    y=2 if z is between cutpoints[1] and cutpoints[2]
>>>>    . . .
>>>>    y=K if z>cutpoints[K-1]

>>>>
>>>> That means, I think, that we could implement discrete variables
>>>> internally:  if we have an integer-valued parameter

>>>> too, by just defining a preset Zeno-like sequence of cutpoints.
>>>>
>>>> What do you think?
>>>>
>>>> A
>>>>
>>>> P.S.  I tried this out by implementing the standard mixture model using
>>>> the latent-data formulation and then testing
>>>> it out on fake data.  It seemed to work, but it was very very slow to
>>>> converge.  So that's another concern.  But if we
>>>> can get the model set up, improving convergence might be possible using
>>>> various Matt and Mike tricks...
>>>>

messages.body_plain:
> Are you sure it's a problem with summation precision per se?
>
> I want to understand where you need to add numbers of
> vastly different scales AND the lower-order numbers
> matter.  That is, when do you do (1e-30 + 1e10) and
> the 1e-30 term matters in the sum?  We try to handle
> the gradients separately, and in the usual ways to do
> sums (+ and sum()), the gradients are handled independently,
> so you get the right answer there even if the 1e-30 term
> drops out of the sum due to underflow.
>
> So what I'm wondering is where higher-precision summation
> will make a difference.
>
> The integrator we use to simulate the Hamiltonian dynamics
> has a higher error than floating point precision.

Thanks very much for helping me understand the point. I was ignoring the
importance of gradients when I started creating those functions. When I
started reading the files in src/prob/distribution yesterday, however, I
began to get a better idea of how Stan works to calculate log prob and
gradients. And as my model derivatives are all in closed form, I'll try
to write a distribution function for it directly and check if I can get
interesting results :)

> Great. Send us the pull request for sort() and rank() when
> you have them.  Just please make sure to run fairly extensive
> tests.  Testing these functions is usually harder than writing
> them, so it's not doing us much of a favor to write the function without
> extensive testing.  For sort, you'd want to test zero size arrays/vectors
> as input, and cases where all the numbers are the same, and some random
> ones.  There's no issue with gradients here because neither rank() nor
> sort() have gradients to calculate.

Sure, I tested them today and they are working fine. I just sent the
pull request.

messages.subject: diagonal adaptation failing
messages.body_plain:
Hi stan-dev,

I'm rerunning some experiments from the NUTS paper, and discovered
that diagonal adaptation is failing quite badly in some cases on a
simple logistic regression. Here are minimum effective sample sizes
(obtained from bin/print) for 16 independent runs of 1K warmup/1K
sampling:

     0
     3
     6
     7
     7
     8
     9
    24
    59
    77
    92
   122
   144
   205
   212
   227

Averages are similar. Compare with the results for --equal_step_sizes:

     6
    35
    39
    43
    49
    59
    88
   103
   122
   147
   158
   162
   167
   172
   203
   217

I don't like that 6, but at least there's only one single-digit
result, compared with almost half when we use diagonal adaptation!

I checked out an old version from December, and that version of
diagonal adaptation produced much, much more sensible results:

   153
   198
   198
   204
   221
   224
   224
   228
   231
   248
   250
   253
   265
   286
   300
   307

So it seems like something's been broken in the new version of
diagonal adaptation. My question is: what's changed, and how are we
going to fix it?

Matt

>>>>>>>> But, thinking about it, I think it's close to trivial.  For simplicity, suppose our model has only two parameters:  a N-dimensional discrete parameter a (which can take on the values 1,2,ï¿½,K) and an M-dimensional continuous parameter b.  We can define a new continuous parameter z defined on [0,1], along with K probabilities p (i.e., simplex[K] p).

>>
>>>>>>>>
>>
>>>>>>>> Thus, we expand our model from:
>>
>>>>>>>>
>>
>>>>>>>> parameters {
>>
>>>>>>>> integer<lower=1,upper=K> a[N];
>>

>>>>>>>> }

>>>>>>>> parameters {
>>
>>>>>>>> real z[N];
>>
>>>>>>>> simplex[K] p;
>>

>>
>>>>>>>>
>>
>>>>>>>> real<lower=0,upper=1> cutpoints[K]
>>

>>
>>>>>>>>
>>
>>>>>>>> Then, y=1 if z<cutpoints[1],
>>
>>>>>>>> y=2 if z is between cutpoints[1] and cutpoints[2]
>>
>>>>>>>> . . .
>>
>>>>>>>> y=K if z>cutpoints[K-1]
>>
>>>>>>>>
>>
>>>>>>>> This can all be implemented in Stan.
>>
>>>>>>>>
>>

>>>>>>>>

caused by:

test new additions.

We could probably also do with some more written specs in
these situations of major changes so everyone knows what's
proposed.  There was a bit of misunderstanding in rolling out
the new changes and what kind of backward compatibility was
being assumed other than what was being tested by unit tests.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: diagonal adaptation failing
messages.body_plain:
Ok, here we go:
2024218701
2024256492
2024318542
are all pretty bad.

Also, Mike's right, the diagonal adaptation seems to be giving
basically reasonable results, insofar as it's roughly matching the
marginal variances. Which leads me to a hypothesis, one that we've
discussed previously on this list.

The mass matrix is effectively adjusting the overall step size,
insofar as multiplying the mass matrix by a scalar is equivalent to
multiplying the step size by the square root of that scalar. This
wasn't a problem in the old implementation, where the overall scale of
the mass matrix was held constant. Here it is a problem, because every
change to the mass matrix's overall scale is effectively a shock to
the step size adaptation problem that the dual averaging algorithm is
trying to solve. And if there's one final change at the end of the
adaptation period, then the step size adaptation never has a chance to
recover.

One of two things needs to happen to remedy this: either the mass
matrix adaptation has to keep its overall scale constant, or the step
size returned by the step size adaptation has to be adjusted to
account for the overall scale of the mass matrix.

Also, I'm not sure that the refactored stepsize_adaptation.hpp
correctly implements the dual averaging algorithm. The new
implementation seems to be returning the averaged iterates ("xbar" in
the old implementation) instead of the iterates ("xk") themselves. The
way it's supposed to work is that during adaptation a bunch of
iterates are generated. Then, once adaptation's over, we use a
weighted average of that sequence of iterates. Using the average
prematurely undermines the algorithm's proof of correctness, I think.

Matt

> > Part of the problem here is that it does the function_signature tests in alphabetical order so all the exp_mod_normal_.*stan functions get parsed, compiled, and run at approximately the same time when using multiple cores in parallel. Would anyone mind if the makefile did a random shuffle (see man shuf for details) of the .stan files under src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/ and looped through the shuffled list? That way, it would be unlikely to get several of the most computationally intensive tests at the same time and thus, unlikely to swap.
>
> No, I don't mind. Could you get it working and into the repo?

This patch seems to work for me on Linux and keeps me well under 1GB per processor on average

diff --git a/make/tests b/make/tests
index c1cc03c..e6504f4 100644
--- a/make/tests
+++ b/make/tests
@@ -100,7 +100,7 @@ endif
 ##
 # Builds a single test
 ##
-test/gm/compile_models$(EXE) : test/gm/compile_models.o bin/libstan.a $(patsubst %.stan,%$(EXE),$(wildcard src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/*.stan))
+test/gm/compile_models$(EXE) : test/gm/compile_models.o bin/libstan.a $(shell shuf -e $(patsubst %.stan,%$(EXE),$(wildcard src/test/gm/model_specs/compiled/*.stan)))
        @mkdir -p $(dir $@)
        $(LINK.c) -O$O $(GTEST_MAIN) $< $(CFLAGS_GTEST) $(OUTPUT_OPTION) $(LIBGTEST) $(LDLIBS) $(LDLIBS_STANC)
 ifeq ($(findstring test-,$(MAKECMDGOALS))$(findstring runtest/,$(MAKECMDGOALS)),)

Is that likely to work on Windows and / or is there are more canonical way to do it?

Also, I think we should shuffle the test-models so as to avoid doing several multivariate ones at once. Maybe also test-distributions? Perhaps it would be better to ask is there anything in the test suite that you definitely don't want shuffled?

messages.subject: distance correlations for MCMC
messages.body_plain:
I was thinking about the distance correlation

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_correlation

which is a measure of multivariate dependence on [0,1] and is implemented by the energy package for R

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/energy/index.html .

My thought was to estimate the distance correlation between consecutive MCMC iterations. For each iteration, you can get a "sample" whose rows are equal to the number of chains and whose columns are equal to the number of monitored quantities from the posterior distribution and then calculate the distance correlation to the next "sample". An R function for doing this is pretty simple:

dependence <- function(stanfit) {
  stopifnot(is(stanfit, "stanfit"))
  stopifnot(stanfit@mode == 0)
  pars <- dim(stanfit)[3]
  arr <- extract(stanfit, permuted = FALSE, inc_warmup = TRUE)
  arr <- array(apply(arr, "chains", function(x) cbind(x[-nrow(x),], x[-1,])),
                 dim = c(nrow(arr) - 1, 2 * pars, ncol(arr)))
  apply(arr, 1, function(x) dcor(t(x[1:pars,]), t(x[-c(1:pars),])))
}

Trying this out on the dogs example

stopifnot(require(rstan))
stopifnot(require(energy))

fit <- stan_demo("dogs", chains = 8)
dcors <- dependence(fit)
plot(dcors, type = "l", ylim = 0:1, las = 1,
     xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Distance Correlation",
     main = paste(fit@model_name, "model"))
lines(lowess(dcors), type = "l", col = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = 1000, col = 3, lty = 3)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Value", "Smoothed", "End Warmup"),
       col = 1:3, lty = 1:3, cex = 3/4)

yields the attached plot which shows that this measure of dependence slowly trends downward during the warmup period and levels off at about 0.7 on average.

What is interesting to me is that (1 - 0.7) * 8000 = 2400, which is in line with the average of the marginal effective sample sizes that we calculate (2247). It is somewhat intuitive that the quantity one minus the average distance correlation times the total number of retained iterations would be a multivariate measure of effective sample size that would be appropriate in the extreme cases where the average distance correlation were 0 or 1. And if you do this on an example like mvn_orange where the defaults yield crappy sampling, the average distance correlation is near 1 and the marginal effective sample sizes are usually in the single digits. But I don't have much of an idea for a proof that it would be a reasonable multivariate measure of effective sample size for intermediate values of the distance correlations, nor much of an argument that setting the exponent equal to 1.0 is best.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] distance correlations for MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Ben
This is interesting, it seems worth thinking about in the larger context of methods for measuring mixing.  So I'm ccing Kenny.
A

On May 5, 2013, at 12:34 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> I was thinking about the distance correlation
>
> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_correlation
>
> which is a measure of multivariate dependence on [0,1] and is implemented by the energy package for R
>
> http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/energy/index.html .
>
> My thought was to estimate the distance correlation between consecutive MCMC iterations. For each iteration, you can get a "sample" whose rows are equal to the number of chains and whose columns are equal to the number of monitored quantities from the posterior distribution and then calculate the distance correlation to the next "sample". An R function for doing this is pretty simple:
>
> dependence <- function(stanfit) {
>   stopifnot(is(stanfit, "stanfit"))
>   stopifnot(stanfit@mode == 0)
>   pars <- dim(stanfit)[3]
>   arr <- extract(stanfit, permuted = FALSE, inc_warmup = TRUE)
>   arr <- array(apply(arr, "chains", function(x) cbind(x[-nrow(x),], x[-1,])),
>                  dim = c(nrow(arr) - 1, 2 * pars, ncol(arr)))
>   apply(arr, 1, function(x) dcor(t(x[1:pars,]), t(x[-c(1:pars),])))
> }
>
> Trying this out on the dogs example
>
> stopifnot(require(rstan))
> stopifnot(require(energy))
>
> fit <- stan_demo("dogs", chains = 8)
> dcors <- dependence(fit)
> plot(dcors, type = "l", ylim = 0:1, las = 1,
>      xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Distance Correlation",
>      main = paste(fit@model_name, "model"))
> lines(lowess(dcors), type = "l", col = 2, lty = 2)
> abline(v = 1000, col = 3, lty = 3)
> legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Value", "Smoothed", "End Warmup"),
>        col = 1:3, lty = 1:3, cex = 3/4)
>
> yields the attached plot which shows that this measure of dependence slowly trends downward during the warmup period and levels off at about 0.7 on average.
>
> What is interesting to me is that (1 - 0.7) * 8000 = 2400, which is in line with the average of the marginal effective sample sizes that we calculate (2247). It is somewhat intuitive that the quantity one minus the average distance correlation times the total number of retained iterations would be a multivariate measure of effective sample size that would be appropriate in the extreme cases where the average distance correlation were 0 or 1. And if you do this on an example like mvn_orange where the defaults yield crappy sampling, the average distance correlation is near 1 and the marginal effective sample sizes are usually in the single digits. But I don't have much of an idea for a proof that it would be a reasonable multivariate measure of effective sample size for intermediate values of the distance correlations, nor much of an argument that setting the exponent equal to 1.0 is best.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Optimizing chain()
messages.body_plain:
So I'm working on some more vari's for quadratic forms on matrices and
an issue has come up which is a matter of style and optimization.

Consider a (scalar valued) function defined on matrices, f(A,B,C).  So
far the pattern for vari's (eg, det, dot_product) has been that the
vari structure contains pointers to the vari's of A, B and C and the
constructor of the vari simply copies data around and computes the
value of the function.  The chain function then uses the stored vari
pointers to propagate the adjoint information.

This is fine for the typical use case, differentiating lp__, but if we
start computing Jacobians it would be inefficient, as each call would
recompute df/d{A,B,C}.  We can store these values, but that uses more
memory.

The question is, are we likely to be computing Jacobians often?  I
seem to recall that being part of the design for higher order
derivatives but I'm very fuzzy on how all of that is going to fit
together.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Optimizing chain()
messages.body_plain:
Jacobians of R^N -> R^M functions are most efficiently
computing using n forward-mode passes, each computing
dy_m/dx_n for all m in 1:M and a single n.

Hessians of an R^n -> R function get computed with
n forward + reverse passes.

Hessian-vector products are easier.  As are directional
derivatives.

You can see all the code in agrad/autodiff.hpp

We haven't finished all the functions in forward mode,
but Peter's working on it and should have them done by
the end of the summer if not sooner.

We need most of the obscure ops in autodiff.hpp for
Michael's softabs metric-based RM-HMC.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] a (fairly) painless way to implement discrete sampling?
messages.body_plain:
Slightly wrong, I mean DREAM(D), there is another one DREAM(ZS). They are all Vrugt and Ter Braak etc.

Don't ask me whether they really fulfill all MCMC criteria! Proofs seem sketchy, as always with these authors, but they seem to work which is the main thing, I haven't come across a practical alternative.

Just completed a study, 60 parameters, 20 discrete, some of the discrete have 3 discrete values, some have 50 discrete values. Got a good variation in results, which pleased my client. I apply NUTS to the non-discrete parameters. It's no use trying to get NUTS to jump between discrete - it's the same problem as jumping between modes, it won't happen.

Got to be careful when hitting bounds.....I normally reflect, but reflecting with discrete needs to be treated carefully, to get correct reversible probabilities.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] diagonal adaptation failing
messages.body_plain:
I pushed a fix -- now the adaptation spends the last bit of warmup, max(10% total iterations, 100 iterations), adapting the step size.  I also fixed the minor misimplementation of the dual averaging.  Everything looks great on the few examples I ran (including logistic regression with the German Credit data for all there seeds Matt posted) -- let me know if there are any remaining performance issues.

-Mike

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Optimizing chain()
messages.body_plain:
Exactly.  For a single set of calls to chain (computing the gradient
of a scalar valued function) it doesn't matter because the (local)
gradients only get computed once but if there are multiple calls
(computing a Jacobian) then you end up recomputing the gradients for
each set of calls.  At any rate, since it seems like we won't be doing
Jacobians with the reverse mode autodiff, I don't need to worry about
this too much.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: performance testing for 2.0
messages.body_plain:
I don't think we want to release a new version that's
slower than the old version in average n_eff/sec terms
or one that has much variance run to run in n_eff/sec.

So we need some tests.  How about 20 runs or so for all
of the models in our test suite, 4 chains each, with
four measurements per model:

     mean minimum r_hat
     mean average r_hat
     mean n_eff/sec

If we scatterplot that out in three plots and they look OK,
I'd be happy releasing a new way of doing sampling and
adaptation.

Of course, we need to resolve the Mac vs. Windows bug,
too.  Daniel and I are going to sit down and try to closely
code review the adaptation, which is where things seem
to be going wrong in the sense that we're getting different
answers on Windows vs. Mac and the Windows answers look
better.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
Some questions:

Is jittering turned on by default? If so, why?

What exactly are you passing to the step size adaptation to tell it
whether the step size is too small or too large?

How are you deciding whether to use a sample from the new half-tree or
the old half-tree?

I'm concerned that the "refactor" has made some significant changes to
the actual algorithm, and that these changes haven't been adequately
tested.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
> Is jittering turned on by default? If so, why?

Defaults to zero jitter, just as before.

> What exactly are you passing to the step size adaptation to tell it

The average acceptance probability of the tree, just as before.

> How are you deciding whether to use a sample from the new half-tree or
> the old half-tree?

Uniformly based on total valid points in the subtree, just as before.

> I'm concerned that the "refactor" has made some significant changes to
> the actual algorithm, and that these changes haven't been adequately
> tested.

I may very well have made an error somewhere, but every attempt was made to reproduce the old algorithm exactly unless I found an explicit error (as in the stepsize initialization - I can't recall another instance).  In particular I did a bunch of tests on the interaction between stepsize and tree structure and everything behaved as expected.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
Ok, I'll take a closer look at the code and double-check. I got a
little confused by the util.sum_prob, but now I see that it's not
being used to decide which branch to sample from but only as a measure
of integrator accuracy. One minor difference, though, is that in the
old version we only computed the average probability for the most
recent half of the tree, excluding the states in the half-tree nearest
the starting point. This is because the first state is always
acceptable, so including states near the start state biases our
estimate of the average acceptance probability upwards (though
probably only slightly). I think the original behavior could be
brought back by moving

        util.n_tree = 0;
        util.sum_prob = 0;

into the while loop.

BTW, can someone remind me how to set off code so that it looks nice
in these emails? Ben's code snippets always look so much nicer than
mine...

Matt

On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 12:24 PM, Michael Betancourt
<betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Is jittering turned on by default? If so, why?
>
> Defaults to zero jitter, just as before.
>
>> What exactly are you passing to the step size adaptation to tell it
>> whether the step size is too small or too large?
>
> The average acceptance probability of the tree, just as before.
>
>> How are you deciding whether to use a sample from the new half-tree or
>> the old half-tree?
>
> Uniformly based on total valid points in the subtree, just as before.
>
>> I'm concerned that the "refactor" has made some significant changes to
>> the actual algorithm, and that these changes haven't been adequately
>> tested.
>
> I may very well have made an error somewhere, but every attempt was made to reproduce the old algorithm exactly unless I found an explicit error (as in the stepsize initialization - I can't recall another instance).  In particular I did a bunch of tests on the interaction between stepsize and tree structure and everything behaved as expected.

messages.subject: adaptation, exceptions and NaN; this -> _foo; static_cast<bar>(...) vs. bar(...)
messages.subject_clean: adaptation, exceptions and NaN; this -> _foo; static_cast<bar>(...) vs. bar(...)
messages.body_plain:
I didn't see anything in place to handle the exceptional
returns and NaN returns possible when evaluating log probabilities
during adaptation.

I'm worried about examples like the following in init_stepsize() in
base_hmc.hpp:

     if ((direction == 1) && !(delta_H > log(0.5)))
       break;

If delta_H is NaN, then !(delta_H > log(0.05)) will be true, and we
break out of the loop with a bad value and no warning.

Could we instead check if we get a NaN response or exception and
perhaps report something back to the user by throwing an exception
with an appropriate message?  Or, if we want to treat it as 0 probability,
treating it like 0 probability?

- Bob

P.S.  I'm also very distracted by all the uses of (this->_foo) for
       member variables _foo.  You shouldn't need the "this->" part.
       (I know we had some trouble getting things to compile for at
       least one instance, and I'd still like to figure out what was
       wrong there.)

P.P.S.  You don't need static casts like this one in base_hmc.hpp:

         ps_point z_init(static_cast<ps_point>(this->_z));

If you have a non-pointer type like the class ps_point, then

        static_cast<ps_point>(foo)

is just longhand for

        ps_point(foo)

So you'll ge the same result with

         ps_point z_init(ps_point(_z));

and thus with

         ps_point z_init(_z);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
So....I may have been premature.  I found two somewhat serious bugs in the NUTS code -- it's amazing they didn't manifest as more serious sampling problems (and frustrating, because I had extensively checked for those kinds of problems when first writing up the new code -- I have no idea what happened in between).  It seemed like the errors were introducing larger gradients which allowed very small differences in floating point calculations to leak into the sampler, accumulate, and eventually become nontrivial.  But even after fixing those problems and verifying that NUTS behaves as expected, Mac/Windows are different.  I'm still neck deep in code, hopefully something will turn up.

Incidentally, I can at least explain why the Mac/Windows code seems to "diverge".  The numerical differences eventually affect the NUTS criterion, and at a given iteration the tree on one machine reaches a deeper depth than on the other.  This misaligns the random number generators and the resulting sequence of samples.

To do this would either require moving to either (a) expression
templates so we can do it on the C++ side, or (b) code analysis

an efficient inv_sqrt() that efficiently calculates derivatives,
which is the whole point.  It's not for more expressiveness.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.

There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
results.  E.G., is one using x87 instructions while another is using
SSE instructions at some point?  With x87 instructions, some floating
point ops are done at 80bit (long double) precision and the result
gets truncated down to 64bit when they're written to memory or
registers.  This can result in slightly different results on different
platforms.  Unfortunately, there's not too much we can do about that.

Cheers,
Marcus

>> So....I may have been premature.  I found two somewhat serious bugs in the NUTS code -- it's amazing they didn't manifest as more serious sampling problems (and frustrating, because I had extensively checked for those kinds of problems when first writing up the new code -- I have no idea what happened in between).  It seemed like the errors were introducing larger gradients which allowed very small differences in floating point calculations to leak into the sampler, accumulate, and eventually become nontrivial.  But even after fixing those problems and verifying that NUTS behaves as expected, Mac/Windows are different.  I'm still neck deep in code, hopefully something will turn up.
>>
>> Incidentally, I can at least explain why the Mac/Windows code seems to "diverge".  The numerical differences eventually affect the NUTS criterion, and at a given iteration the tree on one machine reaches a deeper depth than on the other.  This misaligns the random number generators and the resulting sequence of samples.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
We're actually trying to understand the fundamental differences in code from v1.3.0 and current master. This is manifesting itself as differences in Mac/Windows right now. There's something else going on and if we knew what it was, we'd be ok with it.

We're not actually too concerned with floating point differences. Now, with that said, we can't draw the same first sample in Mac and Windows in master, which we were able to do in v1.3.0. We should either be able to reproduce that behavior or explain why we have differences.

On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 3:00 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.
>
> There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
> levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
> results.  E.G., is one using x87 instructions while another is using
> SSE instructions at some point?  With x87 instructions, some floating
> point ops are done at 80bit (long double) precision and the result
> gets truncated down to 64bit when they're written to memory or
> registers.  This can result in slightly different results on different
> platforms.  Unfortunately, there's not too much we can do about that.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
> On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 2:54 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Pushed the implementation fixes, I'll spend one more day looking for the source of the Mac/Windows discrepancy tomorrow.
> >
> > On May 7, 2013, at 4:48 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> So....I may have been premature.  I found two somewhat serious bugs in the NUTS code -- it's amazing they didn't manifest as more serious sampling problems (and frustrating, because I had extensively checked for those kinds of problems when first writing up the new code -- I have no idea what happened in between).  It seemed like the errors were introducing larger gradients which allowed very small differences in floating point calculations to leak into the sampler, accumulate, and eventually become nontrivial.  But even after fixing those problems and verifying that NUTS behaves as expected, Mac/Windows are different.  I'm still neck deep in code, hopefully something will turn up.
> >>
> >> Incidentally, I can at least explain why the Mac/Windows code seems to "diverge".  The numerical differences eventually affect the NUTS criterion, and at a given iteration the tree on one machine reaches a deeper depth than on the other.  This misaligns the random number generators and the resulting sequence of samples.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
On 5/6/13 3:34 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Ok, I'll take a closer look at the code and double-check. I got a
> little confused by the util.sum_prob, but now I see that it's not
> being used to decide which branch to sample from but only as a measure
> of integrator accuracy. One minor difference, though, is that in the
> old version we only computed the average probability for the most
> recent half of the tree, excluding the states in the half-tree nearest
> the starting point. This is because the first state is always
> acceptable, so including states near the start state biases our
> estimate of the average acceptance probability upwards (though
> probably only slightly). I think the original behavior could be
> brought back by moving
>
>          util.n_tree = 0;
>          util.sum_prob = 0;
>
> into the while loop.
>
> BTW, can someone remind me how to set off code so that it looks nice
> in these emails? Ben's code snippets always look so much nicer than
> mine...

I just found this out, but there is an add-on in thunderbird called
"Markdown Here" that let's you insert code blocks. It also allows you to
add in LaTeX (haven't figured out how to do it yet though, but there's
another add-on called LaTeXIt! that does this).

>
> Matt
>
> On Mon, May 6, 2013 at 12:24 PM, Michael Betancourt
> <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Is jittering turned on by default? If so, why?
>> Defaults to zero jitter, just as before.
>>
>>> What exactly are you passing to the step size adaptation to tell it
>>> whether the step size is too small or too large?
>> The average acceptance probability of the tree, just as before.
>>
>>> How are you deciding whether to use a sample from the new half-tree or
>>> the old half-tree?
>> Uniformly based on total valid points in the subtree, just as before.
>>
>>> I'm concerned that the "refactor" has made some significant changes to
>>> the actual algorithm, and that these changes haven't been adequately
>>> tested.
>> I may very well have made an error somewhere, but every attempt was made to reproduce the old algorithm exactly unless I found an explicit error (as in the stepsize initialization - I can't recall another instance).  In particular I did a bunch of tests on the interaction between stepsize and tree structure and everything behaved as expected.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
That's almost exactly what I said during the meeting today :-).

What's a bit worrying is that we used to get identical results.

But the algebra's changed, so no reason to believe we still would.

Daniel's working on a test suite, so we can at least do functional
and speed tests cross-platform.  If those work out, I wouldn't be
too worried either (as I also said in today's meeting).

- Bob

On 5/7/13 3:00 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.
>
> There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
> levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
> results.  E.G., is one using x87 instructions while another is using
> SSE instructions at some point?  With x87 instructions, some floating
> point ops are done at 80bit (long double) precision and the result
> gets truncated down to 64bit when they're written to memory or
> registers.  This can result in slightly different results on different
> platforms.  Unfortunately, there's not too much we can do about that.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
> On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 2:54 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Pushed the implementation fixes, I'll spend one more day looking for the source of the Mac/Windows discrepancy tomorrow.
>>
>> On May 7, 2013, at 4:48 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> So....I may have been premature.  I found two somewhat serious bugs in the NUTS code -- it's amazing they didn't manifest as more serious sampling problems (and frustrating, because I had extensively checked for those kinds of problems when first writing up the new code -- I have no idea what happened in between).  It seemed like the errors were introducing larger gradients which allowed very small differences in floating point calculations to leak into the sampler, accumulate, and eventually become nontrivial.  But even after fixing those problems and verifying that NUTS behaves as expected, Mac/Windows are different.  I'm still neck deep in code, hopefully something will turn up.
>>>
>>> Incidentally, I can at least explain why the Mac/Windows code seems to "diverge".  The numerical differences eventually affect the NUTS criterion, and at a given iteration the tree on one machine reaches a deeper depth than on the other.  This misaligns the random number generators and the resulting sequence of samples.

Yeah, it's not that there is a difference but rather that the difference is new and so significant.

On May 7, 2013, at 8:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> That's almost exactly what I said during the meeting today :-).
>
> What's a bit worrying is that we used to get identical results.
>
> But the algebra's changed, so no reason to believe we still would.
>
> Daniel's working on a test suite, so we can at least do functional
> and speed tests cross-platform.  If those work out, I wouldn't be
> too worried either (as I also said in today's meeting).
>
> - Bob
>
> On 5/7/13 3:00 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>> I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.
>>
>> There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
>> levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
>> results.  E.G., is one using x87 instructions while another is using
>> SSE instructions at some point?  With x87 instructions, some floating
>> point ops are done at 80bit (long double) precision and the result
>> gets truncated down to 64bit when they're written to memory or
>> registers.  This can result in slightly different results on different
>> platforms.  Unfortunately, there's not too much we can do about that.
>>
>> Cheers,
>> Marcus
>>
>> On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 2:54 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> Pushed the implementation fixes, I'll spend one more day looking for the source of the Mac/Windows discrepancy tomorrow.
>>>
>>> On May 7, 2013, at 4:48 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>>> So....I may have been premature.  I found two somewhat serious bugs in the NUTS code -- it's amazing they didn't manifest as more serious sampling problems (and frustrating, because I had extensively checked for those kinds of problems when first writing up the new code -- I have no idea what happened in between).  It seemed like the errors were introducing larger gradients which allowed very small differences in floating point calculations to leak into the sampler, accumulate, and eventually become nontrivial.  But even after fixing those problems and verifying that NUTS behaves as expected, Mac/Windows are different.  I'm still neck deep in code, hopefully something will turn up.
>>>>
>>>> Incidentally, I can at least explain why the Mac/Windows code seems to "diverge".  The numerical differences eventually affect the NUTS criterion, and at a given iteration the tree on one machine reaches a deeper depth than on the other.  This misaligns the random number generators and the resulting sequence of samples.

messages.subject: std::cout in API
messages.body_plain:
It'd be nice if we could remove all references to
std::cout in the API code before we release.
Right now, I'm seeing them in verbose_evolve().

I'd much rather see an output stream passed in
to these places from the outside than have things
hard coded to write to std::cout, which we can't
control in some settings.  Then whoever's calling
it can pass in std::cout if they want, or a file-based
stream, or whatever.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure I was totally clear. I was just proposing that we allow
elementwise division to broadcast scalars to vectors. It wouldn't have
a significant effect on speed, it'd just be cleaner.

Is there any speed benefit to specializing 1/x using an inv() function?

Matt

On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 11:45 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> On 5/7/13 2:36 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
>>
>> In matlab, you'd do this using elementwise operators, e.g.:
>>
>> 1./x
>> 1./square(x)
>> 1./sqrt(x)
>
>
>> which I think is cleaner than inventing a bunch of new
>> not-all-that-special functions.
>
>
> To do this would either require moving to either (a) expression
> templates so we can do it on the C++ side, or (b) code analysis
> in the generator.  Either would let us evaluate 1/sqrt(x) with
> an efficient inv_sqrt() that efficiently calculates derivatives,
> which is the whole point.  It's not for more expressiveness.
>
> Is there a third way of doing this I'm not considering?
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>>
>> Matt
>>
>> On Tue, May 7, 2013 at 11:30 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> [now on stan-dev]
>>>
>>> (Peter this would be something good for you to do if you're
>>> looking for something light and distracting until I get the
>>> traits fixed for distributions.)
>>>
>>> More below.
>>>
>>> On 5/7/13 2:05 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> ...
>>>> It might be slightly faster if you would use the square() and sqrt()
>>>> functions instead of the the pow(x,k) function that
>>>> takes an arbitrary exponent. But I doubt that is slowing you down a
>>>> noticeable amount.
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> Not much gain.  We have the following in the code.
>>>
>>>      inline var pow(const var& base, const double exponent) {
>>>        if (exponent == 0.5)
>>>          return sqrt(base);
>>>        if (exponent == 1.0)
>>>          return base;
>>>        if (exponent == 2.0)
>>>          return base * base; // FIXME: square() functionality from
>>> special_functions
>>>        return var(new pow_vd_vari(base.vi_,exponent));
>>>      }
>>>
>>> Now that we have square(), the base * base should be replaced.
>>>
>>> Should I include the negative ones, too?  This is one reason I've
>>> been meaning to add special functions:
>>>
>>>      // precision->variance, variance->precision
>>>      inv(x) = 1/x.
>>>
>>>      // deviation->precision
>>>      inv_square(x) = 1 / x^2
>>>
>>>      // precision->deviation
>>>      inv_sqrt(x) = 1 / sqrt(x)
>>>
>>> These seem to get used a lot in transforms, so they'd absolutely
>>> be worth doing in both basic and vectorized forms (though as Ben
>>> says, the vectorization here would be for convenience, not speed, unless
>>> we want to use some of the nifty tricks Marcus developed for matrices
>>> to reduce virtual function calls).

On Tuesday, May 7, 2013 3:00:51 PM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> I'm not sure it's worth looking too closely for the Mac/Windows discrepancy.
>
> There are a number of reasons that different compilers/optimization
> levels/CPUs/platforms/etc would give slightly different floating point
> results.

That is all true, but now I can get identical output with g++-4.6 and clang++-3.3, although there are floating point differences that starting in the first few iterations when cross-compiled with mingw64.

However, it was not entirely true that there were no differences as of v1.3.0. The attached files are identical through iteration 358. On 359, the first parameter differs in the string sense (-6.58535e-05 vs. -6.58535e-005) but that seems to be irrelevant. That happens a few more times. On iteration 748, there is a difference in the first parameter in the 8th decimal place. And this happens again in some subsequent iterations that accumulate and eventually cause genuine differences.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] differences in dual-averaging
messages.body_plain:
I went through all of the code again this morning, focusing on tracing differences between 1.3.0 NUTS and master NUTS.  Everything looks to be equivalent except for a small difference in the NUTS criterion that can lead to significant differences (not necessarily errors, just differences) in the resulting trees, and hence samples, when we aggressively push the integrator step size.

If we had a perfect integrator then the two algorithms would be equivalent with

rho (new algorithm) = \delta x (old algorithm) \propto \int dt M^{-1} p(t)

When we appeal to the leapfrog integrator, however, these end up being slightly different,

rho = sum_{i} M^{-1} p^{i}

\delta x = sum_{i} M^{-1} p^{i - 1/2}

i.e. the old algorithm aggregates the momenta at the half step whereas the new algorithm uses the momenta after the full step.

When the accuracy of the integrator is limited by a large step size (which may be totally fine for HMC) this difference can be nontrivial, especially when the tree depth is big.  Again, this just explains differences in the exact sequence of samples and possibly different sensitivities to floating point arithmetic; both should yield fine inferences.

-Mike

messages.subject: entropy-based simplex prior?
messages.body_plain:
I'm looking to construct a prior on K-simplexes theta
(theta[k] > 0, sum(theta) = 1) that favors low
entropy theta.  The context is a genomics model of
RNA splice variation, where there are often 1000s
of possibilities, but only a handful that are non-zero.
The Dirichlet's not quite right here.

I was about to mail out a suggestion for a prior on
simplexes I dreamed up,

   p(theta) propto exp(alpha * H[theta])

when I did some searches online and came across this
arXiv paper of Matt's, which introduces the exact
same distribution for the same reasons:

    http://arxiv.org/pdf/1009.5761.pdf

Did you (Matt) invent this or are there other refs?  I
found Rodriguez on "entropic priors", but the motivation is
very max-entropy motivated, and I couldn't line up the ideas.

The alpha term is nice because at 0, it reverts to the uniform
distribution over simplex, if it's positive then you prefer
high entropy and if it's negative you prefer low entropy.
Because the simplex is compact and the H[theta] for a K-simplex
theta is bounded between 0 and K, I think it all normalizes
properly.

Should we add this to Stan?  I think it'd be super-cool if Matt
invented the prior so that we could write it as:

    theta ~ hoffman(alpha);

I was very pleased with myself for coming up with the alpha bit,
and I could being doing much worse than replicating thoughts Matt
had a few years ago!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] entropy-based simplex prior?
messages.body_plain:
It would be super-cool if I'd invented it, but I definitely didn't!
There's a small literature on using these to introduce sparsity in for
audio source separation models, which I believe starts here:
http://www.cs.illinois.edu/~paris/Paris_Smaragdis_page/Paris_Smaragdis_Publications_files/smaragdis-icassp2008.pdf
They reference Matt Brand's paper from 1999:
http://www.merl.com/publications/docs/TR98-18.pdf

I'd second Michael's question about the Dirichlet, though. My
understanding is that the primary reason people prefer the entropic
prior is that it doesn't introduce degeneracies in MAP estimation like
the Dirichlet does.

Matt

Probably not too hard.  We'd need a table that maps functions
to sets of includes.  Or we'd need special include files for
each function that were just indirections to other includes.  That's
because we often need agrad and regular implementations of a function
and will soon have forward-mode, too.

But before taking that step, would you mind running a simple test
by hand to see if it saves any time in compilation?  If it's substantial,
it'll totally be worth doing.  But my experience is that each model
compiles fast UNLESS it involves hairy matrix ops.  So I'm not sure this'll
save a lot of time.

- Bob

I think we're killing RAM when we instantiate templates.
This is only done for code we're using, not for all the
extra templates we read in.

is implemented very wastefully, especially on Windows,
where we had to break translation units apart so as not
to blow out memory during template expansion.

Anyway, this would probably be worth doing for even
a 10% speedup in compilation time at some point.
I think the bigger gains will come from compiling more
into our archive/library.  We can do that with explicit
template instantiations the same way we do for the parser.
We can predict all the implementation types.  The only
downside here is that the archive will be big (but
not necessarily the executables we generate from it).

I tracked down the problem with log1m() when the argument
is greater than 1.

This unit test:

   TEST(AgradRev,log1mErr) {
     AVAR a = 10;
     AVAR f = log1m(a);
   }

causes this error:

   *** set a breakpoint in malloc_error_break to debug
   make: *** [test/agrad/rev/log1m] Abort trap: 6

The root cause is that the constructor for log1m_vari(vari*)
throws an exception if the argument has value >= 1.  So I'm
pretty sure we've had this problem all along but haven't
stumbled across it.

I'm going to clean up the other vari classes that do this,
too so that the calling function throws rather than the
vari construtor.

I'd like to know what's causing the problem --- it's not in
the destructors, so I'm thinking it must be in the way we
allocate/deallocate the memory stacks.

- Bob

messages.subject: Fwd: [stan-users] (R)Stan 1.3.0 released
messages.body_plain:
With my latest push, we are down to 6 examples that fail to run

arch1 garch1_1 gp-multi-sim regression regression_std maQ

all of which are due to not having any data. I fixed about 20 failures by creating foo.data.R files that are associated with foo.stan files under src/models, which is what we have been doing for BUGS examples. Often, this just means copying an existing foo.data.R file to bar.data.R so that bar.stan can use it.

We still have a lot of baz-sim.R files that often have been changed to just do

library(rstan)
source("baz.data.R")
fit <- stan(...)

but these are not really necessary unless they do something that is necessary for the manual. All .stan files should work from R in a more flexible way via the stan_demo() function, although since RStan copies much of the Stan tree it is necessary to call

make install

from the rstan directory to get RStan to recognize a new .stan file.

Ben

messages.subject: contributor copyright agreement?
messages.body_plain:
Now that we're taking contributions from the outside world,
I'd like to rethink our approach to intellectual property.

The basic geography of IP in the United States is:

   * Copyright protects original works of authorship
     (for example, the Stan C++ or RStan R/C++ code or the Stan doc)

   * a patent protects inventions or discoveries
     (for example, the NUTS algorithm)

   * a trademark protects words, phrases, symbols, or designs
     (for example, the name "Stan" or the Stan logo)

You can think of the copyright, patent, or trademark holder
as the "owner" of a piece of intellectual property.

By default, everything a person writes is automatically
copyrighted to the author upon creation.

A copyright owner may transfer copyright to another legal entity,
such as another person or a company such as a university or a publisher.

Licensing is a separate issue.  The owner of a copyrighted work
may license the copyrighted work to another legal entity under
a fixed set of terms layed out in the license.

Our current operating procedure for copyright followed the
Eigen matrix lib approach, so that

   1. Stan, RStan and the Stan documentation is copyright to the development
      team jointly.

Our procedures for licensing are that

   2. Stan C++ code is licensed under the open-source new BSD license,

   3. RStan C++ and R code is licensed under the GPLv3 license, and

   4. Stan doc is licensed under the most liberal Creative Commons license.

I think we all agree that we should keep the licensing as is.  But
what about copyright?

   OPTION A.  Maintain the current approach to copyright, which requires
              all contributors to reassign the copyright for their contribution
              to the development team.

   OPTION B.  Let everyone keep the copyright for whatever they write,
              but require that they license it under 2--4 depending on whether
              it is for Stan, RStan or for doc.

For example, the Coin-OR foundation (http://www.coin-or.org) for
operations research software uses a license following option B:

   http://www.coin-or.org/Ots/license.html

Eigen, the matrix lib we use, follows option A.

Both options require that the developer of the code actually own the
copyright to what they wrote.  This is often not the case due to
employment agreements that broadly assign copyright for all code
created to the employer.

- Bob (who is not a lawyer and already has a headache from all this)

P.S.  This FAQ is useful on US copyright law (I cribbed the bullet points
       above from it):

       http://www.copyright.gov/help/faq/faq-general.html
