messages.subject: Pull request workflow
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

Two thoughts on the pull request workflow now that it looks like
master is back in working order.

First, I was thinking that we should have some guidelines on when we
should do pull requests.  It seems like overkill to do it for really
small and obvious changes/bug fixes.  Here is a proposal, comments
welcome:

Pull requests are not strictly needed if then changes:
 - are sufficiently small and/or obvious
 - consist of things like typo fixes, simple bug fixes, code
reformatting, documentation, etc.

Pull requests should be used if the changes:
 - touch a subsystem you don't usually play in (e.g., if I started
futzing around in the parser)
 - may change exposed/documented behaviour
 - alter the available function signatures/distributions
 - ... or generally if you're not sure

The other thing is how pull requests should work.  E.G., if you submit
a pull request, and someone else gives it a thumbs up who should merge
it.  Or, if no one says anything, what's the default behaviour?  I
would suggest that we leave the final merge up to whoever submitted
the pull request for regular contributors with commit access.  If no
one comments within a reasonable window, I would take it as a green
light.  For pull requests from contributors without commit access,
whoever comments should be responsible for doing the merge unless they
explicitly say otherwise (e.g., "This looks good to me, but it touches
the parser so Bob you should look it over and do the merge").

What we want to avoid is pull requests becoming a major drag on
development.  We should also make sure that external pull requests get
quick feedback.  It's bad form to leave other peoples contributions
languishing for too long.  In fact, looking now, we already have one
pull request which hasn't been commented on by anyone for over a week.

Thoughts?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] contributor copyright agreement?
messages.body_plain:
My understanding is that option A is actually almost impossible to do
without having people sign things and mail them before their code can
be included.  Or, at least, every open source project which requires
copyright assignment that I know of requires this.  It's extremely
tedious and a drag on new contributors.

The primary reason to centralize copyright is to make it easier to
relicense things at a later date.  The other big reason is to make
enforcement of the license easier.  Given that the BSD license is
about as liberal as it gets, both of these seem unlikely, so I would
suggest option B.

Finally, I think the only reasonable thing we can do is assume that
contributors own the code they submit.  Obviously, if someone doesn't
and we find out it will need to be removed, but otherwise I'm not sure
what we can do on that front.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
[back on stan-dev]

On 5/14/13 5:12 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Hey guys,
>
> It looks like I got removed from the Stan project on github.  I'm
> guessing this was an accident, but I just wanted to check to see what
> was going on.

After discussion during the meeting (which everyone's welcome
to join, by the way), we turned off push privileges for everyone
to enforce the pull-based workflow.

We should have waited until we had the process better sorted.
I thought it was going to be simpler.  Daniel had to take off
before getting it documented with pointers to how to do the
various steps.  Hopefully it'll be sorted out tomorrow (Thursday).

I believe Daniel and I still have push privileges intended to be
used for C++/core Stan and Jiqiang and Ben still have push privileges
intended to be used only for RStan.  I'm worried this will be
too much of a bottleneck, so we can extend review/push privileges
back to everyone who had push permission before.  This wasn't intended
to be a rebuke of anyone's code --- I actually thought we could turn
everyone's push priviges off and do everything through pull, but it
looks like you need push privileges to be able to execute someone
else's pull request.

What I don't want to do is have people push things directly.
Hopefully simple changes will be simple pull requests and
get handled quickly.  I wrote to Marco, who has the outstanding
pull requests, and told him we needed (a) unit tests for auto-diff
and (b) were waiting until we had the process sorted.

I think if we're going to do this then EVERYTHING should get
reviewed.  I don't want it to be a judgment call on the part
of the person doing the pushing, or I think it'll quickly devolve
to the old system.

Hopefully the simple changes will be simple and fast.

I have a pending push that I'm still trying to figure out how to
formulate into a pull request.  Looks more complex than I anticipated.
The problem I have with git is that every answer to a question
about git on a blog post or on stack overflow seems to require a
Ph.D. in git to understand.  It's worse than unix man pages.

So we'll see how it goes.  We can always change the process
again at a later date if this experiment is a miserable failure.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Pull request workflow
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, May 14, 2013 5:11:09 PM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> First, I was thinking that we should have some guidelines on when we
> should do pull requests.  It seems like overkill to do it for really
> small and obvious changes/bug fixes.  Here is a proposal, comments
> welcome:

I agree. I think there are at least three kinds of changes

-- Those that don't need any additional action, such as changes to TO-DO, fixing typos in the manual, etc.
-- Those that the pusher should verify pass test-unit but doesn't need someone else to review, such as fixing a build failure, adding more tests, etc.
-- Those that need human review in which case anyone should have the opportunity to raise objections before they go into master

But pretty much anybody should be able to push pretty much anything into a branch that is not master. The big problem is that our workflow has largely been to commit directly to the master branch and push to origin/master as if we were using SVN. Git and GitHub support lots of different workflows such as

gitflow: https://github.com/nvie/gitflow
NoSY:  http://root.cern.ch/drupal/content/suggested-work-flow-distributed-projects-nosy
gerrit: which was recently compared to pull requests from GitHub at http://julien.danjou.info/blog/2013/rant-about-github-pull-request-workflow-implementation

and a bunch of others.

Furthermore, an approved pull request is not much good if it includes individual commits that break the build or are otherwise not good. These should be squashed before pushing or pulling anywhere.

Ben

>
> Pull requests are not strictly needed if then changes:
>  - are sufficiently small and/or obvious
>  - consist of things like typo fixes, simple bug fixes, code
> reformatting, documentation, etc.
>
> Pull requests should be used if the changes:
>  - touch a subsystem you don't usually play in (e.g., if I started
> futzing around in the parser)
>  - may change exposed/documented behaviour
>  - alter the available function signatures/distributions
>  - ... or generally if you're not sure
>
> The other thing is how pull requests should work.  E.G., if you submit
> a pull request, and someone else gives it a thumbs up who should merge
> it.  Or, if no one says anything, what's the default behaviour?  I
> would suggest that we leave the final merge up to whoever submitted
> the pull request for regular contributors with commit access.  If no
> one comments within a reasonable window, I would take it as a green
> light.  For pull requests from contributors without commit access,
> whoever comments should be responsible for doing the merge unless they
> explicitly say otherwise (e.g., "This looks good to me, but it touches
> the parser so Bob you should look it over and do the merge").
>
> What we want to avoid is pull requests becoming a major drag on
> development.  We should also make sure that external pull requests get
> quick feedback.  It's bad form to leave other peoples contributions
> languishing for too long.  In fact, looking now, we already have one
> pull request which hasn't been commented on by anyone for over a week.
>
> Thoughts?
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus

> We need some help in figuring out what the process should be for

> Maybe the privilege revocation should've come as a pull request
> to someone who knew WTF git does.

Let me summarize how I understand the process should work.  Either

1) A contributor does not have push access to our repo.

In this case the contributor forks our repo into their own github account, which gives them a local copy of the repo that tracks any changes we make.  Effectively this is just like them cloning our repo but with the ability to save their commits on their github account.

Once the contributor is happy with their changes they make a pull request, denoting the local branch they want to merge from and the remote branch they want to merge into.  When the merge is done github handles all the logistics of moving branches around.

Once Dan removed my permissions, this is the situation I was in only I wasn't prepared with a proper fork.  It wasn't too hard to fork and then copy over my local changes to the fork.

2) a contributor has access to our repo.

In this case the contributor makes a branch, pushes changes to that branch, and makes a pull request denoting the source (now a branch within the repo instead of in a fork) and the destination (probably master).

Unfortunately there's no way we can allow people to handle merge requests without also allowing them to push to master directly - we just have to be courtious.

Also, it's probably good habit to start mentioning people who might be best suited for handling a particular pull request, especially if we have lots of potential mergers.  Github allows @ mentions for this purpose.

I took a quick look over gitflow and I think from the perspective of
that workflow model
(http://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/), we've never
really had a master branch and we've been treating our master branch
as the develop branch.  If we followed the gitflow model, while the
develop branch was churning with new features, we could have still
branched master for hot fixes and point releases.

I'll look over the other docs when I get some more time, but so far
using something like gitflow seems very reasonable to me.  Master
would remain stable at all times, features would be developed in their
own branches and, when done, merged into develop which would churn
and, when settled, would periodically get merged back into master at
points (maybe not always triggering a release, but rather just marking
a point of stability in the development cycle).

Marcus

On Tuesday, May 14, 2013 8:08:29 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > But I don't think our problems are that strongly related to not using pull requests. We just have poor workflow.
>
> Could you elaborate on what you think a better workflow would be?
> Ideally in terms I can understand that don't involve page after
> page of Git diagrams?  If not, I can try to get through something
> more involved over the next few days.  But I really don't understand
> all of these pages of git instructions.

I think it is probably at least as important that we all standardize on a workflow as it is to debate the merits of the multiple workflows supported by git / github / gerrit / etc. But here are a bunch of things I think

-- If a project has good tests, then that mitigates a lot of problems. But:

---- Our test suite has grown so big that it is not feasible for everyone to run on every commit
---- There are still things that are not easily caught by the unit tests
---- There are some things that pass test-unit with whatever toolchain the author is using but not some other toolchain

To overcome this somewhat, I've emailed to see if we can push to a repository on Hotfoot that would run test-unit in about 2 minutes. That would make it feasible to test every commit and only use the Windows box that Jenkins is on for batches of commits that may be ready for master.

-- Our commits are not good.

---- The commit messages are often not that informative
---- The commits lump together things that should be separate commits
---- Separate commits are used for things that should be lumped together (like "made change, will test and document later")
---- Stuff gets committed that doesn't compile. Note that this is a "git commit" issue rather than a "git push" or "git pull" issue. In other words, this is bad:

Commit A: Add feature, fix bug, whatever
Commit B: Oops, made mistake that broke compilation, now fixed

If you push both of these commits, then (among other reasons) if there is a need to "git bisect" the tree to fix some subtle problem and the bisection lands on Commit B, then git can't tell whether Commit B is good or bad with respect to the subtle problem under investigation because it just terminates in a compiler error. This happened most recently with the different numerical results between g++ (!Windows) and mingw64; I couldn't get to the first commit that exacerbated the numerical differences because it was somewhere in a sequence of about 20 commits that didn't even compile.

The thing to do is either use the --amend flag to "git commit" when committing B to the history, which doesn't actually commit B to the history but instead changes Commit A so that it incorporates the change induced by Commit B and thus (for historical purposes) never breaks the build. Or if you discover that Commit A was faulty after already making some intermediate commits, you can use "git rebase -i" to squash Commit A and Commit B into a single commit (say Commit AB) before pushing anywhere (and thereby making the history essentially irrevocable). If we do that, then "git bisect" often locates the root of the problem quickly and essentially automatically.

-- Stuff is going into master way too soon

--- Where it should go depends on a project's workflow, but there is never a rush to go into master and master should always be usable. In other words, anyone should be able to clone the master branch on GitHub and get a working Stan or RStan so we have to be careful about when and what gets merged into master.
--- Branches are so cheap in git and so easy to work with in GitHub that nothing is lost by saying "I've pushed some stuff into branch foo. Can people test it / comment on it and we'll see about merging it into master later?" We had such a branch with the hmc_refactor thing, but it got merged into master before there was time to figure out all the issues that a change of that magnitude would raise.

-- I don't think pull requests are all that great for Stan in general

---- There are a qualified blessing for outside contributors that happen to have GitHub accounts
---- They are a nuisance if the pull request is just something like "I eliminated some already completed cruft off the TO-DO list"
---- Having someone else give approval is overkill if the pull request is something like "I added a test that passes". 99% of the time there is going to be no objection and the 1% of the time that the test is actually flawed is not worth the hassle of going through the pull request
---- If something merits a pull request, it probably merits a group discussion and testing with multiple toolchains, as opposed to one person approving the pull request. This is because Stan is complicated and most people don't know that much about certain parts of it. In other words, I would favor a process where bigger changes are discussed and tested, objections are resolved, and when there are no more objections, someone pushes it to master.

-- I've never used gitflow myself, but it is widely used and seems to help with discipline

---- There is the master branch and the development branch (among others)
---- New features get pushed to the development branch before they are pushed to the master branch. In other words, the development branch is somewhat like how we have been using the master branch thusfar
---- There are also hotfix branches that fix bugs but do not add new features. A hotfix branch is merged into both the development branch and the master branch.
---- Whenever the master branch changes, you (can) do a release

You probably want some degree of human review before something goes into development (at least if it touches stan/src) and definitely want human review before it goes into master. But you don't want too high of a hurdle for a push to some feature branch that maybe multiple people are working on before it gets pushed to the development branch.

Git is complicated, but it is now beating every other version control system for open source projects, including ones that are bigger or more complicated than Stan. Few projects move away from git and many are moving to it, which causes temporary headaches for people learning the ropes. But we've been using git for a long time now, and it shouldn't be beyond our capability to use it well.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Stan github member
messages.body_plain:
I think I've finally caught up on all the thoughts. Sorry about being unavailable the last few hours.

My opinions differ from most of what's being discussed. I'm first going to restore everyone's privledges for the time being, but I don't think this is the right thing to do. (Ben, what's your GitHub handle? Your commits aren't being picked up by GitHub as a user.)

Here is what I suggest:
- Only a small subset of us have "pull & push" access. Everyone on GitHub has "pull" access by default.
- We use pull requests for everything, even things that seem small. We have Jenkins test it before merging that into master.
- Our main repository should only have a couple branches on it: master and a few big enhancement branches.
- Small enhancements can be done on personal branches.
- All pull requests that get merged into master are tested thoroughly (test-unit, test-distributions, test-models) prior to the merge.

I think the workflow should be:
0. Fork the stan-dev/stan repository to a personal repository.
1. Update the personal/stan master repository.
2. Make changes (either to personal/stan/master or personal/stan/branch).
3. Update master, merge master into current branch (if branch==master, that's fine). Test as much needs to be tested locally.
4. Create a pull request.

For a new feature, bug fix, or anything else, start at 1.

For the pull request:
1. Someone informally code review it and declare it to be ok.
1. Start the build on Jenkins (instructions to come).
3. One of the persons with "pull & push" access merge into master and push the changes.
(Yes, that's two ones. If the pull request is from a trusted source, someone can kick off the build before reviewing.)

The workflow would be similar to the other branches we have for longer development, just replace "master" with the branch of your choice.

One thing that I find myself doing are small commits to fix tests after making a larger commit. This is for both myself and others. For those of you that think that small commits don't break the build, I've actually spent a lot of time going back and making tests pass. I've done this for literally everyone that's committed to Stan. I'm actually the last one to do this -- although the last pull request fixed one of the model tests, the other ones failed. I've had to add another quick patch to make it work. I'm running Jenkins now to verify that all the tests pass.

In early email threads I had suggested our code review be very informal, but we still have pull requests. For example, the last pull request, there isn't a need for anyone to really approve it, but it was quick and Marcus said it looked ok. I wouldn't be comfortable with even something as small as that getting pushed into master without having our tests run. If the goal is for our master to be stable, then we should enforce this behavior.

Hopefully that wasn't too long-winded. The short is, I would rather have everything go through pull requests. If the number of people that can approve it becomes the bottle neck, we can increase the number. I think the real bottle neck will be the number of pull requests that we can test on a daily basis. If Ben can help us get the testing done quicker by pushing to Hotfoot or even some other machines, I think we can deal with that burden for a while. We want to speed up our builds, but it's really f'n hard when master's tests don't pass because we weren't diligent about testing.

> Thanks!  That's the level of description I was
> looking for (and what Marcus sent before).  I particularly
> like the git bisect argument.  And compiling on hotfoot
> would be great.
>
> As to different platforms, we can set up multiple Jenkins-like
> environments with a Windows, Mac, and Linux platform.  It's
> a lot of complexity, though.  But if we're merging to master
> less frequently, then perhaps they don't have to be run that
> often.
>
> In any case, we should go back to giving everyone
> commit permission.  Daniel?
>
> - Bob

>
>
> On 5/14/13 9:35 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> > On Tuesday, May 14, 2013 8:08:29 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >      > But I don't think our problems are that strongly related to not using pull requests. We just have poor workflow.
> >
> >     Could you elaborate on what you think a better workflow would be?
> >     Ideally in terms I can understand that don't involve page after
> >     page of Git diagrams?  If not, I can try to get through something
> >     more involved over the next few days.  But I really don't understand
> >     all of these pages of git instructions.
> >
> >
> > I think it is probably at least as important that we all standardize on a workflow as it is to debate the merits of the
> > multiple workflows supported by git / github / gerrit / etc. But here are a bunch of things I think
> >
> > -- If a project has good tests, then that mitigates a lot of problems. But:
> >
> > ---- Our test suite has grown so big that it is not feasible for everyone to run on every commit
> > ---- There are still things that are not easily caught by the unit tests
> > ---- There are some things that pass test-unit with whatever toolchain the author is using but not some other toolchain
> >
> > To overcome this somewhat, I've emailed to see if we can push to a repository on Hotfoot that would run test-unit in
> > about 2 minutes. That would make it feasible to test every commit and only use the Windows box that Jenkins is on for
> > batches of commits that may be ready for master.
> >
> > -- Our commits are not good.
> >
> > ---- The commit messages are often not that informative
> > ---- The commits lump together things that should be separate commits
> > ---- Separate commits are used for things that should be lumped together (like "made change, will test and document later")
> > ---- Stuff gets committed that doesn't compile. Note that this is a "git commit" issue rather than a "git push" or "git
> > pull" issue. In other words, this is bad:
> >
> > Commit A: Add feature, fix bug, whatever
> > Commit B: Oops, made mistake that broke compilation, now fixed
> >
> > If you push both of these commits, then (among other reasons) if there is a need to "git bisect" the tree to fix some
> > subtle problem and the bisection lands on Commit B, then git can't tell whether Commit B is good or bad with respect to
> > the subtle problem under investigation because it just terminates in a compiler error. This happened most recently with
> > the different numerical results between g++ (!Windows) and mingw64; I couldn't get to the first commit that exacerbated
> > the numerical differences because it was somewhere in a sequence of about 20 commits that didn't even compile.
> >
> > The thing to do is either use the --amend flag to "git commit" when committing B to the history, which doesn't actually
> > commit B to the history but instead changes Commit A so that it incorporates the change induced by Commit B and thus
> > (for historical purposes) never breaks the build. Or if you discover that Commit A was faulty after already making some
> > intermediate commits, you can use "git rebase -i" to squash Commit A and Commit B into a single commit (say Commit AB)
> > before pushing anywhere (and thereby making the history essentially irrevocable). If we do that, then "git bisect" often
> > locates the root of the problem quickly and essentially automatically.
> >
> > -- Stuff is going into master way too soon
> >
> > --- Where it should go depends on a project's workflow, but there is never a rush to go into master and master should
> > always be usable. In other words, anyone should be able to clone the master branch on GitHub and get a working Stan or
> > RStan so we have to be careful about when and what gets merged into master.
> > --- Branches are so cheap in git and so easy to work with in GitHub that nothing is lost by saying "I've pushed some
> > stuff into branch foo. Can people test it / comment on it and we'll see about merging it into master later?" We had such
> > a branch with the hmc_refactor thing, but it got merged into master before there was time to figure out all the issues
> > that a change of that magnitude would raise.
> >
> > -- I don't think pull requests are all that great for Stan in general
> >
> > ---- There are a qualified blessing for outside contributors that happen to have GitHub accounts
> > ---- They are a nuisance if the pull request is just something like "I eliminated some already completed cruft off the
> > TO-DO list"
> > ---- Having someone else give approval is overkill if the pull request is something like "I added a test that passes".
> > 99% of the time there is going to be no objection and the 1% of the time that the test is actually flawed is not worth
> > the hassle of going through the pull request
> > ---- If something merits a pull request, it probably merits a group discussion and testing with multiple toolchains, as
> > opposed to one person approving the pull request. This is because Stan is complicated and most people don't know that
> > much about certain parts of it. In other words, I would favor a process where bigger changes are discussed and tested,
> > objections are resolved, and when there are no more objections, someone pushes it to master.
> >
> > -- I've never used gitflow myself, but it is widely used and seems to help with discipline
> >
> > ---- There is the master branch and the development branch (among others)
> > ---- New features get pushed to the development branch before they are pushed to the master branch. In other words, the
> > development branch is somewhat like how we have been using the master branch thusfar
> > ---- There are also hotfix branches that fix bugs but do not add new features. A hotfix branch is merged into both the
> > development branch and the master branch.
> > ---- Whenever the master branch changes, you (can) do a release
> >
> > You probably want some degree of human review before something goes into development (at least if it touches stan/src)
> > and definitely want human review before it goes into master. But you don't want too high of a hurdle for a push to some
> > feature branch that maybe multiple people are working on before it gets pushed to the development branch.
> >
> > Git is complicated, but it is now beating every other version control system for open source projects, including ones
> > that are bigger or more complicated than Stan. Few projects move away from git and many are moving to it, which causes
> > temporary headaches for people learning the ropes. But we've been using git for a long time now, and it shouldn't be
> > beyond our capability to use it well.
> >
> > Ben

messages.subject: settling on a workflow
messages.body_plain:
Now that I think I understand it better, I'm down with the gitflow.
Let's see if this summary is a little easier (and on target --- Ben?).

I also think a lot of our problems will be solved by separating

    --- master branch:  bug fixes w.r.t. last stable release

    --- dev branch:  new features w.r.t. last stable release

    --- feature branch:  where a new feature or bug fix goes

Merge process is then:

    feature branch -> master: bug fixes

    feature branch -> dev:  new features

    dev -> master: non-patch release

We know we want master to be stable and in an always-releasable
state.  But it brings up some questions:

On Wednesday, May 15, 2013 12:10:28 PM UTC-4, Jiqiang Guo wrote:

> On Wed, May 15, 2013 at 11:44 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > So, you can implement a feature in a feature branch and rewrite your history before merging it into the development branch
>
> How to rewrite history? git rebase?

Mostly, yes. Or if you just need to rewrite the previous commit, then

git commit --amend

Or, if

git rebase -i

is not what you want, you can do

git diff development > /tmp/big_patch.diff
git checkout development
git branch -D feature
git branch feature
git checkout feature
git apply /tmp/big_patch.diff

and then add and commit appropriate chunks of your big_patch as the new history.

The main thing is to not rewrite history if someone else has already branched from some point in the old history because then they can't merge. So, you can only change the history of local branches and possibly public feature branches (because feature branches should generally branch directly from the development branch).

Ben

So technically the gitflow process says only release branches get
merged to master.  In other words:

settles down and we're ready to make a release.

3. Merge release branch back into master.

Just so everyone is clear, we're really talking about two different
things here.  They're related and both of them should be addressed,
but they are distinct.

1. The gitflow discussion relates to how we manage releases and the
main Stan repository.  What goes where, when and in what state.  What
do different branches mean, when do they merge, and in what direction,
etc.  In other words, how all of us work jointly on Stan.

2. The commit history discussion relates to how we work locally.
Ideally every commit should build and, hopefully, pass unit tests.  I
think that's a good goal to keep in mind but a little overly
optimistic, and perhaps even a little counter intuitive because it
will lead to Balkanization of commits.  I.E., instead of committing
often with small changes, this encourages large block commits which
have been fully vetted and makes git bisect similarly useless.  (If it
comes down to a single commit, but that commit touches dozens of files
and changes hundreds of lines of code, that's not terribly helpful.)

For 1) I like the gitflow process, it seems to makes sense, and
ensures that we can always do a release with a bug fix if needed.

For 2) I see Ben has already posted something, but roughly speaking,
it means before we do a git push, we should do a git rebase -i and
clean up our commits.  It's also probably a good idea to do the git
rebase regularly for longer lasting feature branches to keep your
history clean since doing a rebase at the end of a long development
cycle can be painful and require a lot of manual merging.

Cheers,
Marcus

> a hassle, so people do fewer pull requests with more commits each, which are

This is *exactly* what I worry about with doing everything through
pull requests.  There are many many commits which are small and
obvious and do not need a full process of review/compile/test.  If we
make even these commits hard or time-consuming to do, they won't
happen at all or will instead get folded into much larger pull
requests whose correctness aren't at all obvious.

If we're going to require *every* commit to compile and pass unit
tests then we need some a bigger testing infrastructure (i.e., servers
which test every commit in every pull request, automatically and,
ideally, quickly) to do this and it needs to be smooth and painless.
I'm not convinced this is possible with GitHub's pull request
framework, as it seems to struggle with anything other than an
immediate merge.  E.G., if one commit in a large sequence breaks
tests, this is going to require a rebase and a whole new pull request
which is not only tedious, but looses the whole thread of discussion
in the issue tracker.

I really think the solution here is that we all just try to be better
about our workflows and try to make things clean when we do push.
That, combined with a disciplined version of something like gitflow,
should make things much smoother going forward.

Cheers,
Marcus

As a rule (without extreme pain) we can't rebase anything that has
landed into dev, master or any other branch that we expect people to
branch off of.  Rebase rewrites history in a way that breaks anyone
who branched from that history.

>> For 2) I see Ben has already posted something, but roughly speaking,
>> it means before we do a git push, we should do a git rebase -i and
>> clean up our commits.  It's also probably a good idea to do the git
>> rebase regularly for longer lasting feature branches to keep your
>> history clean since doing a rebase at the end of a long development
>> cycle can be painful and require a lot of manual merging.
>
>
> Why does a rebase require any manual merging at all?   Don't we just
> compose the patches into one big patch?

A rebase attempts to replay some or all of your commits as if they
were applied starting from a different point.  Sometimes that doesn't
happen cleanly because of conflicts.  Think of a rebase like this:

Imagine you have a sequence of 10 commits.  Commit 1 was originally
off of the HEAD of master, but there was another commit on master, so
it has a new HEAD and you want commits 1 through 10 to look as if they
happened on this new HEAD and you'd like to combine or reorder some of
them to make things look nicer.

To do this, git rebase creates a sequence of patches from your 10
commits, goes to the new head that you're trying to rebase onto and
then tries to replay these patches on this new head, one at a time, to
create a new set of commits.  There can often be conflicts in this
process.

>

> (i.e., branching from stanfoo/dev for features or stanfoo/master for
> hotfixes).

If there was a way that we could add repos/branches for Jenkins to
watch and send us updates on, that would be great.  Particularly if it
didn't require a pull request, as I'd prefer not to have to open a
browser and login to github every time.

Cheers,
Marcus

>> review policies are before merges happen.
>>
>> That is, do we make everything be a pull request that an admin
>> manages before the merge with dev happens?
>>
>> I think we can all agree that we should be strict about what goes
>> into master and when.
>
> Definitely.  I think we could also agree about what goes into (the
> currently hypothetical) dev and when.
>
>>
>> 4. code review.  What is our process for reviewing code if any.
>> Does a third party have to sign off on a code review for every
>> pull request before an attempt is made to merge with dev and test?
>>
>> The gitflow is agnostic on that point, and the minimal thing to do is
>> just let everything merge back into dev that passes all tests.
>>
>> What I'm worried about specifically on this issue is new
>> features getting added without tests, as that seems to be happening
>> more and more often (I'm not trying to point fingers here --- I'm as
>> guilty as anyone of this;  I was used to checkpointing regularly in
>> SVN this way, but it makes less sense in git to do this outside of
>> your own branch).  For instance, some of the pending pull requests
>> are still pending because there aren't enough tests of the added
>> features.
>>
>> Now what I'd like to be able to do is go into that pull request
>> and modify it to add the tests myself, wrap it up as another
>
> This can be done now.  You can pull that branch into your own local
> repository, add some tests and then merge.  In fact, this is something
> we need to be comfortable doing as we get more contributors who may be
> happy to add some new feature, but may lack the
> skills/knowledge/motivation/etc to fully doc or test it.  If we can't
> do this to some extent, then we need to be OK with loosing
> contributions like those.

It's a delicate balance here.  Testing and doc can take longer than
writing the feature.  And then the problem is if the test fails, who
fixes it?

That's where we're blocked on one of the pull requests -- not enough tests.
I can get around eventually to adding more tests for it, but it's
not a high priority because the feature itself wasn't a high priority.

So we'll get a pileup of incomplete pull requests that we can prioritize
and work on ourselves just reject if the requester isn't willing to do
the work.  I'm leaning more toward the latter these days as I'm feeling
totally overwhelmed with (a) this build process, and (b) the new features
I'm down for, like discrete sampling.

>>> 2. The commit history discussion relates to how we work locally.
>>> Ideally every commit should build and, hopefully, pass unit tests.  I
>>> think that's a good goal to keep in mind but a little overly
>>> optimistic, and perhaps even a little counter intuitive because it
>>> will lead to Balkanization of commits.  I.E., instead of committing
>>> often with small changes, this encourages large block commits which
>>> have been fully vetted and makes git bisect similarly useless.  (If it
>>> comes down to a single commit, but that commit touches dozens of files
>>> and changes hundreds of lines of code, that's not terribly helpful.)
>>
>>
>> We can be sloppy on this and fix it all up later by rebasing.
>> But what I'm wondering is whether that's necessary if we keep the
>> branch history as a branch instead of fast fowarding (that is, keep
>> it as a branch rather than merging its local commits into dev and
>> then into master).
>
> As a rule (without extreme pain) we can't rebase anything that has
> landed into dev, master or any other branch that we expect people to
> branch off of.  Rebase rewrites history in a way that breaks anyone
> who branched from that history.

I thought the idea was to rebase the branch before merging it.

I've only thought about this through bisect --- are there other implications?
I'm not sure what "rewrites history" means here.  (Or what Ben meant about
backing out features creating a circular history.)

>>> For 2) I see Ben has already posted something, but roughly speaking,
>>> it means before we do a git push, we should do a git rebase -i and
>>> clean up our commits.  It's also probably a good idea to do the git
>>> rebase regularly for longer lasting feature branches to keep your
>>> history clean since doing a rebase at the end of a long development
>>> cycle can be painful and require a lot of manual merging.
>>
>>
>> Why does a rebase require any manual merging at all?   Don't we just
>> compose the patches into one big patch?
>
> A rebase attempts to replay some or all of your commits as if they
> were applied starting from a different point.  Sometimes that doesn't
> happen cleanly because of conflicts.  Think of a rebase like this:
>
> Imagine you have a sequence of 10 commits.  Commit 1 was originally
> off of the HEAD of master, but there was another commit on master, so
> it has a new HEAD and you want commits 1 through 10 to look as if they
> happened on this new HEAD and you'd like to combine or reorder some of
> them to make things look nicer.
>
> To do this, git rebase creates a sequence of patches from your 10
> commits, goes to the new head that you're trying to rebase onto and
> then tries to replay these patches on this new head, one at a time, to
> create a new set of commits.  There can often be conflicts in this
> process.

Thanks for the example.  I didn't realize this is what it was doing.

>> Finally, there's the issue of where we set all of this up.  Daniel
>> and I have been talking about isolating the dev and master branches
>> in something like stanfoo where only a couple people have permission
>> to control the merge, and then creating a new repository stanbar where
>> we actually work on all the branches.  I'm still not sure the latter
>> will work if we have to clone a whole remote repository (i.e., all of
>> stanfoo) rather than just being able to branch from a remote branch
>> (i.e., branching from stanfoo/dev for features or stanfoo/master for
>> hotfixes).
>
> If there was a way that we could add repos/branches for Jenkins to
> watch and send us updates on, that would be great.  Particularly if it
> didn't require a pull request, as I'd prefer not to have to open a
> browser and login to github every time.

I don't understand what you're asking here.  Updates about what?

Gack.  It does look like GitHub only lets you do this through the
browser.  I'm with you and hate working through browsers compared
to the command line.  This is all very theoretical for me as I've
never successfully created a pull request myself.  It looks like there
are GitHub projects implementing command-line tools for pull requests,
but I have no idea how stable they are.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: settling on a workflow
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, May 15, 2013 3:37:33 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> My question is what happens to bisect when run on dev.
> I thought we wound up with something like this:
>
>    DEV:  a ---------------> b
>            \                ^
>             \              /
> BRANCH      c ---> d --> e
>
>
> but with fast forward, we get:
>
>           a -> c -> d -> e
>
> When we bisect on DEV in the first case, does it only consider
> a and b, or does it also look at c, d, and e?

git bisect is a commit level concept rather than a branch concept, so it should drill down to the first bad commit in the history between the bracket commits. Although, git bisect would require fewer tests to find the first bad commit if there were a nice simple history between the brackets, it will find it eventually as long as all the commits can definitively test for the problem (as opposed to bombing because of a missing semicolon in a commit)

>
> I was sort of hoping that the bisect on dev would find which branch
> introduced the problem, then bisecting that branch would find the commit.

No, it just finds the commit.

> As a rule (without extreme pain) we can't rebase anything that has
> > landed into dev, master or any other branch that we expect people to
> > branch off of.  Rebase rewrites history in a way that breaks anyone
> > who branched from that history.
>
> I thought the idea was to rebase the branch before merging it.

No one should rebase something that someone else could reasonably have branched from (due to the impossibility of merging later). So, you can't rebase the development branch before branching a release branch from it since people will have branched from development to make a feature branch. That person can usually rebase a feature branch before it is merged into the development branch.

> I've only thought about this through bisect --- are there other implications?
> I'm not sure what "rewrites history" means here.  (Or what Ben meant about
> backing out features creating a circular history.)

The main implication is the ability to merge rather than the ability to bisect. There are a couple of other ways to rewrite history that I mentioned to Mav, namely git commit --amend and making a patch, applying that patch to a new branch, and adding / committing chunks at a time.

Ben

> I'm so far behind on the dev list that I don't know

To summarize a bit:

-- I think several people like gitflow and no one seems to be opposed. To transition to gitflow, we need to get master stable enough to release a new Stan and then immediately branch the development branch off of master. An issue is that we currently have a few public feature-ish branches and who knows how many local branches that have already branched from master. These will become inconsistent with gitflow where nothing branches off of master with the one-time exception of the development branch. So, those orphaned branches will have to be dealt with in one of several ways. But I think no one should start any nontrivial new branches right now.

-- Restricting permission to merge into master or development is workable. In the worst case, we could make a separate repo on GitHub for those two branches, but I think having a pre-push hook locally will work too.

-- On the remote testing front, I got a mostly favorable email about doing this on Hotfoot. But I think that is only going to be possible for Columbia affiliates and is only one toolchain. So, we might need to look into Amazon EC2 in addition.

The good news is that master is in pretty good shape at the moment.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rstan install compiled at -O0?
messages.body_plain:
I think you have used set_cppo('debug') and did not set back to set_cppo('fast').
The flags setting is tricky.  It is not orthogonal to set_cppo(). If set_cppo() is used,
the settings, which stays until a different calling of set_cppo(), will overwrite everything
set in the makefile (use O3 for everything) in package rstan.

On Fri, May 17, 2013 at 12:02 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> It looks like RStan is just using -O0 for building the
> various object files.  This is totally OK for the parser,
> but is there a way to make sure they install at -O3 for
> everything else?  I looked on the R getting started
> guide:
>
> http://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/RStanGettingStarted
>
> and I seem to recall there were instructions for tweaking
> the R compiler config, but I don't see them anywhere in the
> doc.   Can you bring those back?  I think this is orthogonal
> to the set_cppo() usage.

I took them away as if a user has never used set_cppo(), O3 set
in the makefile of rstan package will be used.  If set_cppo() is used,
I am assuming it is always 'fast' while 'debug' is just used temporarily.
Now I guess it is a wrong assumption.

>
> Jiqiang -- could you create for each platform (Mac, Windows,
> Linux) a simple install checklist with checkpoints that
> the user can test are installed successfully (checkpoints
> like you did for Rcpp).

I tried to do that but did not find a satisfying results.  I will try again.

>  I think
> that'll make it a lot easier for relative novices in R like
> me to make sure I'm installing things the right way.  Otherwise,
> I'm worried people will do what I just did and wind up
> with a slow install of Stan.

Absolutely right. The solution is to delete file
~/.R/Makevars or set_cppo('fast') before removing the older package.
I should more words to the getting started wiki webpage, thought it would be wordy,
but it should avoid such problem.

>
> - Bob
>

These two jumped out at me:

UTILITIES

R CMD config now make use of personal ï¿½Makevarsï¿½ files under ï¿½~/.Rï¿½ and a site file ï¿½Makevars.siteï¿½, in the same way as
R CMD SHLIB and R CMD INSTALL. This makes the utility more useful in package configure scripts.

On Windows finding the personal files may require the environment variable HOME set.

The old behaviour can be obtained with the new options --no-user-files and --no-site-files.

PACKAGE INSTALLATION

Alternatives to the site and user customization files ï¿½Makevars.siteï¿½ and ï¿½~/.R/Makevarsï¿½ can be specified via the
environment variables R_MAKEVARS_SITE and R_MAKEVARS_USER respectively. These can be used to suppress the use of the

These issues are partly why I thought it'd be a good time to
look at ensembles.  If we want to do something like
parallel tempering we'll have similar design issues.

We definitely want to encapsulate the ensemble somehow
so we can pass it all around by reference.

For threading, the ensembles can be divided up into blocks which
can be independently updated (treating each block as its own
ensemble then recombining when done).

We should have a Rosenbrock banana-type density in our bag
of tests just to keep up with the Joneses.  Michael B had
one in his Geometric NUTS paper --- don't know if it ever
made it into our source.

- Bob

I'm also not sure how this will all play into R-hat
and auto-correlation evaluation.  I think we need
to treat each walker in the ensemble like we treat
a chain now.  I don't think it'll be kosher to just
scramble them together

As to convergence monitoring and effective sample size,
what we'll get looks like this:

                   walker1     ...  walker N
                 -----------------------------
   iteration 1 |   theta[1,1]  ...  theta[1,N]
               |
   iteration m |   theta[m,1]  ...  theta[m,N]

   ...

where theta[m,n] is a vector of all of our parameters for
the model.

I think we need to treat

   theta[1,1], theta[2,1], theta[3,1], ...

like we currently treat a chain.  That is, we can't scramble
the walkers, as in:

   theta[1,1], theta[1,2], ..., theta[1,N], theta[2,1], theta[2,2], ...

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble sampler interfaces
messages.body_plain:
On 5/17/13 12:45 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> So if we can't scramble the walkers together at the end, what's the point of even running an ensemble sampler?

We scramble the walkers together for inference.

They discuss this in the paper --- it's affine invariant.
And also doesn't require gradients, like HMC does, so there's
an issue of speed.  It's also easy to massively parallelize.

Some of the practical proponents claim it's also good for
mode-hopping, but we're skeptical.

We're also worried that in high dimensions, we'll need so many
walkers that just the convergence time will tank the overall
performance.

The big theoretical drawback to its adaptation is that it's global,
not local.  So when you have something like the funnel,
it's still tricky because the geometry changes based
on whether you're in the neck of the wide part of the funnel.
You can also see this issue intuitively with the Rosenbrock
function.  If you move between two members on different halves
of the banana, you won't wind up in a good space.

Looking on the bright side, there are still lots of nice
open research areas :-)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
In my experience, -mtune=native usually has only a small impact on
performance in the best of cases (unless it's compared to something
ridiculous like m-tune=x86 which effectively turns off SIMD
instructions).  For large models which spend a lot of time in calls to
Eigen it might make a noticeable impact.  At any rate, -mtune=native
is ideal for building stan models since the executable will only ever
run on the machine it's built on, so we should turn it on if possible.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Daniel and I have been Gchatting about the transition. I don't know git well enough to make sure we're not stepping into quicksand, so I want to throw this out there to see if anyone can spot a problem:

1) Rename master as develop with

git branch -m master develop

2) Create a new master branch starting at the v1.3.0 tag with

git branch master v1.3.0

3) Pushing everything to github with

git push -f origin master

This idea was based largely based on the commentary in these two posts

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2862590/how-to-replace-master-branch-in-git-entirely-from-another-branch
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2763006/change-the-current-branch-to-master-in-git

The central problem with a transition to the gitflow paradigm is that there are an untold number of branches out there in the world that have branched off our master branch prior to today that in the future need to be capable of being merged into develop and subsequently master. I'm theorizing that with the rename in step 1), git would be able to sort that out because the reflog goes with it.

Another issue is that maybe in the next week or two, we will need to branch the v1.4.0 release branch from the develop branch and when it is ready to release, merge that into master without inducing bad merge conflicts or creating Back to the Future Part II git history that would doom every future git bisect.

And there maybe other problems that I haven't considered yet. So, thoughts?

Ben

> If so, can we

> before we start the above?

messages.subject: Re: Strange unit test failure
messages.body_plain:
Well that was a fun diversion!  Because LDLT operators on a symmetric
matrix, it only ever looks at the lower triangular portion.  Hence,
all the gradients for elements below the diagonal have twice the
expected gradient and all the elements above the diagonal have zero
gradient.

This is an easy fix for the test, but it does raise an issue going
forward with operations on symmetric matrices as the gradient info may
not get propagated to the upper triangular elements of the matrix.
Ultimately this would get fixed with a specialized vari (I don't think
mdivide_left_spd suffers from this), but it's good to keep it in mind.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
First off, thanks everyone for your patience while we go through this change. If you haven't read this blog post (http://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/), please do if you want to contribute. I'm going to walk through our process, but it pretty much mimics the one outlined in the post.

If you don't read anything else, just remember these two things:
Do not push directly into the "master" or "develop" branch.
For working on code: branch from "develop" into a branch called "feature/<some-descriptive-name>", then create a pull request back into "develop".

Permanent Branches

We have two permanent branches:
master
develop

The master branch will always be at our last release. It is currently set to v1.3.0. @nvie calls this production-ready.

The develop branch will be the current working branch. This will be like how we treated master in the past, but with one additional requirement. We will expect this branch to be in a fairly usable state. For the time being, that means it passes all tests: test-unit, test-distributions, test-models.

In order to enforce the good state of the develop branch, all things that get into the develop branch will be done by pull requests.

Note: we are working on an honor system. The active developers will still have the ability to push to the develop and master branches.

Non-Permanent Branches

(quick description. Instructions further below.)

We will have 3 types of non-permanent branches:
feature
hotfix
release

Feature branches are the most common. Any type of new feature, fixing of bugs in a feature that hasn't been released, or pretty much any new development will go in a feature branch. These branch from "develop" and are named "feature/<some-descriptive-name>". After development is complete on the feature, submit a pull request back to "develop".

Hotfix branches are fixes to bugs in the current release. There should be an issue created for the bug in our issue tracker prior to branching. These branch from "master". These are named "hotfix/<next patch version number>". ONce the patch is complete, this will be merged into both "master" and "develop".

Release branches are branches for new releases. These branch from "develop" and are eventually merged into "master". Most developers won't need to worry about this step.

How to Contribute with a Clone of the Repository

(Most of us have been using the repository this way. Using this method, we can share feature branches with ease for collaboration.)
Clone the GitHub stan-dev/stan repository. From the command line:
> git clone https://github.com/stan-dev/stan.git
> cd stan

The default repository is develop and you can verify you are there by typing
> git branch
Create a branch. For a feature branch (most common):
> git checkout develop
> git checkout -b feature/foo
> git push

For a hotfix branch (less common):
If we're currently at v3.2.1
> git checkout master
> git checkout -b hotfix/v3.2.2
> git push

The last command, git push, is to make the branch public. This is necessary for when a pull request is created.
Do work.
Use the regular git commands to work. Collaboration is easy since all the developers have push access to the branch created.
Create a pull request.
A pull request indicates that the work is done and should be merged back to the appropriate place. When the pull request is made, it is expected that the current code passes:
> make manual
> make doxygen
> make test-unit
> make test-distributions
> make test-models

If it does not pass on your local machine, it won't be accepted. Passing these tests do not guarantee acceptance.

For a feature branch:
Merge the current state of "develop" back into the current feature branch:
Update "develop", merge "develop" into current branch (deal with any conflicts using git), push so the changes are available to github.
> git pull origin develop
> git merge --no-ff develop
> git push
Create a pull request.
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Select the feature branch you are working on in the drop-down list. (Below the "Clone in ..." row)
A "Pull Request" button should pop up underneath the feature branch drop-down list. Click it.
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

Alternate directions:
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Click "Pull Request" button. It's towards the top right, on the same row as the repo name "stan-dev/stan"
Select the correct base repo, "stan-dev/stan", and base branch, "develop"
Select the correct head repo, "stan-dev/stan", and head branch, "feature/foo"
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

For a hotfix branch:
Create a pull request.
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Select the hotfix branch you are working on in the drop-down list. (Below the "Clone in ..." row)
A "Pull Request" button should pop up underneath the hotfix branch drop-down list. Click it.
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

Alternate directions:
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Click "Pull Request" button. It's towards the top right, on the same row as the repo name "stan-dev/stan"
Select the correct base repo, "stan-dev/stan", and base branch, "develop"
Select the correct head repo, "stan-dev/stan", and head branch, "feature/foo"
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".
Relax.
At this point, one or more of the developers will check the pull request and do an informal code review. At the same time, our Jenkins box will verify that all tests pass on Windows. If both are good, then the pull request will be accepted, the code will get into the correct branch, and the branch will be deleted.
If the pull request is not accepted immediately, fix the issues.
Check out the branch
> git checkout feature/foo
> git pull origin feature/foo
(Or you can set upstream tracking so you can do "git pull feature/foo")
Do work.
Others can help at this point since the branch is available to everyone else.
The work will update the pull request.
Go back to "5. Relax"

That's it. That's how it works.

How to Contribute with a Fork of the Repository (we should be using a clone)

(This is how some of us have been working. The downside: if you want others to help, you need to give people permissions to your personal fork of the stan repository.)
Fork the GitHub stan-dev/stan repository. Done through either the web or the GitHub application.
Create a branch. For a feature branch (most common):
> git checkout develop
> git checkout -b feature/foo
> git push

For a hotfix branch (less common):
If we're currently at v3.2.1
> git checkout master
> git checkout -b hotfix/v3.2.2
> git push

The last command, git push, is to make the branch public. This is necessary for when a pull request is created.
Do work.
Use the regular git commands to work. If you want collaborators, let them have access to the branch.
Create a pull request.
A pull request indicates that the work is done and should be merged back to the appropriate place. When the pull request is made, it is expected that the current code passes:
> make manual
> make doxygen
> make test-unit
> make test-distributions
> make test-models

If it does not pass on your local machine, it won't be accepted. Passing these tests do not guarantee acceptance.

For a feature branch:
Merge the current state of "develop" back into the current feature branch:
Update "develop", merge "develop" into current branch (deal with any conflicts using git), push so the changes are available to github.
> git pull origin develop
> git merge --no-ff develop
> git push
Create a pull request.
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Select the feature branch you are working on in the drop-down list. (Below the "Clone in ..." row)
A "Pull Request" button should pop up underneath the feature branch drop-down list. Click it.
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

Alternate directions:
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Click "Pull Request" button. It's towards the top right, on the same row as the repo name "stan-dev/stan"
Select the correct base repo, "stan-dev/stan", and base branch, "develop"
Select the correct head repo, "personal/stan", and head branch, "feature/foo"
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

For a hotfix branch:
Create a pull request.
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Select the hotfix branch you are working on in the drop-down list. (Below the "Clone in ..." row)
A "Pull Request" button should pop up underneath the hotfix branch drop-down list. Click it.
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

Alternate directions:
Go to https://github.com/stan-dev/stan (refresh page if necessary)
Click "Pull Request" button. It's towards the top right, on the same row as the repo name "stan-dev/stan"
Select the correct base repo, "stan-dev/stan", and base branch, "master"
Select the correct head repo, "personal/stan", and head branch, "feature/foo"
Fill in form and press "Send pull request".

Relax.
At this point, one or more of the developers will check the pull request and do an informal code review. At the same time, our Jenkins box will verify that all tests pass on Windows. If both are good, then the pull request will be accepted, the code will get into the correct branch, and the branch will be deleted.
If the pull request is not accepted immediately, fix the issues.
Check out the branch
> git checkout feature/foo
> git pull origin feature/foo
(Or you can set upstream tracking so you can do "git pull feature/foo")
Do work.
Others can help if you've given them access. If this workflow is a problem, follow directions for cloning.
The work will update the pull request.
Go back to "5. Relax"

How to Update Your Current Stan Directory

If you have no changes, just follow the above directions on cloning. If that doesn't work, do:
> git pull

That will pull down all the current branches. If you were on working on branch "foo", the new branch will be at "feature/foo".

Commit all changes to foo:
> git checkout foo
> git commit -m "mesage" -a

Check out the new feature branch named "feature/foo"
> git checkout feature/foo

Merge the changes in your current branch:
> git merge foo

Delete old branch:
> git branch -d foo
(shouldn't get warnings -- you've already merged into feature/foo)

Start working like normal. You're at step "3. Do Work" from the sections above.

(Informal) Code Review

We need to define what we're looking for, but to start:
- unit tests
- style
- correctness (by eye)

Here, it helps to be on the shared repo because this will allow other developers to help create tests if you're bogged down to finish out the process.

That should be most of the things we need for developers. If anything is unclear, please let me know. The Stan repo is back to being operational.

Daniel

messages.subject: YIPPEE! Re: [stan-dev] Stan repo is now ready to use.
messages.subject_clean: YIPPEE! Re: [stan-dev] Stan repo is now ready to use.
messages.body_plain:
The writeup looks fantastic.

I'm going to drop Daniel's writeup into our Wiki:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Developer-Process

Feel free to edit, especially if something's unclear and you
can clarify.  It seemed like a steep learning curve to me,
but then I didn't have Daniel's writeup for our concrete case
to work from.

In addition to seconding the thanks to everyone for their patience,
I'd like to thank Daniel and Ben, who hashed the current process out,
as well as everyone who chipped in with critical bits of advice and config.
It's one thing to read about it on the web in pictures and quite another
to move an existing project into it using GitHub without losing our
history.

In retrospect, we should have listened to Ben the first time around when
he suggested the git flow process, but we didn't understand
the benefits of doing it that way or the dangers of doing
it the SVN way.  This all became much more apparent as (a) the
project grew in terms of number of contributors, and (b) we started
to undertake bigger reorganizations of the code.

Next up, I think we're going to split the RStan repository off from
Stan Core.  One reason is that we want to set up permissions so Jiqiang
and Ben control RStan instead of me and Daniel.  Another is to make the
releases independent.

We should also be getting more integrations soon (Python, MATLAB, Julia,
Stata are on our list), and it should be easier all around if
these are separate from Stan Core.   Then the RStan getting
started guide can move to GitHub's wiki.

I'm really psyched to start the new dev process.  It'll probably
take us a while to clear out the clutter of old branches and
catch up with all the pull requests for non-critical features.
So thanks in advance for a bit more patience.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rstan install compiled at -O0?
messages.body_plain:
R 3.0.1 for Mac is out.

I have checked out using R_MAKEVARS_USER environment variable.  If R_MAKEVARS_USER is set, $HOME/.R/Makevars will be replace by what $R_MAKEVARS_USER.  So for installing rstan, we can set it to empty so that the makefile (which sets O3 flag) in rstan package will not be overwritten.

I have changed the RStan getting started a bit: for users who have already installed a version of rstan, executing set_cppo('fast') is suggested before installing.

--
Jiqiang

> On 5/18/13 12:09 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
>>
>> Well that was a fun diversion!  Because LDLT operators on a symmetric
>> matrix, it only ever looks at the lower triangular portion.  Hence,
>> all the gradients for elements below the diagonal have twice the
>> expected gradient and all the elements above the diagonal have zero
>> gradient.
>>
>> This is an easy fix for the test, but it does raise an issue going
>> forward with operations on symmetric matrices as the gradient info may
>> not get propagated to the upper triangular elements of the matrix.
>> Ultimately this would get fixed with a specialized vari (I don't think
>> mdivide_left_spd suffers from this), but it's good to keep it in mind.
>>
>> Cheers,
>> Marcus
>>
>>
>> On Fri, May 17, 2013 at 11:14 PM, Marcus Brubaker
>> <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> So I know we're dealing with process flux, but if someone wants to
>>> investigate something strange, I've got something for you.
>>>
>>> Checkout the inverse_spd branch in my repository at
>>> https://github.com/mbrubake/stan.git .  I added a new function
>>> inverse_spd which computes the inverse using the ldlt factorization.
>>> The function itself is almost trivial:
>>>
>>>      template <typename T>
>>>      inline
>>>      Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>
>>>      inverse_spd(const Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& m)
>>> {
>>>        validate_square(m,"inverse_spd");
>>>        validate_symmetric(m,"inverse_spd");
>>>        Eigen::LDLT< Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic> >
>>> ldlt(m.ldlt());
>>>        if (ldlt.info <http://ldlt.info>() != Eigen::Success)
>>>          throw std::domain_error("Error in inverse_spd, LDLT
>>> factorization failed");
>>>        if (!ldlt.isPositive() || (ldlt.vectorD().array() <= 0).any())
>>>          throw std::domain_error("Error in inverse_spd, matrix not
>>> positive definite");
>>>        return
>>> ldlt.solve(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>::Identity(m.rows(),m.cols()));
>>>      }
>>>
>>> I added unit tests based on the inverse() unit tests (also in the
>>> repository) but somehow inverse_spd gradient tests fail.  Here is one
>>> of the unit tests:
>>>
>>> TEST(AgradRevMatrix,inverse_spd_inverse_spd_sum) {
>>>    using stan::math::sum;
>>>    using stan::math::inverse_spd;

>>>    AVAR a_inv_inv_sum = sum(inverse_spd(inverse_spd(a)));
>>>
>>>    VEC g;
>>>    a_inv_inv_sum.grad(x,g);
>>>
>>>    for (size_t k = 0; k < x.size(); ++k)
>>>      EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(1.0,g[k]);
>>> }
>>>
>>> which fails with:
>>>
>>> src/test/agrad/rev/matrix/inverse_spd_test.cpp:88: Failure
>>> Value of: g[k]
>>>    Actual: 0
>>> Expected: 1.0
>>> Which is: 1
>>> ...
>>> src/test/agrad/rev/matrix/inverse_spd_test.cpp:88: Failure
>>> Value of: g[k]
>>>    Actual: 2
>>> Expected: 1.0
>>> Which is: 1
>>>
>>> I'm puzzled here, there is no fancy varis at play other than the ops

On Sunday, May 19, 2013 4:41:02 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Ben, what are you trying to do? I'm not sure I understand what's going on. There can only be one precompiled header file in the whole build and it needs to be included first. In our models, we generate our includes and at the top sits "#include <stan/model/model_header.hpp>". There's no benefit to compiling any of the other .hpp files. That isn't how precompiled headers work.

I'm not using the precompiled header. I'm just testing whether the header can be precompiled. That is why the precompiled headers were getting sent to /dev/null.

This test is stricter than the tests under src/test/file_includes/ because 1) it automatically applies to all 533 *.hpp files under src/stan instead of just the 117 headers that are tested by the manually created .cpp files under src/test/file_includes/ and 2) precompiling entails parsing but also does a lot more things that could trigger errors. Parsing is mostly just a check for syntax errors, rather than reconciling all the macro expansion, forward declarations, and stuff like that. If you compile the tests under src/test/file_includes/ with optimization, I think the compiler will just get rid of all the code that is #included because none of it is used by EXPECT_TRUE(true). If you precompile the header, even with optimization, the compiler has to get every part of that code into an intermediate binary state so that it can be used by an arbitrary .cpp file.

> If you're looking to hunt down the make error, the only thing that looks iffy is the "@$(MAKE) ..." line. You already have the dependency on $(PCH_TESTS), so I think $(MAKE) $(PCH_TESTS) will run the target again. I haven't thought through make's sweeps over the makefile, so it might already plug in the variable and try to run make again.

I got it figured out now. The primary problem was creating a target out of src/stan/%.hpp .

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, May 20, 2013 3:15:30 AM UTC-4, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Also, it seems that git pull --ff is able to overwrite this config.

Yeah, not a big deal. We're mostly trying to configure things to prevent ourselves from accidentally doing the wrong thing. But, if you want to explicitly git pull --ff to improve the looks of your history, that is fine.

> > I had been presuming that we would rebase feature branches anyway.
> >
> I didn't get very well this point in the other discussions, is it better
> to rebase all your commits to a single one before sending a pull
> request? I think this is related to git bisect, right? But I never used
> it so I don't know what is a desirable history.

We'll try to establish a wiki page about commits soon. It is generally good to git rebase a feature branch but often not to a single commit. Basically, you can git rebase to organize your history retroactively. So, if you had a feature branch like

commit A: add feature
commit B: oops, fix something with commit A
commit C: really fix the problem
commit D: add tests
commit E: add documentation
commit F: add a subfeature, with tests, and documentation

you could rebase this so that commits B through E became part of commit A, so it could publicly look like

commit ABCDE: add feature, plus tests and documentation
commit F: add a subfeature with tests and documentation

This is not only easier to read and understand, if it later becomes necessary to do a git bisect or a git revert, then things go smoother. For example, if git bisect landed on commit B or commit C, it would mark the commit as bad even though it was looking for a different problem. Or if we had to revert the feature committed in A, commit E would still be there documenting a feature that was reverted.

So, the basic principle is to make commits that consist of logical parts, add value, are easy to understand, are easy to bisect, and are easy to revert. And all that is hard to do in one take, so you can use git rebase to accomplish it after the fact. See especially the -i option for an interactive rebase and the ability to execute, for example, make test-unit on every commit.

Ben

In general, rebasing (or in general history rewriting) is a good thing for several reasons --- provided that nothing has branched from the branch whose history is being rewritten. I'll put something on the wiki, but basically

http://git-scm.com/book/en/Git-Tools-Rewriting-History

covers it.

> Is the reason to rebase to make it easier to use git bisect to
> debug and keep our dev branch history cleaner?  That is, if
> we don't rebase and merge a feature branch into develop
> with commits on it that are broken, then git bisect will break
> when applied to develop?

This scenario with git bisect landing on a bad commit is one reason. Having a clean revert mechanism is another. I gave an example like this to Marco:

commit A: implement feature
commit B: add tests
commit C: add documentation

In this case, if commit A later gets reverted, commits B and C (will likely) stay, in which case you have tests that refer to code that is no longer there and documentation of a feature that is no longer there. If you

git rebase -i HEAD~2

the editor will say something like

pick A: implement feature
pick B: add tests
pick C: add documentation

and you can change it to

pick A: implement feature
squash B: add tests
squash C: add documentation

in which case the result will be something like

commit ABC: implement feature, add tests, add documentation

which is better all around in addition to being clean to revert if necessary. The same could be accomplished by reverting the commit that merges the branch (this is one of the reasons why we disallow fast-forward merges) but that would be overkill if the branch also had commit DEF that was good.

On 13-05-20 05:54 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
> We'll try to establish a wiki page about commits soon. It is generally
> good to git rebase a feature branch but often not to a single commit.
> Basically, you can git rebase to organize your history retroactively.
> So, if you had a feature branch like
>
> commit A: add feature
> commit B: oops, fix something with commit A
> commit C: really fix the problem
> commit D: add tests
> commit E: add documentation
> commit F: add a subfeature, with tests, and documentation
>
> you could rebase this so that commits B through E became part of
> commit A, so it could publicly look like
>
> commit ABCDE: add feature, plus tests and documentation
> commit F: add a subfeature with tests and documentation
>
> This is not only easier to read and understand, if it later becomes
> necessary to do a git bisect or a git revert, then things go smoother.
> For example, if git bisect landed on commit B or commit C, it would
> mark the commit as bad even though it was looking for a different
> problem. Or if we had to revert the feature committed in A, commit E
> would still be there documenting a feature that was reverted.
>
> So, the basic principle is to make commits that consist of logical
> parts, add value, are easy to understand, are easy to bisect, and are
> easy to revert. And all that is hard to do in one take, so you can use
> git rebase to accomplish it after the fact. See especially the -i
> option for an interactive rebase and the ability to execute, for
> example, make test-unit on every commit.

Thanks, I'll try to follow this principle from now on.

messages.subject: naming & scope of header "compilation" tests
messages.body_plain:
I think it's easier to understand and more future proof if tests
are named after the functionality they test rather than the
way in which they test it.

So I like Daniel's suggestion to call these "test-headers".
I like this better than "test-precompile-headers" (what Ben's
doing) or "test-compile-headers" (what our old file_includes tests
did).

We can start with our existing preprocessing test and later
add compilation tests (or even better, instantiation tests).

What we did before with the file include tests is compile a file
like stan_agrad_agrad_test.cpp:

   #include <stan/agrad/agrad.hpp>
   #include <gtest/gtest.h>

   TEST(stanAgradAgrad,parses) {
     EXPECT_TRUE(true);
   }

and then run it.  This will at least make sure that stan/agrad/agrad.hpp
is well-formed and exists and that all the function calls inside templated
methods exist.  For example, if I have this in foo.cpp:

   #include <iostream>

   template <typename T>
   T foo() {
     return bar();
   }

   int main() {
     std::cout << "HELLO" << std::endl;
   }

Then I get a compiler error because bar() isn't defined.
Everything compiles fine if I add this above the definition of foo():

   std::string bar() {
     return 1;
   }

It even compiles fine if there's no definition, just a declaration:

   std::string bar();

But then compilation fails if I add this line to main():

   std::cout << foo<double>() << std::endl;

The issue is that foo()'s template parameter T can't be
instantiated with T=double without an implementation of bar()
that returns a double.

So without the instantiations we care about, all of these tests
are technically too weak.  (But better than nothing of course!)

"Precompiling" a header just saves the result of an intermediate
step of the preprocessing (and parsing?) process. I've never understood
how much, but not so much as it makes much of a difference in compiling
a model (I think maybe a 10% speedup if I remember correctly).

The Wikipedia does call what the compiler does to precompile a header
"compiling":

   To reduce compilation times, some compilers allow header files
   to be compiled into a form that is faster for the compiler to process.
   This intermediate form is known as a precompiled header, ...

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precompiled_header

But then I think the author was being paid by the use of "compil".
In particular, I don't believe precompilation instantiates anything.

Anything that we test via creating precompiled headers (whether we keep
the precompiled header or throw it away is irrelevant), could probably
be tested in the same way we tested before, by compiling a trivial unrelated
program (like gtests's TEST macro) and running it through
g++ or clang++ (whether we want to call what g++ or clang++ does
"compilation" or not).

- Bob
