messages.body_plain:
In general, you'd have to reject the entire proposal.
It's just a proposal with 0 density, so there's really
nothing special about it.

But for Stan, our variable declarations imply transforms that
make sure all of the parameters are always in bounds.

The generated model code includes the transforms you need.
You can inspect how they work with HMC.

For example, if you have the following model:

   parameters {
     real<lower=0> sigma;
   }
   model {
     sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
   }

Then what you get for the log probability function is NOT

   cauchy_log(sigma,0,5)

What you get is this:

   cauchy_log(exp(sigma),0,5) + sigma;

The exp() transform makes sure the argument to cauchy_log
is positive.

The extra +sigma comes in from the change of scale implied by
the change of variables.  In the univariate case on the log scale,
you add the log of the absolute value of the derivative of the
transform exp() at sigma.

If you don't understand univariate changes of variables or its
generalization (which involves the determinant of the Jacobian of
the transform), check out the variable transformation section near
the end of the Stan manual.  It goes over the general idea and also
the specific transforms used by Stan for various constraints.

- Bob

messages.subject: rebasing feature branches
messages.body_plain:
I think we should make rebasing optional, but

   1.  we should encourage users to make commits which don't break
       the unit tests, but

   2.  we'll only enforce that users make merge requests that don't break
       unit tests.

I'm a little uncomfortable asking people to blow away their
commit history by rebasing.  (There's no getting it back after
a rebase unless you make a duplicate copy, right?)

I'm pretty sure we'll mostly be backing out whole feature branch
merges if we have to back out anything.  After all, that's all we'd
be able to do with rebasing.  My guess is that we're only going to
be backing things out soon after they are created.  Later on, it'll
probably be easier just to patch over them than do surgery on the
commit chain.

As usual, I may be misunderstanding something here or there may
be trouble lurking where I don't expect it, so discussion's more
than welcome.

- Bob

messages.subject: contributor copyright ownership OK with everyone?
messages.subject_clean: contributor copyright ownership OK with everyone?
messages.body_plain:
Does anyone object to switching to an intellectual property
model where each individual contributor (or their assignee)
owns copyright to their own work and makes

   * the code available under the new BSD licensee and

   * the doc available under Creative Commons BY 3.0 license?

All this will require is that each contributor explicitly
provide their contributions under these licenses.

Git provides a nice official record of who contributed what.

If this is all OK with everyone, we need to answer the question

   * what do we need to keep on file?

If it's just an e-mail agreement, we can keep those in the
Stan distribution itself.  If there need to be signatures involved,
we should get them in duplicate and keep copies at two separate
physical locations.  Left to my own devices, I'd just go with
e-mail agreements from contributors.  But do let me know if you
think we should do more (and ideally why).

I believe the official license will then need to list all of
the individual copyright holders and at the same time indicate
that the whole is licensed under new BSD (or CC BY 3.0 for the doc).

This is similar to the Boost model, though each module is only
licensed to a couple people despite getting contributions from
lots of others.

- Bob

>
>
> I'll change everything to test-headers.

Thanks.

 > This is another use case for git rebase.

And thanks for educating us all (or at least me) on git!

>     "Precompiling" a header just saves the result of an intermediate
>     step of the preprocessing (and parsing?) process. I've never understood
>     how much, but not so much as it makes much of a difference in compiling
>     a model (I think maybe a 10% speedup if I remember correctly).
>
>
> This link is in one of the commit messages for the branch:
>
> http://clang.llvm.org/docs/PCHInternals.html

The key to me is the terminology, which is clearer than Wikipedia's:

    The resulting PCH file contains the serialized form of the compilerï¿½s internal
    representation after it has completed parsing and semantic analysis.
                                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

> although it may differ for clang++ than g++, but either is supported by the test-headers target. The speedup varies if
> it is used.
>
> Did you have a thought on whether it would work to add
>
> #ifdef TEST_ME
> instantiations ...
> #endif
>
> to the .hpp files and passing -DTEST_ME when we test precompile them?

Yes, that could work, but we'd need to do more than precompile them at
that point.

I'd like to stay away from #ifdef and other preprocessor directives
to the extent possible.

To speed up compilation, we really want .o files, though the downside
is that it prevents unfolding/inlining across translation units.
But we'd like to keep our C++ usable through header only operation.
The solution we've found workable is to follow the strategy laid out
in Vandevoorde and Josuttis's book (awesome, by the way --- the one thing
everyone should read about templates and metaprogramming), is to break
the code into three files, with suffixes:

       .hpp   header declarations
   _def.hpp   definitions
  _inst.cpp   instantiations

Then we won't even need to test the instantations because they'll be
"tested" whenver Stan's archive is compiled.

The one example we have of this layout is in src/stan/gm/grammars.
We had to do this to keep the size down for Windows.

- Bob

> that (hopefully) all commits build and pass the unit tests, I think
> forcing people to always rewrite their history to a single commit is
> too much.

I don't think anyone is arguing in favor of always rebasing a branch to one commit. It is a question of whether to merge a branch that has

commit A: implement a feature
commit B: implement said feature correctly
maybe more commits

or whether to force a squash of that history to commit AB and maybe more commits.

> Isn't part of the point of something like git over sending
> patches around the fact that we can keep the development history of
> our contributions?

Which history is sought in the above example, with A and B separate or together?

> On top of that, I like to see things nicely split up so that the
> development process is not such a mystery.  Plus sometimes commits
> will come from multiple people (e.g., one person implements, others
> doc and unit test), I see no reason to squash those down.

The main reasons to squash doc and unit tests into implementation is that it is easier to understand the rationale for the implementation and to take out all three if the implementation gets reverted. I guess if you squash patches that someone else wrote, it would be reasonable to make the other person the author and you as the committer in the final version.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: rebasing feature branches
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, May 20, 2013 5:05:42 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I think we should make rebasing optional, but
>
>    1.  we should encourage users to make commits which don't break
>        the unit tests, but
>
>    2.  we'll only enforce that users make merge requests that don't break
>        unit tests.

That is using git as if it were SVN or CVS. And if commit discipline is voluntary, it won't happen in part because it is extra work and in part because it doesn't do much good for one person to have commit discipline in a project without commit discipline. The guidelines for the Linux kernel

http://www.linuxfoundation.org/content/53-patch-preparation

are pretty good and largely informed by the people who developed git from the outset.

I continue to think that under the old workflow bad pushes were more a symptom of deeper problems than a major problem in their own right. The deeper problems are

-- Bad commits
-- A test suite that has outgrown the capacity of regular laptops to be run often
-- Platform / toolchain / etc. differences

If magically those three problems went away, then pushes / pulls would be a breeze. It looks like we're going to be able to use Hotfoot for testing soon but that is only a partial solution.

> I'm a little uncomfortable asking people to blow away their
> commit history by rebasing.  (There's no getting it back after
> a rebase unless you make a duplicate copy, right?)

I see it more as replacing bad history with good history. Why would you want the bad history back?

> I'm pretty sure we'll mostly be backing out whole feature branch
> merges if we have to back out anything.  After all, that's all we'd
> be able to do with rebasing.  My guess is that we're only going to
> be backing things out soon after they are created.  Later on, it'll
> probably be easier just to patch over them than do surgery on the
> commit chain.

Under SVN / CVS, you rarely revert anything and just add more fixes to the trunk. In the Linux kernel, they revert stuff all the time. Reverting a whole branch is viable but can be a blunt instrument if the branch contains some commits that are good on their own. But you don't really know how long it is going to take before the problem becomes apparent, particularly if you don't have commit discipline so that you don't realize some commit is messed up until a git bisect trips over it.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Currently, I'm testing metropolis against the binormal model. For metropolis with dense metric, the results are at the bottom of this email; the stepsize just keeps growing.

I think the problem may be coming from the way I'm treating prop_cov. Currently, it's being treated as if it were the covariance matrix, but is it actually the covariance matrix or its inverse?

If it is the inverse, then shouldn't the propose method for dense metropolis  look like
      void propose(std::vector<double>& q,
                   BaseRNG& rng) {
        Eigen::VectorXd init(q.size());
        for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); i++)
           init(i) = q[i];

        Eigen::VectorXd prop(q.size());
        prop = this->_nom_epsilon
          * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov.inverse(), this->_rand_int);

        for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); i++)
          q[i] = prop(i);
      }
where we have

       prop = this->_nom_epsilon
          * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov.inverse(), this->_rand_int);

instead of

prop = this->_nom_epsilon * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov, this->_rand_int);
After running the former propose method, we get better results, but the step-size still seems to be increasing as it was previously.

This may have something to do with the init_stepsize() method in base_metro.hpp:
      void init_stepsize() {
        std::vector<double> params_r0(_params_r);
        std::vector<int> params_i0(_params_i);

        this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
        double log_p0 = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);

        this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);

        double log_p = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
        double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;

        int direction = delta_log_p > log(0.5) ? 1 : -1;
        while (1) {

          this->seed(params_r0, params_i0);

          this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
          double log_p0 = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);

          this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);

          double log_p = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
          double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;

          if ((direction == 1) && !(delta_log_p > std::log(0.5)))
            break;
          else if ((direction == -1) && !(delta_log_p < std::log(0.5)))
            break;
          else
            this->_nom_epsilon = ( (direction == 1)
                                   ? 2.0 * this->_nom_epsilon
                                   : 0.5 * this->_nom_epsilon );

          if (this->_nom_epsilon > 1e300)
            throw std::runtime_error("Posterior is improper. Please check your model.");
          if (this->_nom_epsilon == 0)
            throw std::runtime_error("No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?");
        }
      }
Should the line
          double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
actually be
          double delta_log_p = log_p - log_p0;
It was originally the former to mirror the init_stepsize in base_hmc.hpp; I believe the latter gives better results:

messages.body_plain:
There's a lot of literature out there on how Metropolis
works.  I'd suggest looking it up and making sure your
implementation matches.

You are going to be estimating covariance.  But whether you
take the inverse or not before plugging it into your
multivariate normal RNG depends on how you generate random
numbers (looks like you're using multi_normal_rng, which you
wrote, I believe).  Whatever you do, make sure you don't have to do
matrix solving at each iteration --- if you do need to solve,
make sure to do it only once.

Also, you aren't going to be estimating step size and covariance
here (well, you could), but it's not like HMC where there's a number
of steps (corresponding to time intervals).

- Bob

On 5/21/13 4:01 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> Currently, I'm testing metropolis against the binormal model. For metropolis with dense metric, the results are at the
> bottom of this email; the stepsize just keeps growing.
>
> I think the problem may be coming from the way I'm treating prop_cov. Currently, it's being treated as if it were the
> covariance matrix, but is it actually the covariance matrix or its inverse?
>
> If it is the inverse, then shouldn't the propose method for dense metropolis  look like
>
> |       void propose(std::vector<double>& q,
>                     BaseRNG& rng) {
>          Eigen::VectorXd init(q.size());
>          for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); i++)
>             init(i) = q[i];
>
>          Eigen::VectorXd prop(q.size());
>          prop = this->_nom_epsilon
>            * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov.inverse(), this->_rand_int);
>
>          for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); i++)
>            q[i] = prop(i);
>        }|
>
> where we have
>
> |        prop = this->_nom_epsilon
>            * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov.inverse(), this->_rand_int);
>
> |
>
>
> instead of
>
> |prop = this->_nom_epsilon * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov, this->_rand_int); |
> After running the former propose method, we get better results, but the step-size still seems to be increasing as it was
> previously.
>
> This may have something to do with the init_stepsize() method in base_metro.hpp:
>
> |       void init_stepsize() {
>          std::vector<double> params_r0(_params_r);
>          std::vector<int> params_i0(_params_i);
>
>          this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>          double log_p0 = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>
>          this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>
>          double log_p = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>          double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
>
>          int direction = delta_log_p > log(0.5) ? 1 : -1;
>          while (1) {
>
>            this->seed(params_r0, params_i0);
>
>            this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>            double log_p0 = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>
>            this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>
>            double log_p = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>            double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
>
>            if ((direction == 1) && !(delta_log_p > std::log(0.5)))
>              break;
>            else if ((direction == -1) && !(delta_log_p < std::log(0.5)))
>              break;
>            else
>              this->_nom_epsilon = ( (direction == 1)
>                                     ? 2.0 * this->_nom_epsilon
>                                     : 0.5 * this->_nom_epsilon );
>
>            if (this->_nom_epsilon > 1e300)
>              throw std::runtime_error("Posterior is improper. Please check your model.");
>            if (this->_nom_epsilon == 0)
>              throw std::runtime_error("No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?");
>          }
>        }|
>
> Should the line
>
> |           double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
> |
>
> actually be
>
> |           double delta_log_p = log_p - log_p0;|
>
> It was originally the former to mirror the init_stepsize in base_hmc.hpp; I believe the latter gives better results:
>

> lp__        -1.4     0.1  1.5 -5.9 -1.8 -0.9 -0.4  -0.0   206  1.0
> stepsize__   1.3     0.0  0.0  1.3  1.3  1.3  1.3   1.3  1000  1.0

messages.body_plain:
Just for curiosity, does one of those 3 (unit_metro, diag_metro or full matrix) use the algorithm proposed by Hario et al <http://www.math.unm.edu/%7Emichele/Teaching/SC/material/Haario2001_adaptiveMCMC.pdf> or something similar?

A while ago I used this one and the results weren't bad, they also propose a form of calculating the (adaptative) proposal covariance matrix without the need to recalculate the correlation of all other steps for every step. But for it work, I found necessary to use greedy adaptation in the begging, that is, use only the accepted steps for updating the proposal's distribution covariance matrix.

On 13-05-21 05:19 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There's a lot of literature out there on how Metropolis
> works.  I'd suggest looking it up and making sure your
> implementation matches.
>
> You are going to be estimating covariance.  But whether you
> take the inverse or not before plugging it into your
> multivariate normal RNG depends on how you generate random
> numbers (looks like you're using multi_normal_rng, which you
> wrote, I believe).  Whatever you do, make sure you don't have to do
> matrix solving at each iteration --- if you do need to solve,
> make sure to do it only once.
>
> Also, you aren't going to be estimating step size and covariance
> here (well, you could), but it's not like HMC where there's a number
> of steps (corresponding to time intervals).
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reference.

We're currently adapting in blocks, just like we do for HMC.
This is partly for stability and partly to avoid the overhead
matrix solvers running at every iteration during warmup.

- Bob

On 5/21/13 4:46 PM, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Just for curiosity, does one of those 3 (unit_metro, diag_metro or full matrix) use the algorithm proposed by Hario et

> al <http://www.math.unm.edu/%7Emichele/Teaching/SC/material/Haario2001_adaptiveMCMC.pdf> or something similar?

>
> A while ago I used this one and the results weren't bad, they also propose a form of calculating the (adaptative)
> proposal covariance matrix without the need to recalculate the correlation of all other steps for every step. But for it
> work, I found necessary to use greedy adaptation in the begging, that is, use only the accepted steps for updating the
> proposal's distribution covariance matrix.
>
> On 13-05-21 05:19 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> There's a lot of literature out there on how Metropolis
>> works.  I'd suggest looking it up and making sure your
>> implementation matches.
>>
>> You are going to be estimating covariance.  But whether you
>> take the inverse or not before plugging it into your
>> multivariate normal RNG depends on how you generate random
>> numbers (looks like you're using multi_normal_rng, which you
>> wrote, I believe).  Whatever you do, make sure you don't have to do
>> matrix solving at each iteration --- if you do need to solve,
>> make sure to do it only once.
>>
>> Also, you aren't going to be estimating step size and covariance
>> here (well, you could), but it's not like HMC where there's a number
>> of steps (corresponding to time intervals).
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> On 5/21/13 4:01 PM, Peter Li wrote:
>>> Currently, I'm testing metropolis against the binormal model. For metropolis with dense metric, the results are at the
>>> bottom of this email; the stepsize just keeps growing.
>>>
>>> I think the problem may be coming from the way I'm treating prop_cov. Currently, it's being treated as if it were the
>>> covariance matrix, but is it actually the covariance matrix or its inverse?
>>>
>>> If it is the inverse, then shouldn't the propose method for dense metropolis  look like
>>>
>>> |       void propose(std::vector<double>& q,
>>>                     BaseRNG& rng) {
>>>          Eigen::VectorXd init(q.size());
>>>          for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); i++)
>>>             init(i) = q[i];
>>>
>>>          Eigen::VectorXd prop(q.size());
>>>          prop = this->_nom_epsilon
>>>            * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov.inverse(), this->_rand_int);
>>>
>>>          for(size_t i = 0; i < q.size(); i++)
>>>            q[i] = prop(i);
>>>        }|
>>>
>>> where we have
>>>
>>> |        prop = this->_nom_epsilon
>>>            * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov.inverse(), this->_rand_int);
>>>
>>> |
>>>
>>>
>>> instead of
>>>
>>> |prop = this->_nom_epsilon * stan::prob::multi_normal_rng(init, _prop_cov, this->_rand_int); |
>>> After running the former propose method, we get better results, but the step-size still seems to be increasing as it was
>>> previously.
>>>
>>> This may have something to do with the init_stepsize() method in base_metro.hpp:
>>>
>>> |       void init_stepsize() {
>>>          std::vector<double> params_r0(_params_r);
>>>          std::vector<int> params_i0(_params_i);
>>>
>>>          this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>>>          double log_p0 = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>>>
>>>          this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>>>
>>>          double log_p = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>>>          double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
>>>
>>>          int direction = delta_log_p > log(0.5) ? 1 : -1;
>>>          while (1) {
>>>
>>>            this->seed(params_r0, params_i0);
>>>
>>>            this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>>>            double log_p0 = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>>>
>>>            this->propose(_params_r, _rand_int);
>>>
>>>            double log_p = log_prob(_params_r, _params_i);
>>>            double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
>>>
>>>            if ((direction == 1) && !(delta_log_p > std::log(0.5)))
>>>              break;
>>>            else if ((direction == -1) && !(delta_log_p < std::log(0.5)))
>>>              break;
>>>            else
>>>              this->_nom_epsilon = ( (direction == 1)
>>>                                     ? 2.0 * this->_nom_epsilon
>>>                                     : 0.5 * this->_nom_epsilon );
>>>
>>>            if (this->_nom_epsilon > 1e300)
>>>              throw std::runtime_error("Posterior is improper. Please check your model.");
>>>            if (this->_nom_epsilon == 0)
>>>              throw std::runtime_error("No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not
>>> continuous?");
>>>          }
>>>        }|
>>>
>>> Should the line
>>>
>>> |           double delta_log_p = log_p0 - log_p;
>>> |
>>>

messages.body_snippet:
Thanks for the reference.

We're currently adapting in blocks, just like we do for HMC.
This is partly for stability and partly to avoid the overhead
matrix solvers running at every iteration during w

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Dense Metropolis (and potentially diag metro) not working
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Dense Metropolis (and potentially diag metro) not working
messages.body_plain:
As Bob noted, whether to use the covariance or its inverse depends on how you generate the proposal.  Because we want to avoid unnecessary matrix ops I would compute the proposal by hand.  In particular,

1. Compute Cholesky decomposition of the covariance.
2. Sample a vector of N(0, 1) variates, z.
3. Solve L dx = z for dx.
4.  x_{propose} = x_{current} + dx

You were also correct about the init stepsize - it should be log(target accept) = log p_{propose} - log p_{current}.  Make sure it's consistent here and in the actual transition!

To debug, start with a simple Gaussian model with known covariance.  Then make sure Metropolis works with no adaptation, then with stepsize adaptation, then finally with stepsize and covariance adaptation.  The latter is eased by knowing what the true covariance should be.

Also watch the log posterior after each iteration.  If you have the accept stat wrong then the log prob will shrink during convergence instead of grow.

We don't use a scheme like Haario, for reasons Bob mentioned and more.  We do use the banana for testing, though!

On May 21, 2013, at 9:46 PM, Marco Inacio <marcoig...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Just for curiosity, does one of those 3 (unit_metro, diag_metro or full matrix) use the algorithm proposed by Hario et al <http://www.math.unm.edu/%7Emichele/Teaching/SC/material/Haario2001_adaptiveMCMC.pdf> or something similar?
>
> A while ago I used this one and the results weren't bad, they also propose a form of calculating the (adaptative) proposal covariance matrix without the need to recalculate the correlation of all other steps for every step. But for it work, I found necessary to use greedy adaptation in the begging, that is, use only the accepted steps for updating the proposal's distribution covariance matrix.

> > numbers (looks like you're using multi_normal_rng, which you
> > wrote, I believe).  Whatever you do, make sure you don't have to do

> > make sure to do it only once.
> >
> > Also, you aren't going to be estimating step size and covariance

On 5/21/13 6:24 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Wow, I didn't realize that the Eigen benchmark results were that compelling.

> take advantage of things like SSE?

Egads!  It looks like it's not on by default.  And we
haven't turned them on explicitly in the makefiles.

Any advice on how to configure g++ and clang++ to do
this in a cross-platform compatible way?

A quick scan indicates that for g++ and clang++ indicates
that we need something like

   -march=native

to enable an architecture that supports SSE(2) and then
we need to explicitly set  the SSE2 flag:

   -msse2

Do we also need to set just SSE?

> 2. Are we letting Eigen parallelize matrix operations?

Not that I know of.  This we should also check for config.
If we're running multiple chains in parallel, we probably don't
want to parallelize matrix ops.  Otherwise, we probably do.

Is there a way we can turn it on at run time or is it a compile-time
option?

> 3. Do we have specialized adjoint computations for matrix ops yet? 1
> and 2 won't do much good until we do.

Yes, we have them for most ops and Marcus has been
continuing to add more.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebasing feature branches
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, May 21, 2013 3:39:38 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Could you put these comments into the form of
> a recommended practice for developers TODAY?

Today, I don't think it is feasible to do very much. We don't have the machine capacity to test every commit in a pull request; it takes > 10 hours to test the whole pull request (just) on Windows. A human reviewer should at least scan the commit messages and the diffs, and if there is a message like "oops, fix build failure on the previous commit", the human reviewer could say, why don't you rebase this and resubmit the pull request? But if the person submitting the pull request were inclined to rebase, he would have already done so.

It is reasonably simple to do

make clean-all
rebase -i -cmd "make -j8 test-all" HEAD~7

which will run make test-all (or test-unit or whatever) on each of the last 7 + 1 commits. In principle, if you only do make clean-all once at the outset, make should only recompile the affected files on each commit (after the first make -j8 test-all). So, in principle, that should only take about 110% of the time that one make clean-all && make -j8 test-all would take.

In practice, that doesn't work very well. The function_signature*.stan tests generate new function_signature*.cpp files from stanc which thus have a timestamp that is later than the function_signature*.exe binaries, so make will rebake those. Same for test-distributions and for test-models. And for reasons I don't quite understand, make also feels the need to rebake the dependencies of these tests (i.e. bin/stanc.exe). So, the incremental run of make -j8 test-all only omits recompiling bin/libstan.a (which only takes about 5 seconds anyway) and the *_test.cpp files under stan/test/ (which do take a few minutes).

Also, I don't think the test box that Jenkins runs on can do -j8 without swapping, so it does -j4 last I checked. But there are only a couple of places in test-all with extreme RAM spikes (the 2000 line function_signature*.stan tests and bin/stanc), so you end up running the whole test-all with fewer (virtual) cores just to avoid grinding to a halt at a couple of places. With a i7 processor, -j8 isn't twice as fast as -j4 but it's a bit faster on my laptop (where I can do -j8 without swapping as long as I use clang++, O=0, and shuffling).

These problems can be mitigated a lot if you instead utilize ccache ( https://ccache.samba.org/ ) and call the cmd "make -j8 CC='ccache clang++' test-all" iff you first set

export CCACHE_SLOPPINESS=include_file_mtime

which omits the check for the last modification time when comparing the hash of a .cpp file to the hashes of the .cpp files in its cache that it has already compiled. So, make test-all can regenerate a bunch of .cpp files with later timestamps but identical content so that you get a ccache hit.

But there are two problems with ccache. First, it is essentially not available for Windows (it can be used in a full cygwin environment but that doesn't help us much). Second, Stan's practice of utilizing meta-headers such as model_header.hpp and all the src/stan/*.hpp files implies that if any .hpp file in any subdirectory under stan/src/ gets changed, one or more meta-headers will change, and any .cpp file that #includes the changed meta-header will cause a ccache miss even if the .cpp file in question is not actually using the .hpp file that got changed. In other words, if you change just about any header, that will affect model_header.hpp, and cause every .cpp file generated by stanc in test-all to get recompiled even if the resulting optimized binary is identical to what it was before (i.e. the change to the original header doesn't alter the source after the optimization gets rid of the unused code).

So, it isn't really feasible to require pull requests to satisfy test-all at every commit or to require the submitter to first verify on the honor system that test-all is satisfied at every commit. And even if it were, that would just be at O=0 and 1 or 2 platforms. And I don't think saying that people should make their best effort to ensure their commits are good will have much effect because that failed miserably under the old workflow.

> Perhaps with a transition plan for where you'd like
> us to get to in the FUTURE?

1) Have me pull request the feature/test-headers branch so that we can git rid of src/test/file_includes/ . This actually creates more work for test-all but it makes less work for test-unit. Thus, an individual developer can easily verify that the affected .hpp files precompile by doing make CC=clang++ foo.pch and can do test-unit more often.

2) Split the function_signatures*.stan tests out of test-unit and into test-signatures and include test-signatures in test-all. This will have much the same effect as 1) but I believe will make it possible to eliminate the dependency of test-unit on bin/stanc. Thus, test-unit can be done more often, with more cores, and allow the developer to verify the individual function_signatures tests for the distributions affected by his patch(es), if any.

3) Allow the tests conducted by test-distributions to be conducted individually with a make target. Do this often when you know your changes are affecting a particular distribution.

4) Split a test-grad make target out of test-models that just compiles the models, runs them with --test-grad, and returns 0 iff the lp__ is finite and the AD gradient is close enough to the numerical gradient. Include test-grad in test-all but do test-grad more often than test-models. It is somewhat important to occasionally run a model for a lot of iterations to see if it crashes, but otherwise there is currently too much variability in how the samplers perform to get anything definitive as to whether the model is working or not.

5) Get a Windows server with more capacity than the box Jenkins runs on and put it on Amazon EC2 or something where individual developers can test stuff on Windows before submitting a pull request.

6) Get Hotfoot set up for testing. This is actually close to happening. However, we have to get to the point where each individual test conducted by test-all consumes less than 2GB of RAM because the primary Hotfoot server has a 2GB of RAM per core limitation. With clang++, ccache, and all those cores each doing an individual test, I think we could do (the equivalent of) a make test-all in about 5 minutes.

7) Enable --std=c++11 on Hotfoot so that Stan is C++11 compliant even if it is not using any new C++11 features. This should reduce undefined behaviors, so have people verify that their stuff works on Hotfoot (linux) before testing on the quirkier cases of Windows or Mac llvm-g++-4.2. To get there, we only have to fix two parser bugs (scary warnings about the precedence of >> vs > when overloaded and the implicit template instantiation errors in ast.hpp)

8) Get rid of model_header.hpp and replace it with a lookup table that matches functions used by a particular model to the headers where they are defined. Maybe do something similar with the other meta-headers. Utilize ccache on everything that is not Windows.

9) Then get strict about every commit.

10 World domination.

Ben

This has to do with bin/print skipping over one of the rows for NUTS: depth. It's just coded to skip that parameter, which happens to be the 3rd parameter.

I think the right solution is to:
1) when sampling, create an object that encapsulates the sampler's parameters. I think the creation of the object should belong in command.hpp.
2) serialize the object to the output file.
3) in bin/print, unserialize the object to get back the sampler's parameters.
4) in bin/print, branch on the type of sampler. For example, in NUTS, the first parameter is the 4th one listed. Of the first 3 columns, only the first 2 are displayed.

First off, the file src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_test.hpp is parse by a program in src/test/agrad/distributions/generate_tests.cpp. This program then generates individual unit test files that really stresses the distribution. We have written a target for test/*.o to search for a src/test/*_test.cpp file. In this case, it wants to find a src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00000_generated.cpp. This hasn't been generated yet, but we've written a specific target in our make/tests, line 53, that depends on the generate_tests executable and the cauchy_test.hpp. It then passes the cauchy_test.hpp file through the executable, which generates a number of cauchy_generated_*****_test.cpp.

  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00001_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00002_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00003_generated
  make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00004_generated

To do a 5 minute test-all on Hotfoot we really just need a different set of scripts rather than a Hotfoot make target or a revised set of make targets. I've got it all planned out. The best way to think about Hotfoots batch1 queue is an internet cafe with 256 single core machines each with 2GB of RAM but networked. In this situation, we need a script that calls make hundreds of times.

You can think of the batch4 queue as like a single computer with 12 cores and 16 GB of RAM as you need. There you could just do make -j12 test-all and it would be done in an hour or two iff 12 cores and 16 GB of RAM are available. If not, you have to wait up to 3 days for the job to even start.

test-headers # will put in pull request tomorrow
test-libstan # basically all the *_test.cpp files under src/test/ excluding src/test/models; avoid dependency on bin/stanc
test-stanc  # all the stuff under src/test/gm
test-distributions # but with subtargets such as test-distribution-cauchy
test-grad # compile all the models and run with --test-grad, check that output is sensible
test-models # depends on test-grad and runs a lot of iterations of each model but doesn't check gradients

Then have test-unit be {test-headers, test-libstan, test-stanc, test-grad} and test-all be {test-unit, test-distributions, test-models}.

Ben

On 5/21/13 5:25 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> As Bob noted, whether to use the covariance or its inverse depends on how you generate the proposal.  Because we want to avoid unnecessary matrix ops I would compute the proposal by hand.  In particular,
>
> 1. Compute Cholesky decomposition of the covariance.
> 2. Sample a vector of N(0, 1) variates, z.
> 3. Solve L dx = z for dx.
> 4.  x_{propose} = x_{current} + dx

This is how the multi_normal_rng that I created works. The problem
before was that I was multiplying by the stepsize last for some reason,
so x_{current} was being multiplied by the step-size too, so all the
proposals were larger than they should've been and I guess that's what
caused metropolis to get stuck.

>
> You were also correct about the init stepsize - it should be log(target accept) = log p_{propose} - log p_{current}.  Make sure it's consistent here and in the actual transition!
>
> To debug, start with a simple Gaussian model with known covariance.  Then make sure Metropolis works with no adaptation, then with stepsize adaptation, then finally with stepsize and covariance adaptation.  The latter is eased by knowing what the true covariance should be.
>
> Also watch the log posterior after each iteration.  If you have the accept stat wrong then the log prob will shrink during convergence instead of grow.

Good question. Yes, there is a programmatic way of determining it, but it's determined by the annotation in the cauchy_test.hpp file. This is the line that gives us that information:
   // Arguments: Doubles, Doubles, Doubles

Here, we have 3 vectorized double arguments. This line indicates that each of the three parameters can be one of these 8 types:
1. double
2. std::vector<double>
3. Eigen::Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>
4. Eigen::Matrix<double, 1, Eigen::Dynamic>
5. var
6. std::vector<var>
7. Eigen::Matrix<var, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>
8. Eigen::Matrix<var, 1, Eigen::Dynamic>

That's 8^3 = 512 tests. I broke the tests into groups of 100. (I tried not breaking up the tests, but unfortunately, Windows craps out.) So for cauchy, this creates 6 tests.

messages.subject: Fwd: Re: BUGS Model Performance
messages.body_plain:
I'm attaching Michael's output plots.

The executive summary is that the results are still way off
in most of the BUGS models.

Michael --- does your calculation of R-hat and effective sample
size match bin/print and RStan?

Why is the overall frequency of v1.3.0 samples so much lower?
These plots would be much easier to read if they involved the same
number of iterations for both systems.
(Are you sure you're throwing away the warmup iterations for
the new stuff and also including all the multiple chains for v1.3.0?)

For many of the test cases, the accuracies are comparable.  But
for many, they're not and in all the incomparable cases, the new code
looks much much worse in terms of accuracy vs. known values.
Oddly, the time per effective sample is much lower in the
new code.  Something seems to be fishy.

I'd be inclined to start debugging with  Rats, because it's a very
simple model and both systems think they've converged, but the new
implementation is way off in its estimates for a whole batch of
the parameters.

I'm particularly bothered by lsat, which has low R-hat values,
but very far off estimates.

Because it could be an issue with estimating sd or MCSE,
can we skip the error estimates in the mean difference plots
and just do something like a relative difference calculation?

     rel_error(a,b) = 2 * abs(a - b) / (abs(a) + abs(b))

- Bob

OK -- I did misunderstand the original.  Leading with "May be
a bug" threw me :-)    I agree that the increased n_eff
is good.

Daniel just explained what you were doing and we looked
at a couple of cases with big outliers that actually looked
OK.  I think the problem is in the plot.

We can't plot differences on a per-sample basis.  What we
care about here is

    for each parameter,
      for each approach,
         plot relative error of sample mean vs. known value

where the following should work for relative error:

   rel_error(a,b) = 2 * abs(a - b) / (abs(a) + abs(b))

Also, we want to test timing, too.  Is there still no way to
get that for v1.3.0?

- Bob

Is there a simple change we can do that would allow calling

make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00001_generated

(or any other number that is not 00000) without having first called

make test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/cauchy_00000_generated

first?

On Hotfoot, this will be an issue because both 00000 and 00001 will be called at (essentially) the same time. Since 00000 takes longer, 00001 will return an error. As a workaround, we could do all the foo_00000_generated tests first, and then do all the tests that were not 00000, but that is a bit more work.

Ben

messages.subject: Hotfoot
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, May 22, 2013 10:06:13 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > The latter would be best I think. That way, their number can simply be counted rather than trying to predict it. And counting would work even if we change the batch size ever.
>
> Yeah, that's definitely do-able. That was how the tests were originally set up. I split it out into two steps because it was taking too long. Just so you're aware, if you generate all the test cpp files, they get picked up by test-unit.
>
> Can you spec out what you're envisioning? What exactly do you want to type? And what should it generate?

In general, I think anybody should be able to type make test-distribution-cauchy to build and run all the cauchy tests. But that is a bit removed from what I was actually trying to do today, which was move forward with Hotfoot. Here is the body of a test.sh script

cd ${STAN_HOME}
TEST=${TEST_ARRAY[${PBS_ARRAYID}]}
OUT=${TEST//"/"/"-"}
/usr/bin/time --output=${OUTPUT}/${PBS_JOBNAME}_timings.txt --append -f "%C: %E" \
make CC=${CC} ${TEST} > ${OUT}.txt 2> ${OUT}.txt

where

TEST_ARRAY is a large array of individual make targets
PBS_ARRAYID is a counter whose maximum is the number of cores

so basically, for the unit tests, it calls something like

make CC=clang++ test/prob/transform_test.cpp > test-prob-transform_test.txt 2> test-prob-transform_test.txt

and stdout and stderr get redirected to different directories so it is okay that they have the same filename. And the script writes the walltime to a line of a file.

So, we have to build up big arrays of individual make targets. For the distributions tests, this can be accomplished in a somewhat complicated fashion with

unset TEST_ARRAY i
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' file; do
    TEST=${file/"src/stan/prob"/"test/agrad"}
    TEST=${TEST/".hpp"/""}
    TEST_FILE=src/${TEST}_test.hpp
    if [ ! -e  $TEST_FILE ]
      then continue
    fi
    ARGS=`grep "^// Arguments:" ${TEST_FILE} | sed 's@// Arguments: @@' | wc -w`
    let "N_BATCHES=$[(8 ** $ARGS) / 100]"
    for ((j=0;j<=N_BATCHES;j++)); do
      NUM=`printf "_%05d_generated" ${j}`
      TEST_ARRAY[i++]=${TEST}${NUM}
    done
done < <(find src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/ -type f -name "*.hpp" -print0)

So that looks under src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/ for all the .hpp files, finds the corresponding _test.hpp file, finds the number of trailing words in its "// Arguments:" line, calculates the number of batches of tests, and then appends something like test/agrad/prob/distributions/cauchy_XXXXX_generated to the TEST_ARRAY. And I discovered that was wrong for trunc_normal because it should be 2^5 instead of 8^5.

If there were a step where we could just make all the foo_XXXXX_generated.cpp files for all distributions, then this could basically just be find all the *_generated.cpp files under test/agrad/prob/distributions/univariate and stick them into TEST_ARRAY after chopping off the .cpp.

Ben

messages.subject: c++: how to test types?
messages.body_plain:
Is typeid() safe to use for testing types for individual platforms? http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typeid

I want to lean on some of our template metaprograms that return types, like return_type. We currently don't have any unit tests for these functions. I want to get some unit tests in there to verify that return_type does the right thing for a combination of template arguments like double, var, fvar<double>, fvar<var>, fvar<fvar<double>>, ...

I know that typeid() is platform dependent, but is it going to work cross platform if I test strings? (I can't see how that wouldn't work, except if on some system it shows var and fvar as the same thing, like "object".)

Is there a better way to approach it?

Daniel

Complexity of the algorithms is unfortunately only the surface.
I've been assuming you wouldn't have even tried this if the
basic algorithm complexity wasn't similar.

What we want to look for is gotchas in the implementation, like
forgetting to pass a big matrix by reference, that can massively
slow things down in practice.

For testing, I didn't mean anything deep.  I just want a sense of
how long the suite of model tests takes to run 2000 iterations under
v1.3 and how long it takes on v2.0.  I'd even be convinced by half
a dozen randomly chosen models.  That shouldn't include compilation time.

We should also be running the new system through a profiler to see
if there are any gotchas there.  I've never even tried that, but
I hear you can do it pretty easily through Xcode.  I should get off my
butt and try it myself.

I'm very psyched about RM-HMC!  And that our auto-dif's getting cleaned
up as much as our HMC.  If I can clean up the AST and generator code,
I'll really be happy.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I've been thinking some more about the testing framework. The way I set up the new framework, all of the model tests are run for all samplers, but I'm not sure that's what we want. Will there be models that we do not want to test against certain samplers just because it would take so long?

If so, a different set-up for the framework would be to have separate test files for each sampler. (i.e. for bugs_examples/vol/blocker, we could have blocker_nuts_test.cpp, blocer_unit_metro_test.cpp, etc.). Then, if we do not want to test a certain sampler we just don't include that file. But if we do it this way, I think it would end up compiling the model as many times as we want to test it, which would significantly increase the amount of time it takes to run test-models. That's one of the main reasons why I opted to setup the tests the other way. However, another plus for this is that we can create make commands (if that's what they're called) that will test all the models against certain samplers in case we don't want to run all of the models against all the samplers (NUTS, unit/diag/dense metro and later RM-HMC, Ensemble (with a few variations)).

We could also opt to keep the current setup and just have an if/else statement inside the model_test_fixture that doesn't run the tests if the number of iterations is greater than 500k or whatever upper bound we choose. As for being able to just test certain samplers, that would not be difficult, but I don't see a way to just give a command that does that--we'd have to go into model_test_fixture and comment out the tests that call the other samplers. This still wouldn't be difficult, but it just wouldn't be systematic.

Peter

Ideally, we would test everything --- every sampler in
every configuration on every model.  I think of this as more of a functional

of time that not every model is going to be fittable with every

unit tests for the models.  Tests that exercise all of the functions
being generated by the model rather than how they run as a whole.

Then, we can back off and run the functional/regression tests
much less frequently than every pull request.

- Bob

On Thursday, May 23, 2013 2:53:22 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What I'd really like to see is something that looks more like
> unit tests for the models.  Tests that exercise all of the functions
> being generated by the model rather than how they run as a whole.

I do think we need a test-grad metatarget that just compiles all the models, runs them with --test-grad, and returns 0 iff lp__ is finite and the AD gradient is close to the numerical gradient. But that is more of a unit test of the libstan and stanc than a test of a particular sample. To test a sampler, I think we need something like

-- Generate a random correlation matrix
-- Maybe scale with random standard deviations to get a covariance matrix
-- Generate lots of multivariate normal data with mean zero and that covariance matrix
-- Run a sampler
-- Verify that posterior is not too far from the population parameters

You could play around with how the population gets generated, but in general, we need a set of tests with known populations to supplement all the toy BUGS models.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble samplers
messages.body_plain:
For the ensemble sampler, I'm still unsure of how we want to treat the end results of each walker. For instance, what should bin/print show? Do we want to print each walker out by itself? Or should we just take the best one? Or just the average of the walkers?

As for the actual sampling, I feel like we'd have to rewrite most of command.hpp. Perhaps we could just change all of the methods to take in a vector of samples instead of just a sample. Then, for metropolis, RM-HMC, NUTS the vector will be of size 1 and for ensemble it can be whatever is optimal. From there, base_ensemble would have transition which takes in the vector of samples and it would call walker_transitions for each walker.

Peter

On 5/23/13 4:51 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> Do we still need to implement the special functions inv(x), inv_square(x), inv_sqrt(x)? If so, I'll get on this. Are
> there any other special functions we want to implement?

Yes, that'd be great.  Then add them as special cases
to the pow() implementations, which is where they'll
probably get used the most.

There are many functions we'd like to have listed in
the to-do.  But I'd recommend cleaning up some of what you
have done for fvar already before doing any new functions.
Make sure there are no repeated expensive sub-operations,
like exp() or log().  And fix up the matrix ops like
mdivide_left to do the derivatives explicitly.  The way
it is now, using a direct auto-dif on inverse will be both
slow and have bad numerical properties.  Try to follow
the way it's done for reverse-mode and look at the Giles
paper I sent.

There's also log_minus_exp().  You should take a look
at the attached paper.  One thing you could do is look
more seriously at our arithmetic accuracy in functions
like this and log_sum_exp and related functions.  There's
a ref to get started next to the log_minus_exp() discussion
on the to-do list.

A much trickier request we got was for Chebyshev
polynomials.  I don't really even understand what the
original poster was asking for, but if you can
figure that out and implement it using Boost, that'd
be nice.  Especially if you could come up with an application
example.

Even a crude Kronecker product (just the brute force
multiply) would be good to have.

A function to_vector() that applies to matrices and
dumps them out in column-major order would be nice.

It would also be good to expose the special functions that
were added as helpers in doing the cumulative distributions.

Some other harder operations include things like a quadratic
form for matrices, also listed in the to-do list.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble samplers
messages.body_plain:
On 5/23/13 3:30 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> For the ensemble sampler, I'm still unsure of how we want to treat the end results of each walker. For instance, what
> should bin/print show? Do we want to print each walker out by itself? Or should we just take the best one? Or just the
> average of the walkers?

bin/print consolidates multiple chains into a single output
and we want to treat each walker as an individual chain.

We can't average them or just get the posterior mean.  The
whole point of MCMC is to get samples representing the posterior
(co-)variation.

We can't take the "best" one because (a) we have no way to know
which is best, and (b) even if we did, it probably wouldn't satisfy
detailed balance.

> As for the actual sampling, I feel like we'd have to rewrite most of command.hpp. Perhaps we could just change all of
> the methods to take in a vector of samples instead of just a sample. Then, for metropolis, RM-HMC, NUTS the vector will
> be of size 1 and for ensemble it can be whatever is optimal. From there, base_ensemble would have transition which takes
> in the vector of samples and it would call walker_transitions for each walker.

The impact on command is one of the reasons I think it's important
to think about this sooner rather than later.

For design, always work backwards from what we want out.

For the walker setup, we essentially want to treat each walker
as its own chain.  That means we shouldn't have to modify bin/print
at all, and hopefully won't have to modify RStan much.

Andrew wants to run multiple instances of these
ensemble methods, too.  But that should also be OK -- just more
chains to go in the mix.

So to get the output we need, it suffices to have walker n
in ensemble m write to its own samples_M_N.csv file.

Then we just need the input config.  That's going to have to vary
for each class of samplers.  Here, the issue is that we need to
initialize each walker in each ensemble.  In RStan, we can provide
an initialization function, so it can be run multiple times and perhaps
have some randomness in it.  We haven't done anything like that for
command-line Stan, so it'd be OK for now to only allow random initialization
for the ensembles.  (Eventually I'd like to get an initialization
value and then add some noise around it --- that is, recenter the
init=0 at a given value.)

The rest of the changes are going to be internal state.  This you
are certainly going to have to do differently for the ensembles.  But
that doesn't mean you have to do it by generalizing what we already have.
You can write a new base class for ensemble samplers and use that.
You can reuse the sample class for a single position of a single walker.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] adding inv(), inv_square(), inv_sqrt() & speeding up pow()
messages.body_plain:
On 5/23/13 6:04 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> What if we don't know if x is auto-diff or double, as is the case with most of the fvar functions since x could be an
> fvar or rev?

I'd go with (x * x) in that case.

To squeeze more efficiency out, you can always specialize.
So instead of having fvar<T>, you'd have
fvar<fvar<T>> or fvar<var>, which could use pow() because
you know they'll be called with either an fvar or a var.
The plain old T case can then do it with (x * x).

What we do in the probability functions is use trait templates
like so:

   if (is_arithmetic<T>::value)
     y = x * x;
   else
     y = pow(x,2);

where is_arithmetic is a Boost type traits class.

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/type_traits/doc/html/boost_typetraits/reference/is_arithmetic.html

The compiler will evaluate the boolean at compile time and
should be able to eliminate the unneeded branch and avoid
any branch prediction or evaluation at run time.

Whether this is worth it or not depends on the cost savings
and how many times it gets called.  If neither are expected
to be high, I'd go with something simpler.  The downside for
something more complex like the above is that it is harder to
read for others looking at the code later.

- Bob

> I do think we need a test-grad metatarget that just compiles all the models, runs them with --test-grad, and returns 0 iff lp__ is finite and the AD gradient is close to the numerical gradient. But that is more of a unit test of the libstan and stanc than a test of a particular sample.

> -- Maybe scale with random standard deviations to get a covariance matrix

messages.subject: fvar and var types for arguments and returns
messages.subject_clean: fvar and var types for arguments and returns
messages.body_plain:
I want to work backwards from the functionals defined in
stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian, Hessian-vector
product, etc.) to the types that we need in arguments
for the auto-diff functions.  In all of these applications, the top level
input to the function is a mixture of arithmetic types (double
and int) and a *single auto-diff type*.  The single auto-diff type we'd call
them with would depend on the operation, but it will be one of:

    var
    fvar<double>
    fvar<fvar<double>>
    fvar<var>

Some of the functionals are written more genericaly, but
only in terms of these:

     fvar<T>
     fvar<fvar<T>>

All the same arguments will hold no matter what type T is.

If the inputs start out as homogenous auto-diff types (that is, just one
of the above fvar types) and doubles, then a simple inductive argument
shows that you only ever get a few patterns of auto-diff vars in
subsequent function calls.

For instance, suppose the auto-diff type is fvar<T>.
If the args start out as fvar<T> (and double), you only get
this:

    (fvar<T>, fvar<T>)  ===> (T,T)
    (fvar<T>, double)   ===> (T,double)

In particular, you won't ever call an operation between
a T and fvar<T>.

If T == fvar<T2>, then the same argument applies, and we
only get operations on the following types:

    (fvar<T2>, fvar<T2>) ===> (T2,T2)
    (fvar<T2>, double)   ===> (T2,double)

As before, no mixing of T2 and fvar<T2>.

Therefore, I think these should be the signatures for operations on fvars:

     fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, fvar<T>);
     fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, double);
     fvar<T>  op(double, fvar<T>);
     fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, int);
     fvar<T>  op(int, fvar<T>);

(Of course, those are all const references.)

We should not need to do promotion anywhere, so shouldn't
need signatures that look like this:

     fvar<promote<T1,T2>::type> op(fvar<T1>, fvar<T2>);

We could use Boost's enable_if on an arithmetic type S
to combine int and double cases.

     template <typename S, typename T>
     enable_if<is_arithmetic<S>::value,
               fvar<T> >::type
     op(fvar<T>, S);

Does anyone see if I'm missing anything in this reasoning?

- Bob

messages.subject: Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
Peter brought up the question of how to interface ensemble samplers with Stan, but if you step back the real question is how to interface ensembles of chains in Stan (in the simplest case an ensemble sampler is a single chain with all of other walkers just part of the proposal mechanism; it's easy to assign a single chain to each walker and then have them mix in the proposal stage, but this just generates more chains, not more samples).  So, just how do we want people to do inference with multiple chains?

One option is to interleave the chains (carefully as to preserve detailed balance) and then do inference on the mega-chain.  My concern here is that the mega-chain might have a very weird autocorrelation structure (aliasing, single-frequency modes) that would invalidate most autocorrelation estimators (can't cut off the lags past the first zero anymore).

The other option is to calculate expectations from each chain, and then average them together using the ESS as weights.  This approach is more awkward for the user, as the averaging of the expectations need not commute with other manipulations (marginalization, etc).

Thoughts?

Once we've decided on this it won't be hard to modify command appropriately (for example, adding a chain index as a sampler parameter for ensemble methods or just having multiple output files).

messages.subject: reverting merges
messages.body_plain:
[moved to stan-dev]

I believe that's right: once a merge has been reverted, you need to take the current develop, revert the reverted pull request, then apply changes to it. You weren't able to do that?

One reason not to rebase back to an old state is then we've lost the merges that happened after something like this happens. Hopefully we're able to catch just the last merge, but in this case, there were two merges that were applied before I caught that the build was broken.

Daniel

On Fri, May 24, 2013 at 11:21 AM, Michael Betancourt <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> @syclik <https://github.com/syclik> Nope.
>
> Here's the problem -- whatever revert strategy you used simply deleted the files in the reverted commit (instead of, say, rolling back to the commit before and then adding any files added in future commits) The problem is that this marks all files added in that commit as deleted. Because the head of the branch whose merge had to be committed is behind the reversion commit, those files will always be marked for deletion whenever a merge into/from develop is attempted. The reversion acts like a black hole destroying those files no matter what.
>
> Only solution I could find was to create a new branch and recreate all of the changes from scratch. Not something we want to do every time there's a reversion -- which I hope motivates a review of the previous reversion strategy.
>
> —
> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHub <https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/80#issuecomment-18411419>.

I think that all makes sense.

As a side note, after going through the fvar files, I realized that some of them might not work with fvar<fvar<double>> and fvar<var> so Ill go through and write some tests for each function.

For fvar<fvar<double>> and fvar<var>, what do all the derivatives and values come out to? (i.e a.val_.val_, a.val_.d_, etc.)

Peter

On May 24, 2013, at 3:35 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I want to work backwards from the functionals defined in
> stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian, Hessian-vector
> product, etc.) to the types that we need in arguments
> for the auto-diff functions.  In all of these applications, the top level
> input to the function is a mixture of arithmetic types (double
> and int) and a *single auto-diff type*.  The single auto-diff type we'd call
> them with would depend on the operation, but it will be one of:
>
>   var
>   fvar<double>
>   fvar<fvar<double>>
>   fvar<var>
>
> Some of the functionals are written more genericaly, but
> only in terms of these:
>
>    fvar<T>
>    fvar<fvar<T>>
>
> All the same arguments will hold no matter what type T is.
>
> If the inputs start out as homogenous auto-diff types (that is, just one
> of the above fvar types) and doubles, then a simple inductive argument
> shows that you only ever get a few patterns of auto-diff vars in
> subsequent function calls.
>
> For instance, suppose the auto-diff type is fvar<T>.
> If the args start out as fvar<T> (and double), you only get
> this:
>
>   (fvar<T>, fvar<T>)  ===> (T,T)
>   (fvar<T>, double)   ===> (T,double)
>
> In particular, you won't ever call an operation between
> a T and fvar<T>.
>
> If T == fvar<T2>, then the same argument applies, and we
> only get operations on the following types:
>
>   (fvar<T2>, fvar<T2>) ===> (T2,T2)
>   (fvar<T2>, double)   ===> (T2,double)
>
> As before, no mixing of T2 and fvar<T2>.
>
> Therefore, I think these should be the signatures for operations on fvars:
>
>    fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, fvar<T>);
>    fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, double);
>    fvar<T>  op(double, fvar<T>);
>    fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, int);
>    fvar<T>  op(int, fvar<T>);
>
> (Of course, those are all const references.)
>
> We should not need to do promotion anywhere, so shouldn't
> need signatures that look like this:
>
>    fvar<promote<T1,T2>::type> op(fvar<T1>, fvar<T2>);
>
> We could use Boost's enable_if on an arithmetic type S
> to combine int and double cases.
>
>    template <typename S, typename T>
>    enable_if<is_arithmetic<S>::value,
>              fvar<T> >::type
>    op(fvar<T>, S);
>
> Does anyone see if I'm missing anything in this reasoning?
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure, but just in general I think it's important for our paradigm to be that we return to the user a set of simulations which he or she can use to represent the posterior distribution.  Calculating expectations is fine but that's just one thing that can be done with the simulations, I don't think it should be the paradigmatic activity.  And I really really don't want to be handing out weights--not unless there's a really really good reason to do so!
A

On May 24, 2013, at 7:32 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> Peter brought up the question of how to interface ensemble samplers with Stan, but if you step back the real question is how to interface ensembles of chains in Stan (in the simplest case an ensemble sampler is a single chain with all of other walkers just part of the proposal mechanism; it's easy to assign a single chain to each walker and then have them mix in the proposal stage, but this just generates more chains, not more samples).  So, just how do we want people to do inference with multiple chains?
>
> One option is to interleave the chains (carefully as to preserve detailed balance) and then do inference on the mega-chain.  My concern here is that the mega-chain might have a very weird autocorrelation structure (aliasing, single-frequency modes) that would invalidate most autocorrelation estimators (can't cut off the lags past the first zero anymore).
>
> The other option is to calculate expectations from each chain, and then average them together using the ESS as weights.  This approach is more awkward for the user, as the averaging of the expectations need not commute with other manipulations (marginalization, etc).
>
> Thoughts?
>
> Once we've decided on this it won't be hard to modify command appropriately (for example, adding a chain index as a sampler parameter for ensemble methods or just having multiple output files).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
But is an aggregation of samples equivalent to a reversible Markov chain?  For example, if we

1) randomly sample a walker
2) evolve it
3) take the evolved state as a sample

then we can consider the process as a mixture of Markov transitions.  Because each transition converges to the same stationary distribution, the mixture will, too.

But if we

1) evolve all walkers
2) append all evolved states as samples

then I don't think we have the same guarantee.  I'm not so much worried about convergence but the behavior of the autocorrelation estimators, in particular when/how we can terminate the lags in computing the ESS.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Chain Ensembles
messages.body_plain:
On 5/24/13 12:54 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> But is an aggregation of samples equivalent to a reversible Markov chain?

I don't think so.

> For example, if we
>
> 1) randomly sample a walker
> 2) evolve it
> 3) take the evolved state as a sample
>
> then we can consider the process as a mixture of Markov transitions.  Because each transition converges to the same
> stationary distribution, the mixture will, too.

Right.

> But if we
>
> 1) evolve all walkers
> 2) append all evolved states as samples
>
> then I don't think we have the same guarantee.  I'm not so much worried about convergence but the behavior of the
> autocorrelation estimators, in particular when/how we can terminate the lags in computing the ESS.

I don't think we do, either.

For convergence and ESS, we want to keep the ensemble members separate.

For inference and posterior estimation, we want to throw them all together.
Andrew also wants to randomize the thrown-together samples to protect vs. client
code that might do something non-random, like take the first 200.

If the ensemble goes long enough, then the effect of just laying the
ensemble members end to end will diminish, so it should be the same in
the limit.  But we hope to stop long before that happens!  So what would
happen is that we'd underestimate autocorrelation by crossing ensemble
member boundaries.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] fvar and var types for arguments and returns
messages.body_plain:
If you think of an fvar<T> as (a, da/dx) for some x,
then an fvar<fvar<T>> is going to represent two first
order partials and a second-order partial:

    ( ( a,  da/dx ), ( da/dy,  d^2a/dxdy ) )

Initializations are

    x -> ((x,1),(0,0))

    y -> ((y,0),(1,0))

    z -> ((z,0),(0,0))

The magic is that you only need the rules for first-order
auto-dif, and they just propagate.

I've attached some notes that explain the math in more detail.
This is going to go into a paper on our auto-diff system.

- Bob

On 5/24/13 12:16 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> I think that all makes sense.
>
> As a side note, after going through the fvar files, I realized that some of them might not work with fvar<fvar<double>> and fvar<var> so Ill go through and write some tests for each function.
>
> For fvar<fvar<double>> and fvar<var>, what do all the derivatives and values come out to? (i.e a.val_.val_, a.val_.d_, etc.)
>
>
> Peter
>
> On May 24, 2013, at 3:35 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> I want to work backwards from the functionals defined in
>> stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian, Hessian-vector
>> product, etc.) to the types that we need in arguments
>> for the auto-diff functions.  In all of these applications, the top level
>> input to the function is a mixture of arithmetic types (double
>> and int) and a *single auto-diff type*.  The single auto-diff type we'd call
>> them with would depend on the operation, but it will be one of:
>>
>>    var
>>    fvar<double>
>>    fvar<fvar<double>>
>>    fvar<var>
>>
>> Some of the functionals are written more genericaly, but
>> only in terms of these:
>>
>>     fvar<T>
>>     fvar<fvar<T>>
>>
>> All the same arguments will hold no matter what type T is.
>>
>> If the inputs start out as homogenous auto-diff types (that is, just one
>> of the above fvar types) and doubles, then a simple inductive argument
>> shows that you only ever get a few patterns of auto-diff vars in
>> subsequent function calls.
>>
>> For instance, suppose the auto-diff type is fvar<T>.
>> If the args start out as fvar<T> (and double), you only get
>> this:
>>
>>    (fvar<T>, fvar<T>)  ===> (T,T)
>>    (fvar<T>, double)   ===> (T,double)
>>
>> In particular, you won't ever call an operation between
>> a T and fvar<T>.
>>
>> If T == fvar<T2>, then the same argument applies, and we
>> only get operations on the following types:
>>
>>    (fvar<T2>, fvar<T2>) ===> (T2,T2)
>>    (fvar<T2>, double)   ===> (T2,double)
>>
>> As before, no mixing of T2 and fvar<T2>.
>>
>> Therefore, I think these should be the signatures for operations on fvars:
>>
>>     fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, fvar<T>);
>>     fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, double);
>>     fvar<T>  op(double, fvar<T>);
>>     fvar<T>  op(fvar<T>, int);
>>     fvar<T>  op(int, fvar<T>);
>>
>> (Of course, those are all const references.)
>>
>> We should not need to do promotion anywhere, so shouldn't
>> need signatures that look like this:
>>
>>     fvar<promote<T1,T2>::type> op(fvar<T1>, fvar<T2>);
>>
>> We could use Boost's enable_if on an arithmetic type S
>> to combine int and double cases.
>>
>>     template <typename S, typename T>
>>     enable_if<is_arithmetic<S>::value,
>>               fvar<T> >::type
>>     op(fvar<T>, S);
>>
>> Does anyone see if I'm missing anything in this reasoning?
>>
>> - Bob
>>

messages.body_plain:
On 5/24/13 10:14 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Things are different.  Best that can be said is that the new adaptation takes slightly longer to converge.

Nice plot, not so nice result.

The green seems shifted about 1/2 an e to the right on average,
but up to a whole e to the right at the far end.  So it looks
like the new code's taking 50% to 150% longer or so.

If you have the data, could you scatterplot these
by model (ideally with 1.3 on x-axis and 2.0 on the y-axis)?

This is ringing a bell --- Daniel mentioned that the new
code seemed to be more literal in the way it computes leapfrog.
We're not having to compute two gradients per leapfrog
step are we?  That is, we can combine the half steps at
the end of one leapfrog step and the beginning of the next?
Or at least save the gradient so we just do the increment
twice?

 > I'm not
> going to do anything else until the pull queue clears out and I can run without hacking local branches everywhere.

I was worried the pull queue was going to start slowing
down our work.  But I'd think you could just keep going
on your branch and continue to merge in develop branch
as you go.

- Bob

Ah.. So it turns out that I did have the prop cov matrix inverted. The difference wasn't apparent for binormal, but when I ran unit and full metro against the BUGS blocker model for 500k iter, the new full metro had 2x or more neff than unit metro.

Peter

On 5/24/13 1:11 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

 > ESS is already OK that way, I guess.

Let us know if there's a better way to do this.  Goodman has
an approach I haven't dove into in his ACOR code:

   http://www.math.nyu.edu/faculty/goodman/software/acor/

which is also part of the Python package Dan Foreman-Mackey
used in the emcee sampler:

   https://pypi.python.org/pypi/acor

I see, so it's not how to compute split R-hat, but a new R-hat that
would involve splitting into 2, splitting into 3 (or 4), splitting
into 4 (or 8), and so on.  No idea how to do it, but it does remind
me of how FFT works.

Too bad all our theory people are busy working on code.   Your call is
important to us and we'll get to it as soon as our next agent is free :-)

(By the way, it's very odd getting e-mail from you before 4 PM --- I can
feel the time difference.)

- Bob

This is what I tried:

git checkout remotes/origin/feature/mcmc_writer

70a660b Format zero values appropriately

I am not sure that 100% of your commits are there, but if they are there, then they should have different SHAs than on remotes/origin/feature/mcmc_writer. For example,

5f398ea Slight tweak to bin/print to remove duplicate rows
8b09b53 Merged develop

The "Slight tweak to bin/print to remove duplicate rows" commit has a different SHA now.

YMMV, so definitely try that in a detached head state before trying it on your local feature/mcmc_writer that you have been working on.

Ben

messages.subject: stan's slow optimization
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I'm still reflecting upon the fact, reported by Bob, that Stan-optimize is at least an order of magnitude slower than glm for simple logistic regression.  What bothers me about this is that glm uses iterative least squares, which itself is not supposed to be a very fast algorithm.  My impression is that the fastest logistic regression algorithms solve the optimization problem directly without wasting their time with least squares.
I can see that Stan will not be the fastest thing out there--after all, it was not designed for optimization--but should we try to understand why it is so slow?  I'm thinking about this with regard to my plan to have Stan be a replacement for lmer/glmer.  If we're so slow at basic optimization, I'm worried about these more complicated algorithms.
A

On 5/25/13 5:12 PM, Marco Inacio wrote:
> Thanks, I've fixed the formatting issues you pointed. Also, is there any special reason for some (a lot) of functions be
> defined as log1p(const T x) { } instead of log1p(const T& x) { }. I could also include this in the patch, but maybe the

The right thing to do for a templated argument is:

   T:         only arithmetic types (double, float, int, long, size_t, etc.)

   const T&:  class types (var, fvar, etc.)

If you're going to instantiate with both, use the const reference.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan's slow optimization
messages.body_plain:
Actually, the speed of the optimizer that Bob reported is no longer an issue.  It was due to an old, known-to-be slow algorithm.  I tested the BFGS-based optimizer that I implemented recently and found that it's basically about the same speed as glm.  (Well, that was on one problem, I haven't done the more thorough testing that Bob did of varying data and parameter size but I expect the results to generalize.)

The BFGS optimizer has a few minor issues yet which I'm resolving right now but I hope to make it the default optimizer for the next release.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Sat, May 25, 2013 at 9:31 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi all.  I'm still reflecting upon the fact, reported by Bob, that Stan-optimize is at least an order of magnitude slower than glm for simple logistic regression.  What bothers me about this is that glm uses iterative least squares, which itself is not supposed to be a very fast algorithm.  My impression is that the fastest logistic regression algorithms solve the optimization problem directly without wasting their time with least squares.
> I can see that Stan will not be the fastest thing out there--after all, it was not designed for optimization--but should we try to understand why it is so slow?  I'm thinking about this with regard to my plan to have Stan be a replacement for lmer/glmer.  If we're so slow at basic optimization, I'm worried about these more complicated algorithms.

messages.subject: Re: stan's slow optimization
messages.body_plain:
I wouldn't be surprised if BFGS optimization in Stan were always slower than a specialized optimization algorithm for a particular problem where analytic gradients are available. But if researchers were only interested in the mode, then lmer / glmer are probably adequate. For Stan to add value here, I think you need to convince interested people that MCMC would be better than mode finding (shouldn't be too hard to do that) and to implement an interface to those models that is as easy as glmer's (which is what I have been pushing for with a rstanarm package that someone like Alexej could work on).

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: stan's slow optimization
messages.body_plain:
I actually think the same arguments that support Stan over BUGS/JAGS in the MCMC context, apply to the mode-finding context.  Yes, a specialized algorithm for a specific class of models should always be faster than a general purpose algorithm but then you're stuck with the specific model.

At any rate, with BFGS I think we're basically competitive with glm if we're comparing mode finding speed.  We probably require a lot more memory which may hurt with enough parameters and/or data, but if that comes up it wouldn't be too much work to implement L-BFGS.

Cheers,
Marcus
