messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stan's slow optimization
messages.body_plain:
I think of the "least squares" algorithm as being any of the non-iterative solutions of the least-squares problem.

Logistic regression is of course not a least squares problem at all; there are various iterative least squares algorithms that solve logistic regression by starting with a guess, then linearizing the derivative of the log likelihood at that guess, then doing weighted least squares, then linearizing around this new guess, etc.  This algorithm is very natural (to statisticians) but is slow (for big problems) and can be unstable (even for small problems, as we discussed once on the blog).

A

GENERATED_AGRAD_TESTS := $(shell find src/test/agrad/distributions -type f -name '*_test.hpp')

    @mkdir -p $(dir $@)
    $(LINK.c) -O$(O_STANC) $(CFLAGS) $< $(OUTPUT_OPTION)

    @echo "--- Generating tests for $(word 2,$^) ---"

.PHONY: test-distributions

    @$(MAKE) $(patsubst src/%_test.cpp,runtest/%,$(shell find src/test/agrad/distributions -type f -name '*_generated_test.cpp'))

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ensemble samplers
messages.body_plain:
I spent some time this weekend thinking about ensemble samplers, and I think the most general way to approach them is via Neal's ensemble state methods.  That is, we consider mappings between single states and ensembles that preserve detailed balance.  The only difficulty is that we're not mapping from (single state -> ensemble -> single state), but rather (many states -> ensemble -> many states) the mappings aren't hard to manipulate (basically a uniform distribution on the permutation group will do) but I'm not sure if there are any issues with using multiple states while preserving a true Markov chain.

In any case, the encapsulation I was considering would be of the form

class ensemble_sampler: public sampler {

public:

  vector<sampler> samplers;

  transition() {
    for (sampler in samplers) sampler.transition()
  }

  write_state() {
   random_permute(samplers)
    for (sampler in samplers) sampler.write_state()
  }

}

We'd have to tweak our flow a bit (transition would have to use the internal state of sampler and not a given sample, mcmc_writer would have to be tweaked slightly) but then we'd be able to add any ensemble method (including multiple chains) without changing command.hpp.

My main concern is that the user isn't going to know what to do with a bunch of output files.  But if we give them a single output file then they can go about their business without any trouble.

> > On May 23, 2013, at 11:12 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >

> > >
> > >
> > > On 5/23/13 3:30 PM, Peter Li wrote:
> > > > For the ensemble sampler, I'm still unsure of how we want to treat the end results of each walker. For instance, what
> > > > should bin/print show? Do we want to print each walker out by itself? Or should we just take the best one? Or just the
> > > > average of the walkers?
> > >
> > > bin/print consolidates multiple chains into a single output
> > > and we want to treat each walker as an individual chain.
> > >
> > > We can't average them or just get the posterior mean.  The
> > > whole point of MCMC is to get samples representing the posterior
> > > (co-)variation.
> > >
> > > We can't take the "best" one because (a) we have no way to know
> > > which is best, and (b) even if we did, it probably wouldn't satisfy
> > > detailed balance.
> > >
> > > > As for the actual sampling, I feel like we'd have to rewrite most of command.hpp. Perhaps we could just change all of
> > > > the methods to take in a vector of samples instead of just a sample. Then, for metropolis, RM-HMC, NUTS the vector will
> > > > be of size 1 and for ensemble it can be whatever is optimal. From there, base_ensemble would have transition which takes
> > > > in the vector of samples and it would call walker_transitions for each walker.
> > >
> > > The impact on command is one of the reasons I think it's important
> > > to think about this sooner rather than later.
> > >
> > > For design, always work backwards from what we want out.
> > >
> > > For the walker setup, we essentially want to treat each walker
> > > as its own chain.  That means we shouldn't have to modify bin/print
> > > at all, and hopefully won't have to modify RStan much.
> > >
> > > Andrew wants to run multiple instances of these
> > > ensemble methods, too.  But that should also be OK -- just more
> > > chains to go in the mix.
> > >
> > > So to get the output we need, it suffices to have walker n
> > > in ensemble m write to its own samples_M_N.csv file.
> > >
> > > Then we just need the input config.  That's going to have to vary
> > > for each class of samplers.  Here, the issue is that we need to
> > > initialize each walker in each ensemble.  In RStan, we can provide
> > > an initialization function, so it can be run multiple times and perhaps
> > > have some randomness in it.  We haven't done anything like that for
> > > command-line Stan, so it'd be OK for now to only allow random initialization
> > > for the ensembles.  (Eventually I'd like to get an initialization
> > > value and then add some noise around it --- that is, recenter the
> > > init=0 at a given value.)
> > >
> > > The rest of the changes are going to be internal state.  This you
> > > are certainly going to have to do differently for the ensembles.  But
> > > that doesn't mean you have to do it by generalizing what we already have.
> > > You can write a new base class for ensemble samplers and use that.
> > > You can reuse the sample class for a single position of a single walker.
> > >

     inline var fmax(const stan::agrad::var& a,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] profiling develop branch
messages.body_plain:
After profiling via Instruments and running various tests, the only cause I can offer at this point are copy constructors.

Firstly, the leapfrog code is pretty even, with the new code about 20% slower.  I believe a nontrivial amount of this is due to converting between Eigen::VectorXd and std::vector when calculating the gradient, the rest would be due to temporary allocations that arise in the refactoring (depending on how smart the template expressions are).

Secondly, Eigen copy constructors are f'ing slow.  At least 100 times slower than the std::vector copy constructor (estimate from my tests is about 200 times slower).  Because the new code uses Eigen for everything with lots of local copy constructions, it seems like this difference is adding up over the course of a long run and causing a big performance hit (the copy constructor of ps_point is almost 10% of the execution time).  I tried "#define EIGEN_NO_DEBUG" but it didn't have any effect on performance.

Thoughts?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: gamma_cdf?
messages.body_plain:
But since rate is inverse scale (or scale for the inverse gamma) it's
easy to account for this:

gamma_cdf(x*beta, alpha) = 1 - invgamma_cdf(1/(x*beta), alpha).

It's easier to see that you can get away with this when you
log-transform x. On the log-scale, the inverse-gamma pdf is the gamma
pdf reflected around the y axis (and the log of the rate parameter
becomes a location parameter). Then you can work out the identity
using simple addition and subtraction, rather than getting reciprocals
involved.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] profiling develop branch
messages.body_plain:
I just ran some profiling and found some curious behavior.
The following two functions take the same amount of
time:

   double fun1(const MatrixXd& x) {
     MatrixXd y(x);
     return y(0,0);
   }
   double fun2(const MatrixXd& x) {
     MatrixXd y(x.rows(),x.cols());
     std::memcpy(&y(0,0),&x(0,0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
     return y(0,0);
   }

Effectively all of the time's spent in either the copy constructor
or the memcpy (the matrix ctor in fun2 takes 0.1% of the time and
memcpy 99.9%.)

Then I tried vectors, and it's a very different story.
For vectors, fun1 takes 47% of the total time, fun2 25%,
and fun3 20%!

   double fun1(const VectorXd& x) {
     VectorXd y(x);
     return y(2);
   }
   double fun2(const VectorXd& x) {
     VectorXd y(x.size());
     std::memcpy(&y(0),&x(0),x.size() * sizeof(double));
     return y(2);
   }
   double fun3(const VectorXd& x) {
     std::vector<double> y(&x(0),&x(0) + x.size());
     return y[2];
   }

Both fun2 and fun3 spend the same amount of time in memmve,
the rest of fun2's time being spent in the ctor.

WTF, indeed.  So it looks like you can save about half
the amount of time spent in Eigen's copy ctors for vectors
by rolling your own with memcpy.

memcpy should be OK for everything we ever copy (double,
fvar, var).

I'm trying to test var now, but having trouble using var
as a header-only lib.  I'll post a separate message about that.

- Bob

On 5/29/13 1:29 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 5/29/13 8:56 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> After profiling via Instruments and running various tests, the only cause I can offer at this point are copy
>> constructors.
>
> That seems a likely culprit.
>
>> Firstly, the leapfrog code is pretty even, with the new code about 20% slower.  I believe a nontrivial amount of this is
>> due to converting between Eigen::VectorXd and std::vector when calculating the gradient, the rest would be due to
>> temporary allocations that arise in the refactoring (depending on how smart the template expressions are).
>
> This is where most of the time is, so that could account for
> a large part of the issue.
>
>> Secondly, Eigen copy constructors are f'ing slow.  At least 100 times slower than the std::vector copy constructor
>> (estimate from my tests is about 200 times slower).
>
> WTF?  I wonder if it's because they lean so heavily on
> the curiously recursive template pattern that they
> wind up having to iterate over the indices rather than
> just copy memory?  In this case, we could hack around the
> issue by directly copying into their memory.  That is,
> rather than using the copy ctor, use a sized ctor, then
> access it's memory and copy directly there.  We know our
> row and column order are right because we always use the
> defaults.
>
> When do you use copy constructors and can they be replaced
> with references?  I'm guessing Map is going to be even slower
> than a copy constructor.
>
>  > Because the new code uses Eigen for everything with lots of local
>> copy constructions, it seems like this difference is adding up over the course of a long run and causing a big
>> performance hit (the copy constructor of ps_point is almost 10% of the execution time).  I tried "#define
>> EIGEN_NO_DEBUG" but it didn't have any effect on performance.
>
> I'll take a closer look at ps_point and at the copy ctors in
> Eigen and report back.
>
>> Thoughts?
>
> Nice profiling!  I had a rather difficult time trying to read
> through all the template parameters.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vector/matrix ctors for var
messages.body_plain:
Wow, memcpy absolutely smokes it.  Each run constructed the given object 50000 times.

Eigen::VectorXd temp(copy.size());

std::memcpy(&temp(0),&copy(0), copy.size() * sizeof(double));
     2.7e-05 (ms)

Eigen::VectorXd temp(copy);
     0.004721 (ms)

std::vector<double> temp(cont_params);
     3.9e-05 (ms)

I'll revamp the code as soon as I can.

On Wed, May 29, 2013 at 11:17 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Wednesday, May 29, 2013 5:22:10 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > So if copy ctors for Eigen vectors are taking up too much time,
> > I'd just rewrite them as in fun2.  It's still not as fast
> > as std::vector, but there's no Eigen Matrix ctor that takes in
> > either the memory for the vector elements or an iterator.
>
> This whole thing strikes me as odd, so maybe it would be good to ask on the Eigen list? But since we are utilizing stan/math/matrix/EigenDenseBaseAddons.hpp anyway, if it is more convenient for us to write additional Eigen::Matrix constructors, then we could go ahead and do that.

messages.subject: template metaprograms for primitives, var, and fvar
messages.subject_clean: template metaprograms for primitives, var, and fvar
messages.body_plain:
I'm starting to run into some problems with our template metaprograms and how everything is tied together. As of right now, stan/meta/traits.hpp pulls in stan/agrad/rev/var.hpp and stan/agrad/fwd/fvar.hpp, so essentially, everything gets pulled in.

I think the right thing to do is to try to define the base template function in stan/meta/traits.hpp (or even stan/meta/traits/___.hpp), and have var.hpp and fvar.hpp include that as well as a specialization for var or fvar. I guess if we have a generic specialization that can cover both, we could define it at the stan/agrad/ level.

Thoughts? Behavior should be identical to now, the code would need to be rearranged for this to work.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Hotfoot
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, May 22, 2013 11:31:12 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> So, we have to build up big arrays of individual make targets. For the distributions tests, this can be accomplished in a somewhat complicated fashion with
>
> unset TEST_ARRAY i
> while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' file; do
>     TEST=${file/"src/stan/prob"/"test/agrad"}
>     TEST=${TEST/".hpp"/""}
>     TEST_FILE=src/${TEST}_test.hpp
>     if [ ! -e  $TEST_FILE ]
>       then continue
>     fi
>     ARGS=`grep "^// Arguments:" ${TEST_FILE} | sed 's@// Arguments: @@' | wc -w`
>     let "N_BATCHES=$[(8 ** $ARGS) / 100]"
>     for ((j=0;j<=N_BATCHES;j++)); do
>       NUM=`printf "_%05d_generated" ${j}`
>       TEST_ARRAY[i++]=${TEST}${NUM}
>     done
> done < <(find src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/ -type f -name "*.hpp" -print0)
>
> So that looks under src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/ for all the .hpp files, finds the corresponding _test.hpp file, finds the number of trailing words in its "// Arguments:" line, calculates the number of batches of tests, and then appends something like test/agrad/prob/distributions/cauchy_XXXXX_generated to the TEST_ARRAY. And I discovered that was wrong for trunc_normal because it should be 2^5 instead of 8^5.
>
> If there were a step where we could just make all the foo_XXXXX_generated.cpp files for all distributions, then this could basically just be find all the *_generated.cpp files under test/agrad/prob/distributions/univariate and stick them into TEST_ARRAY after chopping off the .cpp.

Is there a simple change I can make to make/tests to accomplish this? In other words, currently if I do something like

make CC=clang++ test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00000_generated

it creates all 6 tests

ls src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_0*
src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00000_generated_test.cpp  src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00003_generated_test.cpp
src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00001_generated_test.cpp  src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00004_generated_test.cpp
src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00002_generated_test.cpp  src/test/agrad/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_00005_generated_test.cpp

but also compiles and runs the normal_0000 test. So, what we need for Hotfoot is a way to create these 6 .cpp files in the first step and then in the second step, compile and run each of them.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Then what to do with fmin/fmax, there seems to be some confusion even in
the manual: page 145 incorrectly uses fmax/fmin for vectors (invalid code).

If min/max is going to cover what they do, then, maybe it would be
better to place them as deprecated and warn the users to use min/max always.

On 13-05-29 02:57 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> No, they don't need specializations.
>
> On 5/29/13 1:28 AM, Marco Inacio wrote:
>> Then should I specialize them for var/fvar?
>
>> Currently, no version of min/max has specializations for var/fvar, and I
>> really find this reasonable.
>
> Yes, they're only defined for int.  But if we change that,
> they'll need to follow fmax.
>
>
>>
>> But fmax/fmin does:
>>
>>      inline var fmax(const stan::agrad::var& a,
>>                      const stan::agrad::var& b) {

That's what I did for our manuals at our company.

The challenge is that they're not whole models, just
fragments.  They could be embedded in whole models, but
those shouldn't go in the manual.

I have some pretty robust Java code that I'm happy to share
that cuts out bits of models and includes those.  It uses code
comments to indicate where to start/stop and what the name of
the resulting file to include is.  Something like:

parameters {
    real a;
}
model {
    /* start block.tex */
    a ~ normal(0,1);
    /* end */
}

would print just

a ~ normal(0,1);

I'd probably have to beef it up for some of our special symbols.

Another nice part about it is that it includes only half vertical
lines for empty lines, which helps with clarity without wasting
ridiculous amounts of vertical space.

The only issue is that it'd introduce a Java dependency on making
the manual.  And make things that much more complex for everyone
else to understand.

On Thursday, May 30, 2013 6:30:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What do others think?  I don't just want to add everything and
> the kitchen sink to Stan as a function.  It'll be confusing to use
> and hard to maintain.  But any distribution that's at all widely
> used should be fair game.

Speaking more philosophically rather than about the K-distribution specifically, I would say that Stan should make some effort to include unpopular distributions. Some distributions are unpopular largely because they do not lend themselves to maximum likelihood or Gibbs sampling but are otherwise plausible distributions for likelihoods or priors. Maybe the K-distribution is an example. Similarly, many distributions have "generalized" variants with additional parameters that aren't used that much because people don't want to specify particular fixed values for them but don't want to optimize over them either (e.g. the exponent in scobit models). Stan could add a lot of value in these situations by making it easy to utilize some unpopular distribution.

Of course, there are an infinite number of distributions and the manual would eventually look like Johnson, Kotz, and Balakrishnan. But I think we should be trying to drive demand a little rather than simply saying we'll try to implement distributions that are in demand.

Ben

messages.subject: more on K distributions
messages.body_plain:
The Wikipedia article

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-distribution

is very confusing because their density function uses two parameters
(nu and L), but they also include a mean parameter mu which appears on the
right-hand side of the density definition but not the left.  It looks
like everyone else is just taking mu = 1.

There's an approximation that might work here:

   http://www.london-research-and-development.com/K-Distribution%20Algorithm.Version2.pdf

It's a bit of algebra, but shouldn't be hard to code in Stan.

There's also a definition in terms of an exponential and
a gamma provided here:

   http://reference.wolfram.com/mathematica/ref/KDistribution.html

under "properties and relations" which is:

    v ~ Gamma(nu, L/nu)

    u ~ Exponential(1)

    --->  sqrt(u * v) ~ K(nu, L)

There's also a simple compound gamma-Rayleigh distribution.  They
don't list a gamma-gamma compound distribution, nor did anything else
I saw.

- Bob

http://blog.wolfram.com/2013/02/01/the-ultimate-univariate-probability-distribution-explorer/

It is not as if anyone really knows what distribution is correct, but you have a better chance with a less restrictive distribution. And it is basically just as easy to use a 3, 4, 5, ... parameter likelihood --- iff said distribution is implemented in Stan --- as it is to use the 2 parameter distribution; you just have to put some reasonable prior on the extra parameter(s). So pushing Stan in this direction would encourage better statistical practice. Like you said, I think LKJ was a step in this direction.

messages.subject: deprecating functions
messages.body_plain:
Marco wrote:
 > Are there other functions that already deprecated?
 > I ask because I want to now the procedure here. I would suggest
 > removing the deprecated functions from the manual and
 > showing the user an error message asking to use the new function
 > and refusing to continue compilation.

The Wikipedia has a nice description of deprecation:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deprecation

What we want to do is maintain backward compatibility by
not disturbing the behavior of existing programs.  Then,
we print warning messages which include instructions on how
to recode so as to avoid the deprecation warnings.

At some release in the future where we break backward
compatibility, we remove the function altogether.  We can
still print warnings, but don't need to at this point.

The idea is that if someone's program compiles without
deprecation warnings, it should work in future releases.

To implement deprecation, we are going to need to create
a set of deprecated function names then match them during
parsing to print a warning message that indicates how to fix
the code so the deprecation warning goes away.

- Bob

I don't think there is a problem for Stan.

We just have to be careful not to break the
expected C++ behavior in our API.  That means leaving
the fmin and fmax functions in place and behaving as
they currently behave.

>> It's going to be tricky, though, with the way Stan compiles.
>> It will just use max() for max() and it will try to call
>> the standard libraries unless we're careful to import our own
>> and our own have better type matches.
 >
> I didn't know that, how does this happen? My guess was that there were a "using std;" in Stan compiled code, but I found
> none, so why would it call std::max? Is there a way I could simulate this behavior in a unit test to check which
> function is being called?

This is very confusing in C++.

Check out this description of abs(), with signature

    int abs(int);

in <cstdlib>:

   http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cstdlib/abs/

You don't need an include to compile this program in
file abs.cpp:

   #include <iostream>
   int main() {
     std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
   }

It has this rather unexpected behavior:

   ~/temp2$ clang++ abs.cpp
   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
   abs(-2.3)=2

What's happening is that the double value -2.3 is getting
cast to an integer (-2) and then run through abs().

Turns out there's another abs() in <cmath> with three
overloaded signatures.  Now compare this program:

   #include <cmath>
   #include <iostream>
   int main() {
     std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
     std::cout << "std::abs(-2.3)=" << std::abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
   }

which as you might expect does this:

   ~/temp2$ clang++ abs2.cpp
   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
   abs(-2.3)=2
   std::abs(-2.3)=2.3

An explicit "using" seems to force the std::abs version
as seen in abs3.cpp:

   #include <cmath>
   #include <iostream>
   int main() {
     using std::abs;
     std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
     std::cout << "std::abs(-2.3)=" << std::abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
   }

which produces this:

   ~/temp2$ clang++ abs3.cpp
   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
   abs(-2.3)=2.3
   std::abs(-2.3)=2.3

Good unit test should be able to catch all this if there are
different behaviors.  Otherwise, it's not really unit testable.
For lgamma, the error behavior was different.

I wouldn't worry about deprecation for the moment.  Feel
free to just leave fabs() and fmin() and fmax() and change the
doc to indicate they're there for C++ lib compatibility.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: more on K-distributions
messages.body_plain:
Here's how I thought it through. Let

u = y^2 / v

So, we have the fact that

f(u,v | ...) = |J| * f(y,v | ...)

where J is the Jacobian matrix of the "bivariate" transformation from (u,v) to (y,v). So, with the independence assumptions,

f(y | ...) * f(v | ...) =

Thus, we have the "4" partial derivatives:

dy / du  = sqrt(v) / (2 * sqrt(u)) dy / dv = sqrt(u) / (2 * sqrt(v))
dv / du  = 0                       dv / dv = 1

Those collectively form J, whose determinant is sqrt(v) / (2 * sqrt(y^2 / v) = v / (2y). So, log(abs(det(J))) = log(v) - log(2 * y) and log(2 * y) is a constant, leaving log(v). But we are dividing by |J| above so that gets negated when we log.

Ben

it is a bit tricky here to think about transformation as we need to specify distribution for both y and v, data and parameters.
An easy way for this case is to consider that we need to specify the joint distribution of
p(y, v, nu) or p(y^2, v, nu), the posterior distribution of (v, nu) up to a constant.

p(y^2, v, nu) = p(y^2 | v, nu) p(v, nu)

then p(y^2 | v, nu) = (1/v) * p(y^2 / v | v, nu)

So the term -log(v) should be added to lp__.

messages.body_plain:
There have been some changes in the autodiff code for multivariate model that may have made chain() a little slower, but it should balance out with reduced computation elsewhere.  Plus, most of the BUGS models don't use the multivariate distributions, so it shouldn't have such a consistent across the board hit.

I would benchmark grad_log_prob() for a single model to see if it's there.

And yeah, between calls to check_range, check_not_nan, etc, there is a big speedup to be had if we can ever reduce the need for repeatedly checking variables like this.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] R install from GitHub? RStan Wiki on GitHub?
messages.body_plain:
For each file on github, you can access it through the "raw" method.  But github only does https, which is not supported by R's install.packages function. And that is why devtools uses package RCurl.  Currently Google code somehow allows http.  And we are not using Google code download for rstan, so I do not know if it will be shut down or not in the future.

Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] min max for double
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the explanation. I see now where the trouble comes from, it's
indeed pretty trick this heritage from C without namespaces. I'll test
this to make sure no double will be converted to int by the C++/C libs,
I just hope there's no substantial difference between compilers in this
area.

It would be cool if the parser had the ability to change min into min_
and the same for max and abs, do you find this worth implementing one
day? I know nothing about parsers, so I can't help with that.

On 13-05-31 03:46 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 5/31/13 1:37 AM, Marco Inacio wrote:
>>
>>> Here's a nice discussion of the distinction in C++:
>>>
>>> http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1632145/use-of-min-and-max-functions-in-c
>>>
>>>
>>> We absolutely need to keep the distinction as-is in the
>>> C++ library for C++ compatibility, but that's a different
>>> issue than keeping it in Stan.
>
>> Nice SO link! Even after reading it though, I couldn't saw any
>> problems arriving provided there's the specialization for
>> (int, int).
>
> I don't think there is a problem for Stan.
>
> We just have to be careful not to break the
> expected C++ behavior in our API.  That means leaving
> the fmin and fmax functions in place and behaving as
> they currently behave.
>
>>> It's going to be tricky, though, with the way Stan compiles.
>>> It will just use max() for max() and it will try to call
>>> the standard libraries unless we're careful to import our own
>>> and our own have better type matches.
> >
>> I didn't know that, how does this happen? My guess was that there
>> were a "using std;" in Stan compiled code, but I found
>> none, so why would it call std::max? Is there a way I could simulate
>> this behavior in a unit test to check which
>> function is being called?
>
> This is very confusing in C++.
>
> Check out this description of abs(), with signature
>
>    int abs(int);
>
> in <cstdlib>:
>
>   http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cstdlib/abs/
>
> You don't need an include to compile this program in
> file abs.cpp:
>
>   #include <iostream>
>   int main() {
>     std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
>   }
>
> It has this rather unexpected behavior:
>
>   ~/temp2$ clang++ abs.cpp
>   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
>   abs(-2.3)=2
>
> What's happening is that the double value -2.3 is getting
> cast to an integer (-2) and then run through abs().
>
> Turns out there's another abs() in <cmath> with three
> overloaded signatures.  Now compare this program:
>
>   #include <cmath>
>   #include <iostream>
>   int main() {
>     std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
>     std::cout << "std::abs(-2.3)=" << std::abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
>   }
>
> which as you might expect does this:
>
>   ~/temp2$ clang++ abs2.cpp
>   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
>   abs(-2.3)=2
>   std::abs(-2.3)=2.3
>
> An explicit "using" seems to force the std::abs version
> as seen in abs3.cpp:
>
>   #include <cmath>
>   #include <iostream>
>   int main() {
>     using std::abs;
>     std::cout << "abs(-2.3)=" << abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
>     std::cout << "std::abs(-2.3)=" << std::abs(-2.3) << std::endl;
>   }
>
> which produces this:
>
>   ~/temp2$ clang++ abs3.cpp
>   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
>   abs(-2.3)=2.3
>   std::abs(-2.3)=2.3
>
> Good unit test should be able to catch all this if there are
> different behaviors.  Otherwise, it's not really unit testable.
> For lgamma, the error behavior was different.
>
> I wouldn't worry about deprecation for the moment.  Feel
> free to just leave fabs() and fmin() and fmax() and change the
> doc to indicate they're there for C++ lib compatibility.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vector/matrix ctors for var
messages.body_plain:
On 5/31/13 12:41 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The temporaries all need to be in memory at the same time -- in particular you need something like \sum_{i = 1}^{n} i =
> n (n  + 1) / 2 objects in memory when building a tree of depth n.

Could you remind me why we need more than log n?

- Bob

> On Fri, May 31, 2013 at 5:23 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com <mailto:marcus.a...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>
>     Also, is it possible to use an Eigen::Map instead of copying the vectors around?  You may need to rewrite some
>     functions using the techniques from here: http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html but it
>     could avoid all these temporary allocations.
>
>     Cheers,
>     Marcus
>
>
>     On Fri, May 31, 2013 at 12:03 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com <mailto:betan...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>
>         I updated the constructors and ran through the first volume of BUGS examples again only to see....no change.
>           The copy constructor does seem to be using less space, but now a huge amount of time is spent freeing objects.

I wonder if we could allocate a pool of these objects and
just re-use them?  They're all double vectors of the same size.
Boost has a pool package:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/pool/doc/html/index.html

I'd rather not introduce a static pool, but we could attach
it to one of the sampler objects.

>         v1.3.0 Time    New Time     Name
>         3 %                11.3 %         szone_free_definite_size
>         6 %                9.4 %           grad_log_prob
>         6 %                9.4 %           chain()
>         6 %                7.5 %           free
>         3 %                7.5 %           tiny_malloc_from_free_list
>         9%                 5.6%            check_not_nan
>         NA                 3.7%            ps_point(ps_point const&)
>
>         I do use slightly more temporary objects in the new code, but grad_log_prob and chain() are noticeably slower,
>         too.  Has anyone benchmarked the autodiff code by itself?

I haven't, but we should.  The only change is that there's
a new virtual delete() function, but it shouldn't be called.
And there's a bit of cleanup for the new stack Marcus introduced,
but that should also be trivial.

The "tiny_malloc_from_free_list" also seems to indicate
that htere are more smaller objects getting allocated and
de-allocated.  That's a problem, but it won't be coming
from auto-diff.

>         Also, why is check_not_nan so slow?  In the sampler code I use the (var != var) trick which seems much faster.

No idea --- it's a Boost implementation.

We need to fix it for the next release.  I just created an issue.

- Bob

messages.subject: opinions on pruning Boost in Stan
messages.subject_clean: opinions on pruning Boost in Stan
messages.body_plain:
For the sake of maintenance, I would rather not prune. Right now, it's really easy to drop a new Boost into Stan. We just unpack it into lib/, delete the old folder, update the make target. If someone could script something really robust that would work, then that's fine too -- I'd need the script in hand to be convinced.

And disk space is cheap.

>
> Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: test that all manual code runs
messages.body_plain:
Regarding pull requests for manual changes: hopefully it doesn't slow you down too much.

I'd suggest just writing a comment saying that this affects the manual only, that you've built the manually successfully on your machine, and that it could be merged immediately. If I see that (from you), I'll merge it.

I wish there was a way to have multiple pull request builders, but I'm not trying to be a Jenkins ninja and do crazy stuff with it.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vector/matrix ctors for var
messages.body_plain:
You need to store rho and the state (at the very least momentum) at the boundary of each subtree -- maybe that scales as log(n)?  I'm pretty sure the code is as tight as it can be without appealing to pools or the like.

On May 31, 2013, at 8:29 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 5/31/13 12:41 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> The temporaries all need to be in memory at the same time -- in particular you need something like \sum_{i = 1}^{n} i =
>> n (n  + 1) / 2 objects in memory when building a tree of depth n.
>
> Could you remind me why we need more than log n?
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Fri, May 31, 2013 at 5:23 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com <mailto:marcus.a...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>>
>>    Also, is it possible to use an Eigen::Map instead of copying the vectors around?  You may need to rewrite some
>>    functions using the techniques from here: http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html but it
>>    could avoid all these temporary allocations.
>>
>>    Cheers,
>>    Marcus
>>
>>
>>    On Fri, May 31, 2013 at 12:03 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com <mailto:betan...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>>
>>        I updated the constructors and ran through the first volume of BUGS examples again only to see....no change.
>>          The copy constructor does seem to be using less space, but now a huge amount of time is spent freeing objects.
>
> I wonder if we could allocate a pool of these objects and
> just re-use them?  They're all double vectors of the same size.
> Boost has a pool package:
>
> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_53_0/libs/pool/doc/html/index.html
>
> I'd rather not introduce a static pool, but we could attach
> it to one of the sampler objects.
>
>>        v1.3.0 Time    New Time     Name
>>        3 %                11.3 %         szone_free_definite_size
>>        6 %                9.4 %           grad_log_prob
>>        6 %                9.4 %           chain()
>>        6 %                7.5 %           free
>>        3 %                7.5 %           tiny_malloc_from_free_list
>>        9%                 5.6%            check_not_nan
>>        NA                 3.7%            ps_point(ps_point const&)
>>
>>        I do use slightly more temporary objects in the new code, but grad_log_prob and chain() are noticeably slower,
>>        too.  Has anyone benchmarked the autodiff code by itself?
>
> I haven't, but we should.  The only change is that there's
> a new virtual delete() function, but it shouldn't be called.
> And there's a bit of cleanup for the new stack Marcus introduced,
> but that should also be trivial.
>
> The "tiny_malloc_from_free_list" also seems to indicate
> that htere are more smaller objects getting allocated and
> de-allocated.  That's a problem, but it won't be coming
> from auto-diff.
>
>>        Also, why is check_not_nan so slow?  In the sampler code I use the (var != var) trick which seems much faster.
>
> No idea --- it's a Boost implementation.
>
> We need to fix it for the next release.  I just created an issue.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: merging pull/88?
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, May 30, 2013 2:09:17 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Was there anything else I needed to do for that?
>
> Looks like Ben says it compiles with C++11 now:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/88#issuecomment-18517933
>
> The above comment also mentions a separate issue with Boost
> local, which is a separate issue.  I still don't think this
> is our issue, but we should try to isolate it and add it
> to the ongoing issues they're having with references to
> temporaries, some of which seem to occur only at higher
> optimization levels:
>
> https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/5190
>
> https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/6126
>
> https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/8489

So, after the merge, it does indeed work for clang++ with -std=c++11 and O_STANC=0 (the default). And, as we know, stanc doesn't work for clang++ with -std=c++11 and O_STANC>0. However, I was surprised to find that stanc also doesn't work for g++-4.8 with --std=c++11 and O_STANC=0. The failures messages (attached) for the latter two cases when doing make test/gm/parser are a bit different, suggesting that there is some undefined behavior going on here. However, adding -fsanitize=undefined in the clang++ case didn't flag anything.

Ben
